stem: Which one of the following complications is least associated with ventricular septal defects?
explanation: VSD complications: heart failure, Eisenmenger, aortic regurgitation, endocarditis. AF reflects atrial overload (ASD, mitral disease), not VSD.

stem: A 3-day-old neonate born prematurely at 34 weeks’ gestation has been slow to wean off the ventilator since birth. On examination, she has been found to have a continuous heart murmur. An echocardiogram has detected a patent ductus arteriosus. No other structural heart abnormalities have been found. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and mildly congested lung fields. What initial treatment should be started to manage this condition?
Which one of the following complications is least associated with ventricular septal defects?

You are helping with school sports physicals and see a 16-year-old boy who has had trouble keeping up with his peers. Which of the following auscultatory findings suggests a previously undiagnosed ventricular septal defect?
option_A: A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border with radiation to the carotids; the murmur is augmented with exercise
option_B: A systolic murmur at the pulmonic area and a diastolic rumble along the left sternal border
option_C: A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border
option_D: A diastolic decrescendo murmur at the mid-left sternal border
option_E: A continuous murmur through systole and diastole at the upper left sternal border
answer_text: A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border
explanation: VSD gives a harsh holosystolic murmur at the mid/lower left sternal border. ASD = pulmonary flow murmur; PDA = continuous machinery murmur.

stem: You are helping with school sports physicals and see a 16-year-old boy who has had trouble keeping up with his peers. Which of the following auscultatory findings suggests a previously undiagnosed ventricular septal defect?
option_A: A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border with radiation to the carotids; the murmur is augmented with exercise
option_B: A systolic murmur at the pulmonic area and a diastolic rumble along the left sternal border
option_C: A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border
option_D: A diastolic decrescendo murmur at the mid- left sternal border
option_E: A continuous murmur through systole and diastole at the upper left sternal border
answer_text: A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border

stem: A 59-year-old man with hyperthyroidism has palpitations and sweating. HR 150 bpm, BP 130/70 mmHg, SpO2 98%. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. TSH <0.01 mU/L with markedly raised free T4; echo shows normal LV function (EF 60%) and no structural heart disease. What is the best initial rate-control therapy?
explanation: Thyrotoxic AF: a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol) controls rate and adrenergic symptoms; antithyroid treatment restores sinus rhythm. Amiodarone worsens thyroid disease.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing heart failure and paroxysmal AF presents with vomiting, dizziness and palpitations after recently starting clarithromycin for pneumonia. She takes digoxin, furosemide and metoprolol. HR 40 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg; ECG shows junctional bradycardia with occasional ventricular ectopics. Potassium 5.9 mmol/L, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). Which ECG finding is most characteristic of digoxin effect?
explanation: Digoxin effect is down-sloping ('reverse tick') ST depression with T flattening and short QT; toxicity shows as brady/junctional rhythms, ectopics or atrial tachycardia with block.

stem: The most common cause of atrial fibrillation is:
explanation: Hypertension is the commonest condition underlying AF (atrial pressure load); others: IHD, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid, alcohol, obesity, sleep apnoea.

stem: Which statement is true of Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree heart block?
option_C: The ECG shows progressive prolongation of the PR interval
option_D: It is treated with a permanent pacemaker
answer_text: The ECG shows progressive prolongation of the PR interval
explanation: Mobitz I: progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat; AV-nodal, often benign, rarely needs pacing. Mobitz II (infranodal) progresses and needs pacing.

stem: All of the following are therapeutic options for atrial fibrillation EXCEPT:
explanation: AF is treated with rate control, rhythm control (cardioversion, drugs, ablation) and anticoagulation. An ICD treats ventricular arrhythmias only.

stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and atrial fibrillation has BP 160/100 mmHg and an irregularly irregular pulse of 120/min at routine follow-up. He takes captopril, furosemide, aspirin and spironolactone. What is the best add-on therapy?
explanation: AF at 120/min with hypertension and IHD: a beta-blocker (metoprolol) controls rate, BP and angina. He also needs a DOAC rather than aspirin.

stem: A patient with acute MI suddenly starts snoring and collapses. The monitor shows a broad-complex rhythm at 168/min with fusion beats. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fusion beats prove AV dissociation and are diagnostic of VT; collapse means pulseless VT, treated like VF with immediate defibrillation.

stem: A 48-year-old man with diabetes has had acute retrosternal chest pain for 3 hours. Pulse 102/min, small volume; BP 110/65 mmHg. ECG shows ST elevation in I, aVL and V1–V4. Later he develops dizziness and palpitations; pulse 36/min and the ECG shows AV dissociation. Which complication has developed?
explanation: A rate of 36/min with P waves independent of QRS is complete heart block; after anterior MI it is infranodal (septal necrosis) and needs pacing.

stem: A 77-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension and heart failure presents with irregular palpitations. Heart rate 135/min, irregularly irregular; BP 70/50 mmHg. She takes metformin and lisinopril. What is the first-line treatment?
explanation: AF with shock (BP 70/50) needs immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation, with heparin, whatever the AF duration.
topics: Atrial fibrillation; Synchronised DC cardioversion; Haemodynamic instability

stem: A 77-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension and heart failure presents with irregular palpitations. Heart rate 135/min, irregularly irregular; BP 70/50 mmHg. She takes metformin and lisinopril. Which of the following should be given to reduce the risk of complications?

A 77-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension and heart failure presents with irregular palpitations. Heart rate 135/min, irregularly irregular; BP 70/50 mmHg. She takes metformin and lisinopril. After she is stabilised, which drug is given to reduce her risk of thromboembolism?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc = 6 (age ≥ 75 ×2, female, HTN, diabetes, HF): long-term anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC (rivaroxaban/apixaban). Antiplatelets are not adequate.
topics: Atrial fibrillation; Anticoagulation; Direct oral anticoagulants

stem: A 77-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension and heart failure presents with irregular palpitations. Heart rate 135/min, irregularly irregular; BP 70/50 mmHg. She takes metformin and lisinopril. If she remains symptomatic despite drug treatment, which measure gives long-term relief?
explanation: Symptomatic AF despite drugs in an older HF patient: 'pace and ablate' (pacemaker then AV-node ablation) gives permanent rate control; PV isolation is the rhythm option.

stem: Which of the following drugs is NOT used to control the heart rate in atrial fibrillation?
explanation: Rate control uses beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil or digoxin. Amiodarone is mainly for rhythm control and too toxic for long-term rate control.

stem: In a patient with atrial fibrillation, which of the following is NOT associated with an increased risk of stroke (thromboembolism)?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc: heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, stroke/TIA, vascular disease, female sex. Obesity raises AF risk but is not in the score.

stem: All of the following are recognised causes of a prolonged PR interval EXCEPT:
explanation: PR > 200 ms: AV-nodal drugs, hypokalaemia, rheumatic fever, Lyme disease, inferior MI, fibrosis. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT, not the PR.

stem: A 73-year-old woman has chest discomfort and a slow pulse of 53/min with occasional pauses. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with intermittent pauses of 3 seconds in which no P wave appears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sinus pauses with absent P waves plus bradycardia in an older person is sick sinus syndrome. In AV block P waves are present but not conducted.

stem: A 63-year-old man complains of gradual-onset chest pain. On examination you note his pulse is regular at 60 beats/min. You request an ECG which demonstrates an increasing PR interval which eventually culminates in an absent QRS complex after the P wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 28-year-old man with no past medical history and not on medications presents to the emergency department with palpitations for several hours and was found to have supraventricular tachycardia. Carotid massage was attempted without success. What is the treatment of choice to stop the attack?
explanation: If vagal manoeuvres fail, adenosine (6 mg rapid bolus, then 12 and 18 mg) terminates AV-node-dependent SVT; verapamil if asthmatic.

stem: A 75-year-old smoker with ischaemic heart disease and previous heart failure presents with a 6-hour history of palpitations and increasing breathlessness. He is alert, BP 128/76 mmHg, SpO2 94% on air, with no chest pain, and his chest is clear. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 160/min, and vagal manoeuvres have had no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_A: Slow the heart rate with IV atenolol to help identify the rhythm
option_B: IV lidocaine 50 mg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 mg/min
option_C: IV adenosine to terminate the rhythm or reveal the underlying atrial activity
option_D: Immediate DC cardioversion, because the rhythm may be ventricular tachycardia
option_E: Withhold oxygen because he is a smoker
answer_text: IV adenosine to terminate the rhythm or reveal the underlying atrial activity
explanation: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: after vagal manoeuvres give adenosine, which ends AVNRT/AVRT or unmasks flutter waves. Cardiovert only if adverse features.

stem: A 57-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of a strong family history of heart disease. An ECG shows sinus rhythm with a constant PR interval of 300 ms (0.3 s), and every P wave is followed by a QRS complex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: PR > 200 ms with every P conducted is first-degree AV block (ageing, vagal tone, AV-nodal drugs, inferior MI); no treatment needed alone.

stem: A 75-year-old man is referred by the GP to the cardiology outpatient clinic. The patient has atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 124/80 mmHg and his pulse varies between 90 and 130 beats/min. His last echocardiogram (done 1 month ago) revealed left atrial chamber dimensions that are increased above normal. What is the most effective management?

You are the junior doctor on call and a nurse asks you to review an ECG. It shows regular P waves with a constant PR interval in the conducted beats, but some P waves are not followed by a QRS complex; there is no progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beats. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dropped P waves with a fixed PR in conducted beats is Mobitz II: infranodal, can progress abruptly to complete block, so pace permanently.
topics: Mobitz type II AV block; Heart block

stem: You are a house officer on call when you are bleeped to see a patient complaining of dizziness. On further questioning the patient comments that he has blacked out on several occasions in the past. You perform an ECG which shows regular P and QRS complexes occurring independently of one another. What is the most likely diagnosis?

You are a house officer on call when you are asked to see a 48-year-old man who is found to be unresponsive by the nursing staff. You cannot obtain a palpable carotid pulse and the cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the first appropriate measure?
explanation: Pulseless VF is a shockable rhythm: defibrillate immediately, then 2 min CPR. Adrenaline is given after the third shock; bicarbonate and calcium are not routine.

stem: At an ECG teaching session, a consultant describes a patient admitted to the coronary care unit with a regular atrial rate of 300/min and a regular ventricular rate of 150/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Atrial rate 300/min with ventricular rate 150/min is atrial flutter with 2:1 block; suspect it in any regular narrow tachycardia near 150/min.

stem: A patient on the coronary care unit develops new atrial flutter with an atrial rate of 300/min and a ventricular rate of 150/min; it began about 6 hours ago. He is haemodynamically stable, and a rhythm-control strategy is chosen. What is the most effective first-line treatment to restore sinus rhythm?
explanation: Synchronised DC cardioversion restores sinus rhythm in > 90% of flutter (drugs work poorly); anticoagulate as for AF. CTI ablation prevents recurrence.

stem: A previously well 36-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of attacks of palpitations and sweating. The attacks come on suddenly and are unrelated to food, posture or exercise. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Which of the following investigations is the LEAST useful in evaluating her?
explanation: Paroxysmal palpitations with sweating: check TFTs, metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma), ambulatory ECG and echo. An upper GI study has no role.

stem: A 57-year-old Bangladeshi patient is admitted to accident and emergency (AE) with palpitations. He speaks very little English but tells you he has a ‘heart problem’. On examination you note his pulse is irregular at 145 beats/min. An ECG is performed which demonstrates no P waves. Which management plan would you instigate first?
explanation: Irregular tachycardia without P waves is AF; first-line rate control in a stable patient is a beta-blocker (bisoprolol). Flecainide is for rhythm control.

stem: A 37-year-old woman develops palpitations after recent surgery. Her pulse is regular at 175/min and BP is 125/70 mmHg; she is otherwise well. She has asthma. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
explanation: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (carotid massage if young, no bruit); then adenosine, or verapamil if asthmatic.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after collapsing during football training. He is now alert and orientated, and his vital signs and examination are normal. He remembers feeling dizzy before collapsing but recalls little else. He is normally healthy and takes no regular medication. Blood tests have been sent. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Syncope during exercise is a cardiac red flag (HCM, long QT, WPW, Brugada, ARVC); a 12-lead ECG is the essential first test.
topics: Exertional syncope; Sudden cardiac death; ECG

stem: An otherwise healthy 50-year-old man presents to his GP with palpitations and is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse. The episode lasts less than 2 hours in total and resolves without treatment. Full blood count, biochemistry, thyroid function, ECG and echocardiogram are all normal. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Brief self-terminating AF with CHA2DS2-VASc 0 and a normal heart needs no anticoagulation; antiplatelets are never used for AF stroke prevention.

stem: A 75 year old woman presents to her family physician with a 24-hour history of rapid, irregular palpitations accompanied by fatigue. In an elderly patient, what is the most likely cause of palpitations?
explanation: Rapid irregular palpitations in an older person are most likely AF (prevalence ~10% over 80); confirm with an ECG during symptoms.

stem: A 72 year old hypertensive woman presents with a history of sudden-onset, rapid, irregular palpitation. She has had several episodes over the previous 3 months, which have resolved within 1 hour. She feels tired and slightly lightheaded during episodes. From this history, which of the following most likely explains her symptoms?

An 85 year old man presents with a 6-month history of sudden episodes of lightheadedness, which last up to 15 seconds. He is admitted to hospital with an episode of syncope resulting in facial injury. Examine the rhythm strip below. Which conduction abnormality does this show?
option_C: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
option_E: Wenckebach (Mobitz type I) second-degree AV block
answer_text: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
explanation: Constant PR with sudden dropped P waves is Mobitz II: infranodal, progresses to complete block and causes Stokes–Adams attacks — permanent pacemaker.

stem: Which of the following rhythms is NOT commonly associated with sick sinus syndrome (sinoatrial disease)?
explanation: Sick sinus syndrome: sinus bradycardia, pauses, SA block, often with AF/atrial tachycardia (tachy–brady). VT is not a feature.

stem: A 75 year old woman has a history of hypertension and diabetes. She presents with atrial fibrillation. What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score?
explanation: Age ≥ 75 (2) + female (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 5: high stroke risk; offer a DOAC.

stem: A patient has sudden-onset rapid palpitations; the ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min and he is haemodynamically stable. What should be used first to try to terminate the rhythm?
explanation: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (modified Valsalva), then adenosine 6–12–18 mg rapid bolus. DC shock if unstable.

stem: For which of the following scenarios would a permanent pacemaker be an appropriate treatment?
option_B: Prevention of sudden death due to ventricular fibrillation
option_C: Sick sinus syndrome associated with syncope
answer_text: Sick sinus syndrome associated with syncope
explanation: Permanent pacing for symptomatic bradycardia (sick sinus with syncope), Mobitz II and complete heart block. Athletes' bradycardia is physiological.

stem: Which of the following is associated with excessive alcohol consumption?
explanation: Alcohol triggers AF ('holiday heart') and heavy intake raises AF incidence; abstinence reduces recurrence. It also causes dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: One of the fallowing is true for Mobitz I second degree heart block
option_C: ECG shows progressive prolongation of PR intervals
answer_text: ECG shows progressive prolongation of PR intervals

stem: The following are recognized causes of prolonged PR interval except:
The most important complication of atrial fibrillation is
explanation: The key complication of AF is ischaemic stroke from left atrial appendage thrombus (risk ×5); hence CHA2DS2-VASc and anticoagulation.

stem: A 45-year-old man is found collapsed and an ECG on arrival shows torsades de pointes. Which of his medications is most likely to have contributed?
explanation: Antipsychotics (risperidone, haloperidol) block hERG channels, prolong QT and cause torsades. Treat with IV magnesium and stop the drug.
topics: Torsades de pointes; Drug-induced QT prolongation

stem: Most common cause of AF
The following are therapeutic options for treatment of atrial fibrillation except
option_B: Radiofrequency pulmonary vein isolation with ablation

stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with palpitations. During the cardiovascular examination you notice irregular cannon a’ waves. Which one of the following would account for this finding?
explanation: Irregular cannon a waves mean AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT); regular ones occur in junctional rhythms. AF abolishes a waves.
topics: Cannon a waves; Complete heart block

stem: A patient with known Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190/min (orthodromic AVRT). He is haemodynamically stable and vagal manoeuvres have failed. Which treatment is appropriate?
explanation: Orthodromic AVRT is narrow and AV-node-dependent, so adenosine terminates it. In pre-excited AF (irregular, broad) AV-nodal blockers are dangerous.
topics: Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome; AV re-entrant tachycardia; Adenosine

stem: A 55-year-old woman with no past medical history presents with syncope; her ECG (A) shows advanced AV block, and she has painful red nodules on her shins (B). What is the most likely cause of both the cardiac and skin abnormalities?
explanation: Heart block plus erythema nodosum suggests sarcoidosis: granulomas in the septum/conduction system; confirm with cardiac MRI or FDG-PET.
topics: Cardiac sarcoidosis; Heart block; Erythema nodosum

stem: Which abnormality is shown on this 12-lead ECG?
option_E: S1Q3T3 (McGinn-White pattern) indicative of right ventricular strain
explanation: Broad QRS with rSR' ('M') in V1–V2 and slurred S in I, aVL, V5–V6 is RBBB. LBBB gives a broad QS in V1 and notched R in V6.

stem: A 21-year-old competitive cyclist, asymptomatic and without syncope, has a resting heart rate of 45/min with occasional pauses up to 2.2 seconds. BP 108/72 mmHg; examination is otherwise normal, and the ECG shows sinus rhythm with PR 128 ms and QRS 80 ms. What advice is appropriate?
option_A: Perform electrophysiologic evaluation for consideration of a pacemaker
option_B: He should not compete in the upcoming race due to concern for bradycardia and will need a tilt table test
option_C: No further follow-up is needed. Good luck with the race!
option_E: He should undergo a treadmill stress ECG to determine the presence of chronotropic competence
answer_text: No further follow-up is needed. Good luck with the race!
explanation: Sinus bradycardia, first-degree and Wenckebach block are physiological in asymptomatic athletes; no tests or restriction needed.

stem: A 60-year-old man is undergoing an electrophysiology study for evaluation of syncope. After careful venous cannulation and placement of conductance and pacing catheters and after administration of 0.2 mg/kg of propranolol and 0.04 mg/kg of atropine, his heart rate is 65 bpm. After stopping the drugs and allowing adequate time for washout, his superior/lateral right atrium is paced 140 bpm. On cessation of this overdrive pacing, his next sinus beat occurs 1800 msec later. Based on these observations, this patient can be diagnosed with which of the following?
explanation: A prolonged sinus node recovery time after overdrive pacing (1800 ms) with low intrinsic rate means intrinsic SA node disease.
topics: Sick sinus syndrome; Sinus node recovery time

stem: All of the following are reversible causes of SA node dysfunction EXCEPT:
explanation: Reversible SA node dysfunction: hypothermia, hypothyroidism, raised ICP, drugs, hyperkalaemia, vagal tone. Radiation causes permanent fibrosis.

stem: Which of the following is a risk factor for development of thromboembolism in patients with the tachycardia-bradycardia variant of sick sinus syndrome?
option_E: None of the above; there is no increased risk of thromboembolism with the tachycardia-bradycardia variant of sick sinus syndrome
explanation: Tachy–brady syndrome includes AF/flutter; atrial enlargement (and age, prior stroke, LV dysfunction) adds embolic risk. A pacemaker does not remove it.

stem: Normal cells within the AV node exhibit a property known as decremental conduction. If you wanted to demonstrate this property during an electrophysiology study, what maneuver could you perform?
option_A: Pace the right atrium at serially decreasing cycle length and measure the pace-to-His conduction time
option_B: Pace the ventricle and record right atrial potentials
option_C: Administer atropine 0.04 mg/kg and record AV nodal conduction time by measuring the time it takes an atrial pacing beat to reach the His bundle
option_D: Administer metoprolol 10 mg intravenously and record AV nodal conduction time by measuring the time it takes an atrial pacing beat to reach the His bundle
option_E: Administer adenosine 12 mg intravenously and record the AV nodal recovery time
answer_text: Pace the right atrium at serially decreasing cycle length and measure the pace-to-His conduction time
explanation: Decremental conduction (slower conduction at faster rates) is shown by atrial pacing at shorter cycle lengths with a lengthening AH interval until Wenckebach.

stem: An 87-year-old man with a history of well-treated hypertension and aortic stenosis has become symptomatic from his aortic stenosis over the last 2 months. Yesterday, he underwent surgical aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic 25-mm valve with excellent intraoperative results. He was rapidly weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass and extubated within 24 hours. Per surgical protocol, he had temporary epicardial pacing wires placed on the ventricular surface and has been pacing at 90 bpm. On rounds this morning, you briefly pause his ventricular pacing to check his underlying rhythm. You note an atrial rate of 80 bpm, but a ventricular rate of 32 bpm with a wide QRS complex. There is no relationship between the P waves and QRS complexes. This patient’s ventricular bradycardia is most likely due to which of the following?
option_A: Development of a systemic disease such as sarcoidosis or Lyme disease causing AV node dysfunction
option_B: Endocarditis of the new aortic bioprosthesis causing AV node block
option_D: Slowed AV nodal recovery after overdrive pac ing
option_E: Surgical injury to the AV node
answer_text: Surgical injury to the AV node
explanation: The AV node lies near the aortic annulus, so AVR/TAVI can cause complete heart block; pace permanently if it persists beyond ~5–7 days.
topics: Complete heart block; Aortic valve replacement

stem: An 82-year-old man has had two episodes of sudden syncope without warning in the past week, one causing facial bruising. During a further 'spell' in clinic, the rhythm strip shown is recorded. What type of block is present, matched to the appropriate management?
option_A: Complete SA nodal block - Permanent pacemaker implantation
option_C: Second-degree Mobitz type II SA nodal block - Exercise treadmill study
option_D: Second-degree Mobitz type I AV block - No intervention necessary
option_E: Second-degree Mobitz type II AV node block - Permanent pacemaker implantation
answer_text: Second-degree Mobitz type II AV node block - Permanent pacemaker implantation
explanation: Constant PR then sudden dropped P waves with syncope is Mobitz II; it tends to progress to complete block, so implant a permanent pacemaker.
topics: Mobitz type II block; Permanent pacemaker

stem: A 19-year-old long-distance runner, who finished in the top 10 of the local marathon last year, presents for cardiac evaluation after his primary care physician ordered a Holter monitor for screening purposes. On his Holter report, several episodes of second-degree, Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block were noted, all occurring during sleep. The patient reports no symptoms but thinks he may have a grandfather who had a pacemaker implanted at an advanced age. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_E: Serologic testing including thyroid-stimulating hormone levels
explanation: Nocturnal Mobitz I in an asymptomatic athlete is high vagal tone; it resolves with exercise. Reassure.
topics: Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block; Athlete's heart

stem: A 47-year-old woman with a history of tobacco abuse and ulcerative colitis is evaluated for intermittent palpitations. She reports that for the last 6 months, every 2-4 days she notes a sensation of her heart “flip-flopping” in her chest for approximately 5 minutes. She has not noted any precipitating factors and has not felt light headed or had chest pains with these episodes. Her physical examination is normal. A resting ECG reveals sinus rhythm and no abnormalities. Aside from checking serum electrolytes, which of the following is the most appropriate testing?
option_A: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) with oral and intravenous (IV) contrast
option_D: Reassurance with no further testing needed
explanation: Monitoring depends on symptom frequency: Holter for daily symptoms, event recorder for every few days, implantable loop recorder for rare episodes.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with a normal examination and ECG has brief 'flip-flopping' palpitations every few days. Event monitoring shows that the symptoms correspond to atrial premature contractions only. Which statement is true?
option_A: Atrial premature contractions are less common than ventricular premature contractions on extended ECG monitoring
option_B: Echocardiography is indicated to determine if structural heart disease is present
option_C: Metoprolol should be initiated for symptom control
option_D: The patient should be reassured that this is not a dangerous condition and does not require further evaluation
option_E: The patient should undergo stress test to determine if ischaemia is present
answer_text: The patient should be reassured that this is not a dangerous condition and does not require further evaluation
explanation: Atrial premature complexes are common and benign in a normal heart; reassure and reduce caffeine/alcohol. Beta-blocker only if troublesome.

stem: An 18-year-old volleyball player with rare palpitations and light-headedness has a normal examination; her ECG shows a PR interval of 60 ms, QRS duration of 140 ms and a delta wave (WPW pattern). Which finding is reassuring that she is at low risk and does not need catheter ablation?
option_A: Ability to increase the heart rate to 185 bpm on an exercise treadmill test
option_B: Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway has both antegrade and retrograde conduction properties
option_C: Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway is located in the posteroseptal region
option_D: Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm
option_E: Holter monitoring demonstrating occasional runs of atrial fibrillation
answer_text: Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm
explanation: Sudden loss of the delta wave on exercise shows a pathway with a long refractory period, so low risk of pre-excited AF degenerating to VF.

stem: An 85-year-old woman with no prior cardiac history presents to the emergency department with 2 hours of palpitations. Blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and heart rate are normal, although you note an irregularly irregular rhythm on examination. ECG shows an irregularly irregular, narrow QRS without discernable P waves at a rate of 75 bpm. Echocardiogram reveals no structural heart disease. Despite the nor mal heart rate, the patient is quite symptomatic with her atrial fibrillation and wants to pursue achievement of sinus rhythm. All of the following interventions may be beneficial EXCEPT:
explanation: Recent-onset AF converts with DC shock, flecainide or amiodarone. Adenosine only transiently blocks the AV node and does not convert AF.

stem: A 79-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) and hypertension has no new symptoms; BP 108/56 mmHg, HR 88/min. His rhythm strip is shown. Based on this, he now has a definite (class I) indication for which therapy?
option_D: Systemic anticoagulation with warfarin or a novel oral anticoagulant
option_E: Transesophageal echocardiography followed by direct current (DC) cardioversion
answer_text: Systemic anticoagulation with warfarin or a novel oral anticoagulant
explanation: AF with heart failure, hypertension, vascular disease and age ≥ 75 (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 5): oral anticoagulation is class I. Flecainide is contraindicated.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department after sudden onset of palpitations 30 minutes prior to her visit. She was seated at her work computer when the symptoms began. Aside from low back pain, she is otherwise healthy. In triage, her heart rate is 178 bpm and blood pressure is 98/56 mmHg with normal oxygen saturation. On physical examination, she has a “frog sign” in her neck and tachycardia but is otherwise normal. ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia without identifiable P waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step to manage her tachycar dia?
Which of the following statements regarding restoration of sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation is true?
option_A: Dofetilide may be safely started as an outpatient
option_B: In patients who are treated with pharmacotherapy and are found to be in sinus rhythm, a prolonged Holter monitor should be worn to determine if anticoagulation can be safely stopped
option_C: Patients who have pharmacologically maintained sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation have improved survival compared with patients who are treated with rate control and anticoagulation
option_D: Recurrence of atrial fibrillation is uncommon when pharmacotherapy is used to maintain sinus rhythm
answer_text: In patients who are treated with pharmacotherapy and are found to be in sinus rhythm, a prolonged Holter monitor should be worn to determine if anticoagulation can be safely stopped
explanation: Rhythm control did not improve survival (AFFIRM) and asymptomatic recurrence is common, so anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VASc, not apparent sinus rhythm.

stem: A young woman collapses while jogging and is unresponsive, with BP 50 mmHg (palpable) and a heart rate of about 280/min. Her 12-lead ECG is shown. What is the next most appropriate step?
option_E: Emergent CT scan with contrast to evaluate for pulmonary embolism
explanation: Irregular very fast broad complexes of varying shape are pre-excited AF; with collapse give immediate DC shock. AV-nodal blockers can precipitate VF.

stem: A young woman collapses while jogging (BP 50 mmHg, heart rate about 280/min). Her 12-lead ECG is shown. What is the underlying rhythm?
option_A: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade conduction through an accessory tract
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade conduction through an accessory tract
explanation: Irregularly irregular broad complexes with varying width and RR < 250 ms is AF conducting down an accessory pathway. VT and AVRT are regular.

stem: A 67-year-old man was given thrombolysis 3 hours ago for an anterolateral STEMI. His monitor now shows the rhythm strip below. What rhythm does this represent?
option_B: Complete heart block with a junctional escape
option_D: Normal sinus rhythm with a left bundle branch block
explanation: A regular broad ventricular rhythm at 60–110/min soon after thrombolysis is accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a benign reperfusion marker.

stem: Ms. Milsap is an 18-year-old high school volleyball star with a sports scholarship to the local university. As part of her admission process, she is required to undergo a full medical assessment prior to taking part in collegiate sports. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities, although she reports the rare episode of palpitations and light-headedness. ECG reveals a PR interval of 0.06 msec, QRS duration of 140 msec, and a slurred upstroke or delta wave in the initial part of the QRS. You correctly diagnose this as Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. Which of the following findings is reassuring that Ms. Milsap will suffer no ill effects or need catheter ablation due to this abnormality?
option_A: Ability to increase the heart rate to 185 bpm on an exercise treadmill test
option_B: Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway has both antegrade and retrograde conduction properties
option_C: Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway is located in the posteroseptal region
option_D: Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm
option_E: Holter monitoring demonstrating occasional runs of atrial fibrillation
answer_text: Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm

stem: A 47-year-old woman on methadone takes leftover erythromycin for a respiratory infection and develops palpitations and light-headedness. The rhythm strip shows recurrent non-sustained runs of the arrhythmia shown. IV magnesium sulfate 2 g does not stop the episodes, and her potassium is normal. What is the next most appropriate step?
option_A: Metoprolol 5 mg IV repeatedly until her resting heart rate is 60 bpm
option_D: IV isoproterenol infusion titrated to a rate of 100-120 bpm
answer_text: IV isoproterenol infusion titrated to a rate of 100-120 bpm
explanation: Torsades from methadone + erythromycin persisting after magnesium: raise the rate with isoprenaline or overdrive pacing to shorten QT. Amiodarone worsens it.
topics: Torsades de pointes; Long QT syndrome; Isoprenaline

stem: In an ECG with wide complex tachycardia, which of the following clues most strongly supports the diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia?
option_B: Classic right bundle branch block pattern
option_C: Irregularly irregular rhythm with changing QRS complexes
option_E: Slowing of rate with carotid sinus massage
explanation: AV dissociation (independent P waves, fusion or capture beats) is diagnostic of VT. Prior MI, QRS > 160 ms and chest-lead concordance also favour VT.

stem: An 18-year-old man with no symptoms has an ECG at a pre-university medical showing an irregular rhythm: every QRS is preceded by an identical normal P wave with a constant PR interval, and the rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_B: Electrophysiology study and planned ablation of an ectopic atrial focus
option_D: Holter monitor to define arrhythmia burden
explanation: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (rate rises on inspiration, falls on expiration) is normal, especially in the young; all beats are sinus, so reassure.

stem: A 22-year-old triathlete with type 1 diabetes is recovering from diabetic ketoacidosis. While she is asleep, the monitor shows bradycardia; the ECG is shown (2:1 AV block with narrow QRS complexes). Where is the block most likely to be?
explanation: 2:1 block with narrow QRS in a sleeping young athlete is almost certainly vagally mediated AV-nodal block; infranodal block usually has broad QRS.

stem: A young athlete has 2:1 AV block with narrow QRS complexes while asleep (ECG shown), with the block located in the AV node. What would be expected if IV atropine were given?
option_A: Increase sinus rate and maintain 2:1 AV block
option_B: Increase sinus rate and improve heart block to 1:1 conduction
option_C: Increase sinus rate and worsen heart block to >2:1
option_D: No change in sinus rate and worsen heart block to >2:1
answer_text: Increase sinus rate and improve heart block to 1:1 conduction
explanation: Atropine removes vagal tone at SA and AV nodes, raising the rate and restoring 1:1 conduction in nodal block; in infranodal block it may worsen the ratio.

stem: An 87-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes levodopa. After running out of his medication and failing to obtain a refill, he presents to the emergency department with a parkinsonian exacerbation. On initial evaluation, he has the ECG shown in Figure V-52. Which of the following is the next most appropriate step?
option_B: Check serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and obtain targeted respiratory history
explanation: Parkinsonian tremor artefact (4–6 Hz) can mimic flutter, AF or VT; regular QRS complexes seen through it confirm sinus rhythm, so no treatment.

stem: A 68-year-old man with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension and an unexplained TIA 6 months ago has felt unwell for 5 days; BP 110/78 mmHg, HR 150/min. His ECG is shown. Two doses of IV metoprolol 5 mg slow the rate to 75/min and he feels better, and ablation is planned. What is the next most appropriate step?
explanation: Saw-tooth waves in II, III, aVF with 2:1 conduction is typical flutter; its stroke risk equals AF, and CHA2DS2-VASc is high, so anticoagulate before ablation.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with palpitations. Her ECG (shown) has a short PR interval and delta waves. Where is her accessory pathway likely to be?
explanation: A negative delta wave and LBBB-like QRS in V1 indicate a right-sided accessory pathway; a positive delta in V1 indicates a left-sided pathway.

stem: Mr. Cooper underwent tPA administration for acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction 1 hour previously. He had an excellent response with resolution of his ST-segment elevation and chest pain. However, the nurse pages you to evaluate a change in his rhythm. You note a wide complex ventricular rhythm with a rate of 75 bpm. Mr. Cooper continues to feel well without new symptoms, and his blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. The next most appropriate therapeutic maneuver is which of the following?
option_A: Administer amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
option_C: Administer metoprolol 5 mg IV every 5 minutes × 3
explanation: A wide ventricular rhythm at 75/min soon after successful lysis in a well patient is accelerated idioventricular rhythm: observe. Suppression is harmful.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the coronary care unit with unstable angina and started on appropriate antiplatelet and anti-anginal therapy. She has hypertension; fasting glucose is normal and total cholesterol is 5.2 mmol/L. She is found to be in atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate treatment to reduce her risk of stroke?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc 5: oral anticoagulation. After ACS with AF: brief triple therapy (≤ 1 week), then DOAC + clopidogrel to 12 months, then DOAC alone.
topics: Atrial fibrillation; Anticoagulation; Acute coronary syndrome

stem: A 21-year-old man is on his way home from a party when he experiences the sudden onset of rapid palpitations. He feels uncomfortable but not short of breath and has no chest pain. He goes to the nearest accident and emergency department, where he is found to have a supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) at a rate of 170/ minute. Carotid sinus massage produced transient reversion to sinus rhythm, after which the tachycardia resumed. What would be the next step in your management?

A 29-year-old woman sees her GP with fatigue, palpitations and weight loss without dieting. Her pulse is about 120/min and irregularly irregular, BP 142/89 mmHg and BMI 19 kg/m2; there are no added heart sounds. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Weight loss, fatigue and new AF in a young woman suggest hyperthyroidism: check TSH and free T4 (recommended in all new AF).
topics: Atrial fibrillation; Hyperthyroidism; Thyroid function tests

stem: A 62-year-old man with a previous myocardial infarction presents with palpitations that began 3 hours ago; this is his first known episode. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at about 130/min without acute ischaemic changes. He has mild central chest discomfort, but BP is 128/80 mmHg and he is not distressed. A rhythm-control strategy is preferred. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
option_A: Heparin and digoxin at the standard daily dose
option_B: Heparin followed by synchronised DC cardioversion
option_E: Wait for spontaneous reversion to sinus rhythm
answer_text: Heparin followed by synchronised DC cardioversion
explanation: AF < 48 h can be cardioverted once heparin is started. Prior MI contraindicates flecainide, so use DC cardioversion (or amiodarone).

stem: In the ICU, a patient suddenly becomes pulseless and unresponsive, with cardiac monitor indicating ventricular tachycardia. The crash cart is immediately available. What is the best first therapy?

A 36-year-old man presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
option_B: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes

stem: A 60-year-old woman develops chest pain, respiratory distress, and confusion after right hip replacement surgery. She is confused and appears in respiratory distress. Blood pressure is 80/50, heart rate of 155/minute. ECG reveals atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the best management of this patient’s arrhythmia?

A 69-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and asthma is evaluated. Episodes are infrequent, and echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart. Which statement regarding her management is correct?
option_A: Digoxin effectively prevents recurrences of the arrhythmia
option_C: Sotalol is a suitable choice to prevent recurrences
option_E: Oral flecainide taken as needed may be an effective way to terminate an attack
answer_text: Oral flecainide taken as needed may be an effective way to terminate an attack
explanation: Infrequent paroxysmal AF in a normal heart: 'pill-in-the-pocket' flecainide with an AV-nodal blocker. Sotalol is contraindicated in asthma.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of shortness of breath. His pulse is irregular at 140/min, and the ECG shows atrial fibrillation. What would you expect to see in the jugular venous pulse?
explanation: The a wave is atrial contraction, so it is absent in AF. Cannon a waves = AV dissociation; large v waves = tricuspid regurgitation.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with exertional chest tightness relieved by rest. ECG reveals first degree heart block. Which ECG finding is typical?

A 38-year-old man with no past medical history is referred after an abnormal preoperative ECG, and long QT syndrome is confirmed on repeat ECGs. His father had a heart condition diagnosed in his 20s, and he himself has had episodes of syncope after exertion. He is started on a beta-blocker and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is planned. Loss of function of which of the following is most commonly associated with his condition?
explanation: Congenital long QT is most often loss of potassium-channel function (KCNQ1 LQT1, hERG LQT2); treat with nadolol/propranolol and avoid QT drugs.

stem: A 55-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease presents with palpitations for the past 10 days. His pulse is 130/min and irregularly irregular. He had one previous episode of atrial fibrillation 3 months ago, which was terminated by elective cardioversion after anticoagulation with warfarin. Which term best describes his arrhythmia?
explanation: AF lasting > 7 days (or needing cardioversion after 7 days) is persistent; paroxysmal ends within 7 days, permanent means rhythm control abandoned.

stem: A 72-year-old man with hypertension and ischaemic heart disease presents with light-headedness. He takes bisoprolol, amlodipine and aspirin. Heart rate is 38/min, BP 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on air and temperature 37.1 °C. The ECG shows regular P–P and R–R intervals with no relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes. What would you expect to hear on auscultation of the heart?
explanation: In complete heart block the varying AV interval makes S1 intensity vary (with intermittent cannon a waves). Stop bisoprolol and pace.

stem: A 56-year-old man is brought in by paramedics after fainting this morning; he is now conscious but pale and light-headed, with no injuries. His heart rate is 37/min, respiratory rate 16/min and BP 105/70 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a prolonged PR interval. What is the initial management?
explanation: Bradycardia with an adverse feature (syncope): IV atropine 500 µg, repeat to 3 mg; then transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline/adrenaline infusion.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with pneumonia. Her only past history is a transient ischaemic attack 2 months ago. On admission the ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 103/min. She is treated with IV fluids and antibiotics and improves; two further ECGs overnight show sinus rhythm, and next day she is medically fit for discharge. What is the single most appropriate management of her atrial fibrillation?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc 5 (age 75 = 2, female, prior TIA = 2): anticoagulate (DOAC); AF during acute illness often recurs. Aspirin is not used.
topics: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; Anticoagulation; CHA2DS2-VASc score

stem: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset palpitations. BP is 124/84 mmHg and pulse 150/min. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. Vagal manoeuvres fail, IV access is obtained and adenosine 6 mg is given with no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Adenosine is given 6 mg, then 12 mg, then 18 mg by rapid bolus with flush; repeating 6 mg rarely works. Verapamil if adenosine fails.

stem: Each of the following may cause left bundle branch block EXCEPT:
explanation: LBBB occurs with IHD, hypertension/LVH, AS, cardiomyopathy and conduction fibrosis. Secundum ASD causes RBBB with right axis deviation.
topics: Left bundle branch block; Atrial septal defect

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. The ECG shows sinus rhythm at 85/min, QRS duration 110 ms, PR interval 180 ms and corrected QT interval 500 ms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ECG abnormality?
explanation: QTc 500 ms is prolonged (high torsades risk); hypokalaemia (flat T, U waves) is a common cause. Hypercalcaemia and digoxin shorten the QT.
topics: Long QT syndrome; Hypokalaemia; QT interval

stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted after a collapse, and the ECG shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which one of the following is NOT associated with an increased risk of torsades de pointes?
explanation: Torsades needs a long QT: TCAs, SAH, hypothermia, congenital LQTS, low K/Mg/Ca. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT. Treat with IV magnesium 2 g.
topics: Torsades de pointes; Long QT syndrome; Hypercalcaemia

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 118/min. He has brittle asthma, hypertension and heart failure, and a recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%. What is the most appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
explanation: AF with HFrEF and brittle asthma: rate-limiting CCBs are negatively inotropic and beta-blockers are precluded, so digoxin is used.
topics: Atrial fibrillation; Digoxin; Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with lethargy and palpitations for the past 4–5 days. His pulse is 123/min and irregularly irregular, BP 118/70 mmHg, and his chest is clear. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
explanation: For stable AF without heart failure, first-line rate control is a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil), aiming initially for a resting rate below 110/min. Digoxin monotherapy is reserved for sedentary patients or when other agents are contraindicated, because it controls the rate poorly on exertion. Amiodarone and flecainide are rhythm-control drugs, and amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that does not slow AV-nodal conduction. He also needs CHA2DS2-VASc assessment for anticoagulation.

stem: Which one of the following is NOT an indication for insertion of a temporary pacemaker?
option_A: Complete heart block after an inferior MI, with normal blood pressure
option_B: Complete heart block after an anterior MI, with normal blood pressure
option_C: Bradycardia-dependent torsades de pointes recurring despite IV magnesium
option_D: Mobitz type II heart block after an anterior MI, with normal blood pressure
option_E: Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to drug treatment
answer_text: Complete heart block after an inferior MI, with normal blood pressure
explanation: CHB after inferior MI is nodal (narrow escape, atropine-responsive, usually resolves), so pacing is not needed if stable; after anterior MI it is.
topics: Temporary pacing; Complete heart block; Myocardial infarction

stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted for observation after presenting with dizziness, and the rhythm strip shown is recorded on the monitor. She has no history of cardiac disease, diabetes or hypertension. On questioning she reports several previous episodes of transient dizziness and one brief syncope. Examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best plan of care?
option_A: Reassurance; this is a benign condition and needs no treatment
option_B: Reassurance and advice not to drive until symptom-free; no other treatment
option_C: Nuclear cardiac stress testing, with treatment depending on the result
explanation: Rapid SVT ending in a long pause with dizziness/syncope is tachy–brady sick sinus syndrome: permanent pacemaker, then rate-control drugs safely.
topics: Sick sinus syndrome; Tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome; Permanent pacemaker

stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of palpitations. A 24-hour Holter monitor shows occasional unifocal premature ventricular contractions and premature atrial contractions. Which of the following is the best management for this patient?

An active 78-year-old woman with hypertension presents with a new left hemiparesis; CT excludes haemorrhage, and cardiac monitoring shows atrial fibrillation. She was in sinus rhythm at a check-up 3 months earlier. Optimal management at discharge includes review of her antihypertensive therapy, a ventricular rate-control agent and which of the following?
option_A: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator/permanent pacemaker to avoid the need for anticoagulation
option_C: Antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, without anticoagulation
option_D: Antiplatelet therapy plus warfarin with a target INR of 1.5
option_E: Long-term oral anticoagulation (a DOAC, or warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0)
answer_text: Long-term oral anticoagulation (a DOAC, or warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0)
explanation: Ischaemic stroke with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 6): lifelong anticoagulation, DOAC preferred (or warfarin INR 2–3), started within days depending on infarct size.

stem: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops a viral upper respiratory infection. On the second day he has palpitations and attends the emergency department. His BP is 118/78 mmHg and he is otherwise well. The rhythm strip (lead V1) is shown. What is the best next step in management?
option_E: Initiation of chest compressions and preparation for semielective intubation
explanation: Flutter waves ~250/min with 2:1 block in a stable patient: rate control first with IV metoprolol, then anticoagulation and elective cardioversion/ablation.

stem: An asymptomatic 65-year-old man with diabetes attends the emergency department with a sports-related right shoulder injury. His pulse is irregular, and the rhythm strip shown is recorded; BP and the rest of the examination are normal. What is the best immediate management?
explanation: Progressive PR lengthening until a dropped beat is Mobitz I (AV-nodal, benign): observe and review AV-nodal drugs if asymptomatic.
topics: Mobitz type I AV block; Wenckebach phenomenon; ECG

stem: In the intensive care unit, a monitored patient suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless, and the monitor shows ventricular tachycardia. A defibrillator is immediately available. What is the best first treatment?
explanation: Pulseless VT is managed exactly like ventricular fibrillation: in a monitored, witnessed arrest with a defibrillator at hand, give an immediate unsynchronised shock (biphasic 120–200 J; up to three successive shocks may be given in this setting), then resume CPR. Synchronised cardioversion is for VT with a pulse – in pulseless VT, attempting to synchronise only delays the shock. Adrenaline 1 mg is given after the third shock and then every 3–5 minutes, with amiodarone 300 mg (or lidocaine) after the third shock.
topics: Cardiac arrest; Pulseless ventricular tachycardia; Defibrillation

stem: A 36-year-old male presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
option_B: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 min

stem: A patient has been on the coronary care unit for 24 hours with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He develops the rhythm shown, although his BP remains stable at 110/68 mmHg. What is the best next step in management?
option_B: Pacing (temporary transvenous, then assessment for a permanent pacemaker)
answer_text: Pacing (temporary transvenous, then assessment for a permanent pacemaker)
explanation: Complete heart block after anterior MI is infranodal with an unreliable escape rhythm: pace (temporary, then assess permanent) even if BP is stable.
topics: Complete heart block; Myocardial infarction; Temporary pacing

stem: A 62-year-old man with COPD develops a viral upper respiratory infection and starts an over-the-counter decongestant. Shortly afterwards he has palpitations and attends the emergency department, where the rhythm strip shown is recorded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Regular saw-tooth waves ~300/min with a QRS after every fourth is atrial flutter with 4:1 block; decongestants and lung disease are triggers.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is admitted with dizziness. Monitoring shows atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, which is controlled with a beta-blocker. Echocardiography shows an enlarged left atrium, an ejection fraction of 50% and no diastolic dysfunction. She is now asymptomatic, with BP 130/80 mmHg and an irregularly irregular pulse of about 80/min. What is the best management strategy for her arrhythmia?
option_E: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation
answer_text: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation
explanation: Older patient with dilated LA, now rate-controlled and asymptomatic: continue rate control plus long-term anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 3).

stem: During medical screening of new military recruits, an 18-year-old man reports several episodes of palpitations and syncope over the past few years. Examination is unremarkable. Excerpts from his ECG are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_A: Previous myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery disease
explanation: Short PR, delta wave and wide QRS is pre-excitation (WPW); palpitations or syncope warrant an EP study and pathway ablation.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has progressive exertional breathlessness, angina and presyncope on climbing stairs. BP 138/76 mmHg, HR 78/min. There is a harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge, a soft S2 and a slow-rising (parvus et tardus) carotid pulse. Echocardiography: aortic valve area 0.8 cm², peak velocity 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 48 mmHg, LVEF 42% and moderate concentric LV hypertrophy. What is the best next step?
option_B: Elective surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement
option_D: Medical treatment and repeat echocardiography in 6–12 months
answer_text: Elective surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement
explanation: Symptomatic severe AS (area < 1 cm², mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg) with EF < 50% needs AVR — surgical or TAVI by heart team. No drug improves outlook.
topics: Aortic stenosis; Aortic valve replacement; TAVI

stem: A 36-year-old woman has exertional breathlessness and palpitations. There is a loud S1 and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex, best heard with the bell in the left lateral position and accentuated by brief exercise. Which additional finding most strongly supports mitral stenosis?
option_B: Soft S1 with an apical pansystolic murmur
option_D: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge
option_E: Continuous murmur that increases with inspiration
explanation: An opening snap after S2, with a loud S1 and apical mid-diastolic rumble, is mitral stenosis; the shorter the S2–snap interval, the more severe the stenosis.

stem: A young woman has breathlessness and palpitations, and an early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. Aortic regurgitation is suspected. Which finding argues AGAINST this diagnosis?
option_C: To-and-fro femoral bruit on compression (Duroziez sign)
option_E: Soft mid-diastolic murmur at the apex (Austin Flint murmur)
explanation: Significant chronic AR gives a wide pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic), so 120/95 mmHg argues against it. Acute AR may have a near-normal pulse pressure.
topics: Aortic regurgitation; Pulse pressure; Clinical signs

stem: A 35-year-old man has exertional and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Pulse 82/min regular, BP 135/85 mmHg; there are bibasal fine crackles and a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the left axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Exertional dyspnoea and PND with an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation (rheumatic or prolapse in the young); echo confirms.

stem: A patient with previous rheumatic fever is told he has aortic regurgitation. Which finding is NOT consistent with this diagnosis?

An elderly man with hypertension treated with lisinopril has exertional breathlessness. BP is 165/55 mmHg. There is a grade 2/6 early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex; S1 is normal and there is no opening snap. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Early diastolic murmur with wide pulse pressure is AR; the apical rumble is an Austin Flint murmur, told from MS by a normal S1 and no opening snap.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease for 20 years has breathlessness and fatigue. There is a soft S1, a loud S3 and an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Which investigation will NOT help in the diagnosis of her valve lesion?
explanation: Echo (TTE/TOE) and catheterisation define a chronic valve lesion; cardiac enzymes detect myocardial necrosis and say nothing about valve disease.
topics: Mitral regurgitation; Rheumatic heart disease; Echocardiography

stem: A young woman has breathlessness and palpitations, and an early diastolic murmur is heard at the aortic area. Which sign is NOT consistent with aortic regurgitation?
option_B: High diastolic pressure with a narrow pulse pressure
answer_text: High diastolic pressure with a narrow pulse pressure

stem: A patient has breathlessness, fatigue and leg oedema. There is a raised JVP with large v waves, a left parasternal (right ventricular) heave, a loud P2 and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Echocardiography shows right ventricular hypertrophy with structurally normal tricuspid leaflets and functional tricuspid regurgitation. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Loud P2, RV heave and RVH with functional TR (normal leaflets) means pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure; then find its cause.
topics: Pulmonary hypertension; Tricuspid regurgitation; Right heart failure

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination there is a loud first heart sound and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A loud S1 and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex are the hallmarks of mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic; there may also be an opening snap and, in sinus rhythm, pre-systolic accentuation. Haemoptysis results from raised pulmonary venous pressure (rupture of bronchial veins, pulmonary oedema or infarction). MR and AS cause systolic murmurs, AR an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, and tricuspid stenosis a mid-diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath on exertion and fatigue. On examination you note a soft first HS and a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to her axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 62-year-old man presents with angina and breathlessness. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis; angina, dyspnoea and syncope signal severe disease.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with dyspnoea and orthopnoea. On examination you note a blowing early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic after an echocardiogram showing right ventricular dysfunction. He has a raised JVP and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, with a raised JVP and large v waves, is tricuspid regurgitation.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and breathlessness. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the neck. Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
explanation: Transthoracic echo with Doppler confirms AS and grades it (velocity, gradient, area) with LV function; angiography is done before surgery.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. There is a loud first heart sound and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. An echocardiogram and chest X-ray are requested. All of the following are chest X-ray features of this condition EXCEPT:
explanation: In MS the enlarged LA straightens the left heart border, gives a double right border and splays (widens) the carina; upper-lobe diversion and Kerley B lines.

stem: A 20-year-old student sees his GP with blurred vision; a year ago he had a dislocated lens. On examination he has pectus excavatum, a high-arched palate and joint hypermobility. Which cardiac disorder is often associated with his condition?
explanation: Ectopia lentis, pectus, high palate and hypermobility suggest Marfan syndrome, commonly with MVP; aortic root dilatation is the dangerous lesion.

stem: A 65-year-old man has 3 months of exertional central chest pain and breathlessness that settle with rest, and lately dizziness on exertion. There is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. ECG shows tall R waves in I, aVL and V4–V6 with deep S waves in V1–V3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Exertional angina, dyspnoea and dizziness/syncope with an ejection murmur and LVH on ECG is severe aortic stenosis. HCM is younger, and its murmur does not radiate to the carotids.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever presents with breathlessness on exertion and a malar flush. She is in sinus rhythm, and echocardiography confirms mitral stenosis. Which physical sign is she likely to have?
explanation: In MS with sinus rhythm, atrial contraction causes pre-systolic accentuation of the rumble; it disappears when AF develops.

stem: An 80-year-old man is found to have an incidental ejection systolic murmur, and his family physician feels a systolic thrill at the base of the heart. What is the most likely cause of the thrill?
explanation: A basal systolic thrill with an ejection murmur in an elderly man is most likely calcific aortic stenosis; echo grades severity.

stem: A 43-year-old man has a routine health check at work. He has a murmur, isolated systolic hypertension (180/60 mmHg) and left ventricular hypertrophy on his ECG. Echocardiography shows significant regurgitant flow across the aortic valve. Which clinical sign is he likely to have?
option_C: Head nodding in time with the heartbeat (de Musset sign)
answer_text: Head nodding in time with the heartbeat (de Musset sign)
explanation: Pulse pressure 120 mmHg with significant AR gives hyperdynamic signs: collapsing pulse, Corrigan, de Musset (head nodding), Quincke and Duroziez.
topics: Aortic regurgitation; de Musset sign; Clinical signs

stem: A 58-year-old man with known mitral valve prolapse presents with 4 weeks of fever, malaise and weight loss after a dental extraction. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a vegetation on his native mitral valve with no abscess, and he has no embolic complications. Blood cultures grow viridans streptococci fully sensitive to penicillin, and his renal function is normal. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen to start?
explanation: Penicillin-sensitive streptococcal native-valve IE: IV benzylpenicillin 4 weeks (or 2 weeks with gentamicin if uncomplicated). Vancomycin is for allergy.

stem: A 71-year-old man with rheumatic heart disease for 20 years presents with breathlessness on exertion. BP is 128/78 mmHg. On examination the apex beat is displaced, the first heart sound is soft and the second heart sound is normal. Which valvular lesion is most likely?
explanation: A displaced apex with a soft S1 in rheumatic disease is mitral regurgitation (LV volume overload). MS gives a loud S1 and tapping undisplaced apex.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and chest discomfort. There is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap after S2 and a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. Which valve lesion is most likely?
explanation: Loud S1, opening snap and an apical mid-diastolic rumble are mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic. Tricuspid stenosis is at the lower left sternal edge; aortic stenosis is systolic.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath on exertion. On examination his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular. Auscultation of his chest reveals an early diastolic murmur Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of murmur?

An 87-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 0.76 L), poorly controlled diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease presents with exertional chest pressure, leg swelling, breathlessness and rapidly worsening fatigue. There is a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, an inaudible S2 and slow-rising, delayed carotid pulses. Echocardiography confirms aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.59 cm². The cardiothoracic surgeon declines surgical aortic valve replacement because her predicted in-hospital mortality exceeds 15%. Which statement to her is reasonable?
option_A: For this condition, medications have been shown to reduce the risk of death
option_B: It does not matter that you are not a surgical candidate: your condition carries a low 1- and 5-year mortality, and medication can control your symptoms
option_C: Percutaneous balloon aortic valvotomy is a good non-surgical option with excellent short- and long-term results
option_D: As you are not a surgical candidate, no other procedure can replace your valve, so we should consider hospice care
option_E: We should refer you for assessment for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
answer_text: We should refer you for assessment for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
explanation: Symptomatic severe AS has ~50% 2-year mortality without replacement; at prohibitive surgical risk, refer for TAVI (heart-team assessment).

stem: A 62-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with progressive breathlessness, ankle swelling and abdominal distension. She is in sinus rhythm. Examination shows a raised JVP, a left parasternal heave, tender hepatomegaly and pitting oedema to the knees. What is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
option_B: Progression to pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure
answer_text: Progression to pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure
explanation: Long-standing MS causes pulmonary hypertension and RV failure (raised JVP, RV heave, hepatomegaly, oedema); this indicates valvotomy or surgery.
topics: Mitral stenosis; Pulmonary hypertension; Right heart failure

stem: What is the typical character of the apex beat in a patient with mitral stenosis?
explanation: In MS the apex is undisplaced and tapping (a palpable loud S1) because the LV is protected from overload.

stem: Which auscultatory finding most suggests pulmonary hypertension in a patient with mitral stenosis?
explanation: Pulmonary hypertension causes a loud (even palpable) P2, often with an RV heave. The opening snap and loud S1 come from the mitral valve itself.
topics: Mitral stenosis; Pulmonary hypertension; Heart sounds

stem: In which patient with mitral stenosis is percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy indicated?
option_B: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation
option_C: All patients with any degree of stenosis
option_D: Only in patients with associated atrial fibrillation
answer_text: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation
explanation: Balloon mitral commissurotomy: symptomatic MS (area ≤ 1.5 cm²) with pliable non-calcified leaflets, ≤ mild MR and no LA thrombus on TOE.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends her GP for a routine medical examination and is noted to have a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap. Her blood pressure is 118/71 mmHg and pulse is 66/min. She is entirely asymptomatic and her chest x-ray and ECG are normal. What would be the most appropriate investigation at this point?
A patient admitted with pneumonia is found to have a heart murmur. Which finding points to mitral regurgitation?
option_B: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position
option_C: Murmur louder over the right 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
answer_text: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position
explanation: Mitral murmurs are loudest at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position; MR is pansystolic, radiates to the axilla, louder in expiration.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents with increasing shortness of breath on exertion over the past three months, with no chest pain, cough, or ankle swelling. On examination, BP is 158/61 mmHg, pulse 88/min, and crackles are present at both lung bases. A decrescendo diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 59-year-old man attends for a routine check-up. He is asymptomatic, and examination reveals a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Mid-systolic click then late systolic murmur is mitral valve prolapse (Barlow); standing/Valsalva bring the click earlier, squatting delays it.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and essential hypertension presents with worsening breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance. Which of the following is NOT a clinical sign of mitral stenosis?
option_C: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla
answer_text: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla
explanation: MS signs: malar flush, AF, tapping apex, loud S1, opening snap, RV heave. A pansystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.

stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is told she has mitral valve prolapse after an echocardiogram. Which statement is correct?
option_C: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole
option_D: Significant mitral regurgitation will eventually develop
answer_text: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole
explanation: MVP is systolic displacement of a leaflet > 2 mm into the LA; most are asymptomatic and need no drugs, but echo follow-up is advised.

stem: A 76-year-old male collapses at home but recovers quickly. He also reports increasing shortness of breath on exertion and occasional central chest pain. Examination reveals BP 115/88 mmHg, a few rales at the bases, and borderline LVH on ECG. Which auscultatory finding would you expect?
option_A: Mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex
option_B: Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge
option_C: Diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
option_D: Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the apex
option_E: Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
answer_text: Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge

stem: A 15-year-old student, newly active in football, experiences a syncopal episode during practice. Examination reveals a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and apex, and ECG shows LVH. Which physical finding is most likely?
option_A: A systolic ejection murmur at the apex that diminishes with squatting/handgrip and increases with Valsalva/standing
option_B: A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and murmur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing
option_C: A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla that increases with squatting/handgrip and diminishes with Valsalva/standing
option_D: A blowing holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border which increases with squatting/ handgrip and diminishes with Valsalva/standing
option_E: A low pitched mid systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
answer_text: A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and murmur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing

stem: A 75-year-old patient presents to the ER after a syncopal episode with occasional substernal chest pressure and exertional dyspnea. BP is 110/80 with bibasilar rales. Which auscultatory finding best explains his symptoms?
option_A: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
option_B: A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
option_C: A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
answer_text: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of productive cough, leg swelling and fatigue; he has been afebrile throughout. He had a porcine (bioprosthetic) mitral valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation 12 years ago. Examination shows bibasal crackles, a laterally displaced apex beat and a grade 3/6 low-pitched diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
option_C: Structural degeneration of the bioprosthetic valve
answer_text: Structural degeneration of the bioprosthetic valve
explanation: Bioprosthetic valves degenerate after ~10 years (earlier in mitral position); a new apical diastolic murmur means prosthetic MS. Exclude endocarditis; redo or valve-in-valve.
topics: Prosthetic heart valve; Bioprosthetic valve degeneration
