stem: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 50-year smoking history presents with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. Physical exam shows weak peripheral pulses. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 60-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and dyspnea for 2 months, with nocturnal dyspnea and occasional palpitations. He has type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease. Examination shows bilateral basilar rales. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 4 years ago is reviewed. Which long-term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
option_D: Aspirin + clopidogrel for the first 12 months
explanation: Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin (INR ~2.5–3.5 mitral, 2.0–3.0 bileaflet aortic). DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN).

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with fatigue and exertional breathlessness. He has no significant past history, takes no medication, and does not smoke or drink alcohol. He is very tall (2.08 m) and thin, with a high-arched palate. Auscultation reveals a pansystolic murmur that is loudest in inspiration. What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
explanation: A pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo) is tricuspid regurgitation; in Marfan it may follow tricuspid prolapse.
topics: Tricuspid regurgitation; Marfan syndrome; Carvallo sign

stem: A 45-year-old woman who injects drugs presents with breathlessness and bilateral leg swelling. Her pulse is regular, there is a pansystolic murmur heard loudest at the lower left sternal edge, and there is shifting dullness in the abdomen. What is the most likely finding in her jugular venous pulse?
explanation: TR (e.g. right-sided IE in drug users) gives giant v (cv) waves in the JVP and a pulsatile liver. Cannon a waves mean AV dissociation.
topics: Tricuspid regurgitation; Jugular venous pressure; Infective endocarditis

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with a bisferiens pulse?
explanation: A bisferiens (double-peaked) pulse occurs in mixed aortic valve disease with predominant AR, severe AR and HOCM. Pure AS gives a slow-rising pulse.
topics: Bisferiens pulse; Mixed aortic valve disease; Arterial pulse

stem: Which one of the following is a cause of a soft second heart sound?
explanation: Severe calcific AS gives a soft or absent A2 (and reversed splitting). Pulmonary hypertension gives a loud P2; ASD gives fixed splitting.

stem: Which of the following conditions is NOT associated with the development of aortic regurgitation?
explanation: AR arises from leaflet disease (rheumatic, IE, bicuspid) or root dilatation (Marfan, ankylosing spondylitis, syphilis). DCM causes functional MR/TR.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is seen by his GP because his parents are concerned that he is struggling to gain weight and is excessively breathless on exertion. He has known congenital pulmonary stenosis, managed conservatively so far, and the parents ask whether intervention may be needed. What murmur is likely to be heard on examination?
explanation: Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with click and soft P2; balloon valvuloplasty if severe.
topics: Pulmonary stenosis; Heart murmur; Congenital heart disease

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He is now alert and, in retrospect, describes occasional substernal chest pressure and breathlessness on exertion. His BP is 110/80 mmHg and there are a few bibasal crackles. Which auscultatory finding would best explain his presentation?
option_A: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
option_B: A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
option_C: A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
answer_text: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
explanation: Exertional syncope, angina and breathlessness in an older patient with a narrow pulse pressure (110/80 mmHg) form the classic triad of severe aortic stenosis, whose murmur is a harsh crescendo–decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids, often with a soft A2 and a slow-rising pulse. Once symptoms develop, survival without valve replacement is only a few years (shortest with heart failure), so urgent echocardiography and referral for AVR or TAVI follow. An early diastolic murmur indicates AR, an apical holosystolic murmur MR, a midsystolic click MVP and a rub pericarditis.
topics: Aortic stenosis; Syncope; Ejection systolic murmur

stem: A 72-year-old man has intermittent breathlessness on exertion, palpitations and a cough occasionally productive of blood. On auscultation, a low-pitched diastolic rumbling murmur is faintly heard at the apex. What is the most likely cause of the murmur?
option_C: A silent MI within the past year
explanation: Dyspnoea, AF and haemoptysis with an apical diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, usually a late consequence of childhood rheumatic fever.

stem: A 68-year-old man is intubated in the emergency department because of pulmonary oedema. His BP is 150/90 mmHg. Urgent echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 45% and severe mitral regurgitation. Despite aggressive diuresis with furosemide, he still requires mechanical ventilation for pulmonary oedema. What is the best next step?
option_E: Start IV afterload reduction (e.g. nitroprusside or IV enalaprilat)
answer_text: Start IV afterload reduction (e.g. nitroprusside or IV enalaprilat)
explanation: Severe MR with pulmonary oedema and adequate BP: IV afterload reduction (nitroprusside/nitrates) increases forward flow; IABP if hypotensive; then surgery.
topics: Mitral regurgitation; Afterload reduction; Acute pulmonary oedema

stem: A nurse at a community clinic has listed patients scheduled for a dental extraction who may need antibiotic prophylaxis. Which of these patients is most likely to benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis?
option_A: 17-year-old boy with coarctation of the aorta
option_B: 26-year-old woman with a ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood
option_D: 65-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve
answer_text: 65-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve
explanation: Dental prophylaxis (AHA/ESC) only for highest risk: prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD. NICE does not recommend it routinely.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Antibiotic prophylaxis; Prosthetic heart valve

stem: A 48-year-old woman with breast cancer on recent chemotherapy has 4 days of progressive breathlessness, chest discomfort and fatigue. BP 92/64 mmHg, HR 118, RR 24. JVP is raised, heart sounds are muffled and pulsus paradoxus is 14 mmHg. ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes; echo shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial systolic collapse. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_E: IV fluids and observe for 24 hours
explanation: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus with RA collapse is tamponade (likely malignant): urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis. Diuretics are harmful.
topics: Cardiac tamponade; Malignant pericardial effusion; Pericardiocentesis

stem: A 27-year-old has had sharp, stabbing chest pain radiating to the shoulder and left jaw for 3 days with a low-grade fever. A to-and-fro scratching sound is heard over the precordium and the ECG shows ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2–V5. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 27-year-old man has had sharp, stabbing chest pain radiating to the shoulder and left jaw for 3 days with a low-grade fever. A to-and-fro scratching sound is heard over the precordium and the ECG shows ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2–V5. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Positional pain, friction rub and concave ST elevation across several territories is acute pericarditis; treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.
topics: Acute pericarditis; Pericardial friction rub; ECG

stem: A 27-year-old has had sharp, stabbing chest pain radiating to the shoulder and left jaw for 3 days with a low-grade fever. A to-and-fro scratching sound is heard over the precordium and the ECG shows ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2–V5. Four days later he develops retrosternal oppression; the JVP is raised, pulsus paradoxus is present and BP is 80/45 mmHg. Which complication has developed?
explanation: A new raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus and hypotension days after pericarditis means tamponade; confirm with echo and drain urgently.

stem: A patient with acute pericarditis develops hypotension, a raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus. Which investigation best confirms this complication?
explanation: Echo shows the effusion, RA/RV diastolic collapse and a plethoric IVC, and guides pericardiocentesis. ECG and CXR are insensitive.

stem: A patient with acute pericarditis develops cardiac tamponade (BP 80/45 mmHg, raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus). What is the treatment of choice now?
explanation: Tamponade with hypotension needs urgent pericardiocentesis; diuretics, nitrates and ACEi worsen filling. Fluids only as a bridge.

stem: Which of the following is a bad prognostic sign in acute rheumatic fever?
explanation: In rheumatic fever, carditis and recurrence are commonest when the first attack is in young children, so young age is a bad sign; penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence.
topics: Acute rheumatic fever; Prognosis; Rheumatic heart disease

stem: Which of the following is a major criterion for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
option_B: Three or more positive blood cultures taken over more than one hour
answer_text: Three or more positive blood cultures taken over more than one hour
explanation: Duke major criteria: persistently positive blood cultures (e.g. 3 sets ≥ 1 h apart) or imaging evidence of endocardial involvement. IVDU and emboli are minor.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Duke criteria; Blood cultures

stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of cardiac tamponade?
explanation: Tamponade raises all diastolic pressures, so the JVP is high (blunted y descent); a collapsed JVP means hypovolaemia. Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds.

stem: A patient who had a mitral valve replacement 3 weeks ago develops infective endocarditis. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within weeks of surgery) is mostly coagulase-negative staphylococci or S. aureus acquired peri-operatively.

stem: A middle-aged woman has fatigue, abdominal distension and leg swelling. Her pulse is 112/min, regular and of small volume, there is an early diastolic sound (pericardial knock), and the chest X-ray shows calcification around the heart shadow. Chronic constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which finding is AGAINST this diagnosis?
explanation: Constriction causes systemic congestion (raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, early ascites, hepatomegaly) with clear lungs, so prominent breathlessness argues against it.

stem: All of the following are features of myocarditis EXCEPT:
explanation: Myocarditis gives chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmia and raised troponin; a rub means associated pericarditis. Cardiac MRI is the key test.

stem: The age group most commonly affected by acute rheumatic fever is:
explanation: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and peaks at 5–15 years; it is rare under 3 and uncommon in adults.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has central chest pain and fever, and a pericardial rub is heard. Which ECG abnormality is NOT typical of acute pericarditis?
option_C: T-wave inversion after the ST segments normalise
explanation: Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, then T inversion. Hyperacute T waves are the earliest sign of STEMI.

stem: A 22-year-old man has fever, night sweats and weight loss. There are linear (splinter) haemorrhages under the nails and a new pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Fever, weight loss, a new regurgitant murmur and splinter haemorrhages is infective endocarditis: 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, then echo.

stem: A 22-year-old man has fever, night sweats and weight loss. There are linear (splinter) haemorrhages under the nails and a new pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla. Which investigation should be performed first, before antibiotics are started?
explanation: Take ≥ 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics: they identify the organism and are a major Duke criterion; echo follows promptly.

stem: A 22-year-old man has fever, night sweats and weight loss. There are linear (splinter) haemorrhages under the nails and a new pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla. Three months later he develops right-sided weakness. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Embolisation of vegetations, most often to the brain, makes new focal weakness an embolic stroke; image urgently and consider early surgery.

stem: In infective endocarditis, which of the following is NOT an indication for surgery?
option_A: Persistent fever for more than 7 days despite antibiotics
explanation: Surgery in IE: heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, fungi) or large vegetations with emboli. Age is not an indication.

stem: A 51-year-old man with mitral valve prolapse and type 2 diabetes has had intermittent fever, night sweats and fatigue for 10 days, with mild exertional breathlessness and occasional palpitations. He recently had a dental extraction. T 38.9 °C, pulse 122/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, RR 22/min. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and tender erythematous nodules on his fingertips. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Subacute endocarditis on a prolapsing mitral valve after dental extraction is caused by oral viridans streptococci. S. aureus is acute and fulminant; S. epidermidis infects prosthetic valves.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Viridans streptococci; Dental procedures

stem: A 51-year-old man with mitral valve prolapse and type 2 diabetes has had intermittent fever, night sweats and fatigue for 10 days, with mild exertional breathlessness and occasional palpitations. He recently had a dental extraction. T 38.9 °C, pulse 122/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, RR 22/min. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and tender erythematous nodules on his fingertips. Which of the following findings is most specific to this disease?
explanation: Only the vascular signs (splinter haemorrhages, like his Osler nodes) point specifically to endocarditis; fever, dyspnoea, tachycardia and splenomegaly are non-specific.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Splinter haemorrhages; Osler nodes

stem: A 51-year-old man with mitral valve prolapse and type 2 diabetes has had intermittent fever, night sweats and fatigue for 10 days, with mild exertional breathlessness and occasional palpitations. He recently had a dental extraction. T 38.9 °C, pulse 122/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, RR 22/min. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and tender erythematous nodules on his fingertips. The initial step of management should include:
explanation: Take three sets of blood cultures, then start empirical IV antibiotics and tailor to the organism. Surgery is for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or large emboli.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Blood cultures; Empirical antibiotics

stem: A 51-year-old man with mitral valve prolapse and type 2 diabetes has had intermittent fever, night sweats and fatigue for 10 days, with mild exertional breathlessness and occasional palpitations. He recently had a dental extraction. T 38.9 °C, pulse 122/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, RR 22/min. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and tender erythematous nodules on his fingertips. Which of the following is the most serious potential complication of this disease?
explanation: Leaflet or chordal destruction causes acute regurgitation and heart failure, the commonest cause of death in IE and the main reason for urgent surgery. Pulmonary emboli come from tricuspid IE.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Acute heart failure; Complications of endocarditis

stem: A 23-year-old man who has recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection presents to the AE department with chest pain made worse on breathing. On examination he is febrile, and has a ‘scratchy’ sound heard on auscultation in systole and diastole. ECG reveals widespread saddle-shaped ST segment elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A previously fit and well 30-year-old gym instructor is admitted to hospital following a stab wound to the left side of his chest. He has a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg and heart rate of 125 beats/min. Breath sounds are present throughout but his HSs are muffled. His JVP appears raised. What additional feature is most likely to be present in this patient?
option_A: Diastolic murmur over the praecordium radiating towards the left axilla
option_D: An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration
option_E: An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during expiration
answer_text: An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with chest pain. She comments that the pain is worse on inspiration but is relieved by leaning forward. Her past medical history includes breast carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward is acute pericarditis; with breast cancer consider malignant involvement and check echo.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with known breast cancer has increasing breathlessness. Heart sounds are soft and the apex beat cannot be felt. Which investigation is most likely to make the diagnosis?
explanation: Soft heart sounds and an impalpable apex in a patient with cancer suggest a malignant pericardial effusion; echocardiography confirms it and shows tamponade physiology.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends the emergency department with worsening breathlessness and fevers. The medical team suspects a diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Which of the following is the most suggestive feature of infective endocarditis?
explanation: A new or changing regurgitant murmur with fever is the most suggestive feature of IE; new regurgitation on echo is a major Duke criterion.

stem: A 35-year-old man who injects drugs has night sweats and weight loss. He is febrile (38.5 °C) and infective endocarditis is suspected. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: In people who inject drugs, S. aureus is the commonest cause of IE, usually tricuspid with septic pulmonary emboli; cover MRSA where prevalent.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Injecting drug use; Staphylococcus aureus

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with night sweats. On examination you detect a systolic murmur. She has severe gum and tooth decay and has recently had two teeth taken out. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for her condition?

A 40-year-old man with an underlying cardiac condition is about to have root canal treatment and a new crown fitted. For which of the following conditions is antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis recommended?
option_C: Previous coronary artery bypass grafting involving the use of the internal mammary arteries
option_D: Presence of a dual chamber pacemaker
explanation: Prophylaxis only for highest risk (prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD). ASD, VSD, CABG and pacemakers do not qualify.

stem: Some clinical features of infective endocarditis result from immune-complex deposition. Which of the following is NOT an immune-complex phenomenon?
explanation: Immune-complex phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid factor. Splenic abscess is embolic (vascular), like Janeway lesions.

stem: A 35-year-old man complains of fatigue, night sweats and weight loss. On examination you note a systolic murmur and evidence of splenomegaly. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?

A previously well 45-year-old man has fevers and malaise. He has multiple splinter haemorrhages and a systolic murmur, and infective endocarditis is suspected. Regarding the modified Duke criteria, which statement is INCORRECT?
option_A: The presence of Osler's nodes is a minor criterion
option_B: A positive rheumatoid factor is a minor criterion
option_C: Echocardiographic evidence of new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve is a major criterion
option_D: A single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or a phase I IgG titre > 1:800 is a major criterion
option_E: A definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria
answer_text: A definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria
explanation: Definite IE (modified Duke): 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor. Three minor criteria give only 'possible' endocarditis.

stem: A 45-year-old teacher with known mitral valve prolapse presents to his GP with a 2-week history of fevers, rigors, chest pain and breathlessness. He recently underwent a tooth extraction. On examination he is febrile with multiple splinter haemorrhages. A systolic murmur is heard and appears to have increased in intensity since his last GP visit. What is the most likely causative agent in this case?
explanation: Subacute IE on a prolapsing mitral valve after dental work is most likely viridans streptococci from the mouth; benzylpenicillin-based treatment.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Viridans streptococci; Dental procedures

stem: A 21-year-old man has a recent influenza-like illness with fever, myalgia and headache. He then develops pleuritic-type chest discomfort and breathlessness. His pulse is 105/min and regular and BP is 105/60 mmHg; the JVP is not raised. The first and second heart sounds are normal, and a loud, harsh to-and-fro sound is heard in both systole and diastole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A to-and-fro scratchy sound in systole and diastole after a viral illness is a pericardial rub (acute viral pericarditis); treat with NSAID plus colchicine.
topics: Acute pericarditis; Pericardial friction rub; Viral infection

stem: What is the appropriate initial treatment for the symptoms of acute pericarditis?
explanation: Acute pericarditis: high-dose aspirin or ibuprofen tapered over 1–2 weeks plus colchicine for 3 months (halves recurrence). Steroids are second line.

stem: Which of the following conditions may result in chronic pericardial constriction?
explanation: TB is the commonest cause of constriction worldwide; others are cardiac surgery, radiotherapy, viral/idiopathic pericarditis and connective tissue disease.

stem: A 75-year-old male smoker has a 6-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue, and recently his ankles swell in the afternoon. His pulse is 100/min and regular and BP is 92/60 mmHg. The JVP is raised and rises on inspiration, the heart sounds are quiet with no added sounds, and there is bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. The chest X-ray shows apparent cardiomegaly with a globular cardiac silhouette. A pericardial effusion is suspected. Which of the following statements is true?
option_A: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy
option_B: A pericardial rub is always heard if the effusion is large
option_C: An ECG is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis
option_D: High-dose diuretic therapy will resolve the pericardial effusion
option_E: In symptomatic patients, cardiac surgery is required to remove the pericardial fluid
answer_text: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy
explanation: A large effusion in an older smoker suggests malignancy; a rub is often absent, echo confirms, and diuretics do not help. Drain and send cytology.

stem: An 18-year-old man has sudden-onset sharp chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration or lying flat and relieved by sitting forward and taking shallow breaths. Acute pericarditis is suspected. What is the most specific ECG change in acute pericarditis?
explanation: PR depression (with PR elevation in aVR) is the most specific ECG sign of pericarditis; ST elevation is diffuse, concave and without reciprocal change.

stem: In patients with a pericardial effusion, what is the most important clinical sign to determine whether there is cardiac tamponade?
explanation: Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall > 10 mmHg) is the key bedside sign that an effusion is causing tamponade; echo confirms.

stem: A 50-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever and influenza-like symptoms. He has a heart rate of 105/min and a wide pulse pressure (BP 140/45 mmHg). A murmur was suspected but is not heard on repeat examination. There is no evidence of chest or urinary infection. What are these findings most compatible with?
option_C: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve
option_D: Infective endocarditis affecting the tricuspid valve
answer_text: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve
explanation: Prolonged fever with a new wide pulse pressure suggests aortic valve endocarditis with acute AR; its soft short murmur is easily missed.

stem: An 18 year old woman presents with a sore throat and suspected acute rheumatic fever. Which of the following is a minor manifestation of acute rheumatic fever?
explanation: Jones minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR. Carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and nodules are major.

stem: An 18 year old woman has a raised C-reactive protein, a rash consistent with erythema marginatum and pyrexia. However, the clinician remains uncertain about the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever. Rapid response to which treatment will help to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: Rheumatic arthritis responds dramatically to aspirin within 24–48 h; a rapid response supports the diagnosis.

stem: A 65-year-old man has a 4-week history of general malaise and lethargy. Two courses of antibiotics have temporarily improved his symptoms, but overall he continues to deteriorate, and his GP notes that he has become anaemic. He is admitted with fever; blood cultures are taken and an echocardiogram shows a mass on the mitral valve. Which organism is most likely to grow from his blood cultures?
explanation: An indolent illness with anaemia and partial response to antibiotics is subacute native-valve IE, classically viridans streptococci.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a 4-week illness of malaise, anaemia and fever has a mitral valve mass on echocardiography. Before the blood culture results are known, a junior doctor examines him for signs of endocarditis. Which of the following is the commonest finding?
explanation: Microscopic haematuria (glomerulonephritis or renal emboli) is commoner in IE than splinters, Osler nodes or Roth spots; dipstick the urine.

stem: Which of the following is bad prognostic sign regarding acute rheumatic fever:
Which of the following is not a feature of cardiac tamponade?

A patient with acute myocardial infarction came with repeated severe dyspnea. On examination PR was 112 beats/min with pulsus paradoxus, BP 90/55 mmHg, JVP was elevated, and heart sounds were muffled. The next day, what is the most likely diagnosis?
A middle-aged woman presents with fatigue, abdominal distension and light-headedness. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which of the following findings would be LEAST typical of this diagnosis?
explanation: Constriction gives a raised JVP with rapid y descent, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock and ascites. Pulsus paradoxus is the hallmark of tamponade.
topics: Constrictive pericarditis; Pulsus paradoxus; Kussmaul's sign

stem: A 55-year-old man has progressive shortness of breath and ankle oedema. He is originally from Africa and probably had tuberculosis many years ago. His BP is 105/55 mmHg, the JVP is raised 5 cm with a rapid y descent, and there is marked ankle oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Right-sided congestion with a steep y descent after previous TB is constrictive pericarditis; CT/MRI shows thickening or calcification.
topics: Constrictive pericarditis; Tuberculosis; Jugular venous pressure

stem: Dressler syndrome results from which of the following?
explanation: Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI (antimyocardial antibodies); treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.

stem: A patient with history of mitral valve replacement 3 weeks ago developed infective endocarditis. Which of the following microorganisms is responsible for this endocarditis?
Which manifestation of acute rheumatic fever is responsible for its long-term organ damage?
explanation: Carditis is the only rheumatic fever manifestation causing permanent damage (chronic rheumatic valve disease); arthritis, rash and chorea resolve.
topics: Acute rheumatic fever; Rheumatic heart disease

stem: Which of the following conditions carries the LOWEST risk of infective endocarditis?
option_A: Rheumatic heart disease with mitral regurgitation
explanation: MVP without regurgitation has near-population endocarditis risk. Prosthetic valves and previous IE carry the highest risk.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Mitral valve prolapse; Risk factors

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with pyrexia and found to have infective endocarditis. Which one of the following is most associated with a good prognosis?
explanation: Viridans streptococcal native-valve IE is usually penicillin-sensitive with > 90% cure. S. aureus, prosthetic and culture-negative IE do worse.

stem: Which one of the following is bad prognostic sign of rheumatic fever

A 75-year-old woman with widely metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer is admitted to intensive care with BP 73/52 mmHg after 3–5 days of fatigue and worsening breathlessness. Her neck veins are distended, and the chest X-ray shows a massive, water-bottle-shaped heart shadow without new pulmonary infiltrates. Which additional finding is most likely on examination?
option_A: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration
option_B: Lack of fall of the jugular venous pressure with inspiration
option_C: Late diastolic murmur with opening snap
option_E: Rapid y-descent of jugular venous pressure tracing
answer_text: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration
explanation: Hypotension, distended neck veins and a water-bottle heart in lung cancer is malignant tamponade, so pulsus paradoxus is expected. Kussmaul sign suggests constriction.
topics: Cardiac tamponade; Pulsus paradoxus; Malignant pericardial effusion

stem: A 27-year-old doctor has had 1 week of cough, coryza and low-grade fever. Today he develops rapidly escalating chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration. His 12-lead ECG is shown. His BP is normal, he is now afebrile, and the JVP is not raised, but he is uncomfortable from the pain. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_A: Administer aspirin, intravenous heparin, sublingual nitroglycerin, and clopidogrel
option_B: Emergently obtain transthoracic echocardiogram with possible pericardiocentesis
option_C: Emergently perform coronary angiography to evaluate for acute myocardial infarction
explanation: Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression after a viral illness, no high-risk features: outpatient ibuprofen plus colchicine.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with chest pain following a week of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her cardiac examination reveals distant heart sounds and her chest X-ray shows an increased cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely cause of the increased cardiac silhouette?
explanation: Distant heart sounds with a newly enlarged globular silhouette after a viral illness is pericardial effusion (> 200–250 mL); echo confirms and checks for tamponade.
topics: Pericardial effusion; Acute pericarditis; Chest X-ray

stem: Based on her history and exam, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Which investigation is most important to confirm the diagnosis?
In a patient with a life-threatening pericardial effusion causing hemodynamic compromise, what is the best mode of therapy?
A 32-year-old woman presents with a history of fever, chills, night sweats, and a pansystolic murmur over the apex radiating to the axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which investigation is most indicated to confirm the diagnosis of infective endocarditis in this patient?
Which of the following clinical signs is characteristically associated with infective endocarditis?
explanation: Janeway lesions (painless palmar/plantar haemorrhagic macules from septic emboli) are characteristic of endocarditis; a minor Duke criterion.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has fever, chills, night sweats and a new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Infective endocarditis is suspected and three sets of blood cultures have been taken. She is unwell but haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
option_B: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results
answer_text: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results
explanation: After blood cultures, start empirical high-dose IV bactericidal antibiotics, then tailor to the organism for 4–6 weeks. Surgery only for specific indications.

stem: A 55-year-old man attends the emergency department with a dry cough and severe chest pain that began this morning. Two months ago he had an inferior myocardial infarction treated with a right coronary artery stent. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia and takes aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin and enalapril. Temperature 38.5 °C, pulse 92/min, respiratory rate 22/min, BP 130/80 mmHg. A high-pitched scratching sound is heard best with him leaning forward in expiration; the rest of the examination is normal. The ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and troponin I is 0.2 µg/L (0.2 ng/mL). What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Fever, pleuritic pain, rub and diffuse ST elevation weeks after MI is Dressler syndrome; early infarct pericarditis occurs within 1–3 days.
topics: Dressler syndrome; Post-cardiac injury syndrome; Acute pericarditis

stem: A 41-year-old man with fever and transient pain in both knees and elbows. The right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the week prior to presentation. On physical examination, the patient has a low-grade fever. He has a III/ VI, high-pitched, apical systolic murmur with radiation to the axilla, as well as a soft, mid-diastolic murmur heard at the base. A tender nodule is palpated over an extensor tendon of the hand. There are pink erythematous lesions over the abdomen, some with central clearing. The following laboratory values are obtained: Hct 42%, WBC 12,000/µL with 80% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 20% lymphocytes, ESR 60 mm/h. Which investigation is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?

A 12-year-old girl has high fever and swelling of the left ankle and knee 3 weeks after a sore throat. Two years ago she developed breathlessness and a generalised rash when given dicloxacillin for a skin infection. Temperature 38.8 °C, pulse 87/min, BP 98/62 mmHg. The left ankle and knee are swollen and tender with limited movement, and a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
explanation: Rheumatic fever: eradicate group A strep with penicillin/amoxicillin; with penicillin anaphylaxis use a macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin).
topics: Acute rheumatic fever; Penicillin allergy; Macrolides

stem: A 25-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse develops low grade fever, malaise, and night sweats after a dental procedure. Which investigation is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?
A nurse prepares a list of patients for dental procedures. Which patient is most likely to ben efit from antibiotic prophylaxis?
A 43-year-old man with HIV who injects drugs presents with fever, night sweats and a holosystolic murmur that increases on inspiration. Which complication of his condition is most likely?
option_C: Painful nodules on the finger pads
option_D: Painless haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles
explanation: IE in people who inject drugs is usually tricuspid (murmur louder on inspiration) and embolises to the lungs as septic pulmonary emboli.
topics: Right-sided endocarditis; Septic pulmonary emboli; Injecting drug use

stem: Blood cultures and TEE in a patient with tricuspid vegetations reveal the organism responsible for IE. Which organism is most likely?

A 34-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has fatigue, exertional breathlessness, low-grade fevers and splinter haemorrhages. He was started on empirical IV vancomycin, and blood cultures now grow Cardiobacterium hominis. What is the next step in management?
explanation: Cardiobacterium hominis is a HACEK organism, often beta-lactamase-producing: switch to ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (6 for prosthetic valves).

stem: A 64-year-old man admitted 7 days ago with pancreatitis after abdominal trauma develops fever, breathlessness and a new holosystolic murmur. There is purulent discharge from his central venous catheter site. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: Line-associated healthcare IE is most often S. aureus; remove the line, take cultures and give vancomycin until MRSA is excluded.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Healthcare-associated infection; Staphylococcus aureus

stem: A 41-year-old man with IV drug use presents with a 10-day history of weakness, headache, and night sweats, and a holosystolic murmur on exam. What is the most likely consequence of his condition?
option_A: Painless macules and papules on palms and soles

stem: At autopsy, multiple small sterile nodules composed of immune complexes, fibrin and thrombus are found on both surfaces of the mitral valve, including the ventricular side. In which patient would these findings most likely be found?
option_A: A 71-year-old man with acute high fever and nail-bed haemorrhages
option_C: A 41-year-old woman with a facial rash and non-erosive arthritis
option_D: A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman who injects drugs
option_E: A 6-year-old girl with subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum
answer_text: A 41-year-old woman with a facial rash and non-erosive arthritis
explanation: Sterile vegetations on both sides of the mitral leaflets are Libman–Sacks endocarditis of SLE (malar rash, non-erosive arthritis), especially with antiphospholipid antibodies.

stem: Three weeks after a transurethral resection of the prostate, a 70-year-old man has fever, malaise and limb pain. He has subungual petechiae, tender red papules on the fingers and a new holosystolic murmur. Blood cultures grow a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: IE after a urological procedure with a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus is Enterococcus faecalis: amoxicillin plus ceftriaxone or gentamicin ~6 weeks.

stem: A 77-year-old man is under review on the ward after having a pacemaker inserted earlier that day. He initially presented to the emergency department two days ago with recurrent episodes of collapse, leading to a diagnosis of sick sinus syndrome. In the past hour, he has reported increasing chest discomfort and developed hypotension. On examination, he is cool and clammy peripherally, his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is at 5 cm above the sternal angle, and his heart sounds are indistinct. His current heart rate is 72 bpm with a blood pressure of 88/56 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chest discomfort, hypotension, raised JVP and quiet heart sounds hours after pacing suggest lead perforation with haemopericardium/tamponade.

stem: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department with increasing breathlessness over 7 days, much worse in the last 24 hours, and light-headedness. He has left shoulder pain and mild ongoing chest pain that improves on sitting up. Five weeks ago he had an anterior STEMI treated with a stent to the left anterior descending artery. The JVP is raised, peripheral pulses are weak and the heart sounds are muffled; the chest is clear with good air entry. Pulse 101/min regular, BP 89/50 mmHg (equal in both arms), temperature 36.0 °C, SpO2 95% on air, respiratory rate 20/min. The ECG shows Q waves in V1–V3 without ST change and small-amplitude complexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and low voltages weeks after MI is tamponade from a post-MI effusion: urgent echo and pericardiocentesis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, non-radiating central chest pain that eases on expiration. Cardiorespiratory examination is normal apart from a heart rate of 96/min. The ECG shows widespread ST elevation in the anterior, inferior and lateral leads. FBC and U&E are normal; troponin I is 0.8 µg/L (reference < 0.2 µg/L). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Multi-territory ST elevation with pleuritic pain in a young woman is pericarditis; a small troponin rise means myopericarditis, not ACS.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with several days of progressive chest pain, pleuritic in nature and worse on lying down. He achieves some relief from the pain by sitting forward. On examination, a pericardial rub is noted when leaning forward. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following electrocardiogram (ECG) findings is most specific?
Which one of the following features is not part of the modified Duke criteria used in the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
explanation: A prolonged PR is a Jones (rheumatic fever) criterion, not a Duke criterion; in IE new conduction block may signal an aortic root abscess.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week. She had an aortic valve replacement 2 years ago. According to current ESC guidance, what antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended before this procedure?
explanation: A prosthetic valve is highest risk: ESC/AHA advise single-dose oral amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before extraction. NICE advises against routine prophylaxis.
topics: Endocarditis prophylaxis; Prosthetic heart valve; Amoxicillin

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. On examination, you note several Janeway lesions on his hands. There is a collapsing pulse and you note an early diastolic murmur. You take multiple sets of blood cultures and commence the patient on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed infective endocarditis. A trans-thoracic echo identifies large vegetation on the aortic valve with associated aortic regurgitation. You note the patient has a background of metastatic colorectal cancer and is currently receiving palliative chemotherapy. In light of the patient’s past medical history, which of the following organisms are most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) IE is strongly linked to colorectal neoplasia, so isolating it should prompt colonoscopy.
topics: Infective endocarditis; Streptococcus gallolyticus; Colorectal cancer

stem: A 60-year-old man who had a mitral valve replacement 3 years ago presents acutely with high fever, rigors and fatigue 1 week after a large boil (furuncle) on his thigh. Echocardiography shows a new vegetation on the prosthetic valve, and three sets of blood cultures are taken. Which organism is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Late prosthetic valve IE (> 1 year) resembles native IE; an acute illness after a furuncle points to S. aureus, which usually needs rifampicin and early surgery.

stem: Two weeks after hospital discharge for documented myocardial infarction, a 65-year-old returns to your office concerned about low-grade fever and pleuritic chest pain. There is no associated shortness of breath. Lungs are clear to auscultation and the heart is free of murmur, gallop, or rub. ECG is unchanged from the last one in the hospital. Which therapy is most likely to be effective?
explanation: Fever and pleuritic pain 2 weeks after MI with no new ECG change is Dressler syndrome: aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine. Anticoagulation risks haemopericardium.

stem: A 35-year-old man has substernal chest pain aggravated by inspiration and relieved by sitting up. The lung fields are clear and the heart sounds are somewhat distant. The chest X-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. What is the best next step in evaluation?
explanation: Pericarditic pain with distant heart sounds and an enlarged cardiac silhouette suggests pericarditis with an effusion, and transthoracic echocardiography is the investigation of choice: it confirms and sizes the effusion and shows whether there is tamponade physiology. A lateral decubitus film is used for pleural, not pericardial, fluid, and serial ECGs are non-specific. Cardiac catheterisation and stress imaging are for coronary disease and have no role here.

stem: A 42-year-old female with acute pericarditis develops jugular venous distention and hypotension. The ECG shows electrical alternans. Which of the following is the most likely additional physical finding?
option_A: Basilar rales halfway up both posterior lung fields

stem: An 18-year-old man has fever and flitting pain in both knees and elbows; the right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the previous week. He has a low-grade fever, a grade III/VI high-pitched apical systolic murmur radiating to the axilla and a soft mid-diastolic murmur at the base. A tender nodule is felt over an extensor tendon of the hand, and there are pink erythematous lesions on the abdomen, some with central clearing. Haematocrit 0.42, WBC 12 × 10⁹/L (80% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes), ESR 60 mm/h. His ECG is shown. Which test is most critical to the diagnosis?
explanation: Migratory arthritis, carditis, nodules and erythema marginatum meet Jones criteria, which also need evidence of recent strep infection: a raised ASO (or anti-DNase B) titre.
topics: Acute rheumatic fever; Antistreptolysin O; Jones criteria

stem: A 45-year-old man with newly diagnosed hypertension is referred for baseline investigations. Which test is NOT routinely indicated?
explanation: New hypertension work-up: U&E/eGFR, urine ACR and dipstick, HbA1c, lipids, ECG and fundoscopy. CT aortography is only for a specific clue.

stem: On routine examination a patient with hypertension has a blood pressure of 165/105 mmHg. According to the European (ESH/ESC) and British Hypertension Society classification, this is:
explanation: ESH/ESC grades: 1 = 140–159/90–99, 2 = 160–179/100–109, 3 = ≥ 180/≥ 110 mmHg; 165/105 is grade 2. Confirm with ABPM/HBPM.

stem: Which of the following drugs is NOT first-line treatment for hypertension?
Which of the following drug classes is NOT first-line antihypertensive therapy?
explanation: First-line: ACEi/ARB, dihydropyridine CCB or thiazide-like diuretic. Beta-blockers are used only for compelling indications (angina, MI, HFrEF, AF).

stem: All of the following endocrine diseases are recognised causes of secondary hypertension EXCEPT:
explanation: Addison's disease causes salt loss and hypotension. Conn's, acromegaly and 11β/17α-hydroxylase CAH cause hypertension.

stem: A man has been diagnosed with essential hypertension by his GP and is about to start treatment. Which of the following statements about the treatment of essential hypertension is true?
option_A: Alpha-blockers such as prazosin rarely cause postural hypotension
option_B: Patients of African-Caribbean origin respond well to ACE inhibitor monotherapy
option_C: ACE inhibitors are safe in bilateral renal artery stenosis
option_D: Treatment with bendroflumethiazide may cause hypokalaemia
option_E: ACE inhibitors commonly cause ankle swelling
answer_text: Treatment with bendroflumethiazide may cause hypokalaemia
explanation: Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, gout and hyperglycaemia. Ankle swelling is from dihydropyridine CCBs, not ACE inhibitors.
topics: Thiazide diuretics; Hypokalaemia; Antihypertensive adverse effects

stem: A 50-year-old man has a persistently raised blood pressure of about 185/110 mmHg. He has had headaches for a few weeks but is otherwise well. His ECG shows increased QRS voltages with ST depression in the left ventricular leads, and fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping without haemorrhages or papilloedema. What is the most appropriate management?
option_A: Advise weight loss and see again in 2 months
option_C: Hospitalize and give urgent IV antihypertensive medication
option_D: Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 2 months
option_E: Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days
answer_text: Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days
explanation: Grade 3 hypertension with LVH and grade 2 retinopathy but no acute features: start oral treatment now and review within days.
topics: Severe hypertension; Left ventricular hypertrophy; Hypertensive retinopathy

stem: A 50-year-old white man sees his GP for a blood pressure check, having recently been diagnosed with essential hypertension. His only other condition is type 2 diabetes mellitus without end-organ damage, well controlled on oral hypoglycaemic agents. His blood pressure has remained about 145/90 mmHg despite 3 months of diet and exercise. Which is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?
explanation: In type 2 diabetes NICE starts an ACE inhibitor at any age (ARB if Black or ACEi-intolerant); add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic next.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a mild headache. He is known to have poorly controlled hypertension and is on multiple antihypertensive medications. On examination his blood pressure is 205/110 mmHg and there is no evidence of end-organ involvement. His headache is still present but there is no focal neurology identified. Which of the following is the least appropriate in the management of this patient’s blood pressure?
option_A: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department
option_B: Adjust treatment and follow-up within 24 to 48 hours of presentation in the community
option_C: Initiate a maintenance dose of an oral medication before discharge
option_D: Consider a short observation period before discharge
option_E: Discharge the patient, emphasizing the importance of close follow-up and compliance with medications
answer_text: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department
explanation: Hypertensive urgency (no acute organ damage) is lowered gradually with oral drugs; rapid ED reduction risks stroke and ischaemia.

stem: A 55-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with hypertension and commenced on treatment. He attends his GP to find out more about the condition. Which of the following is the commonest cause of hypertension?
explanation: About 90–95% of hypertension is primary (essential) with no single cause; secondary causes make up only 5–10%.

stem: A 63-year-old retired doctor presents with nausea and headaches. His past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus. On examination you note his blood pressure is 165/76 mmHg. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
A 65-year-old hypertensive patient is reviewed in the outpatient clinic complaining of visual disturbances. On examination you note flame-shaped haemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Keith–Wagener: 1 narrowing/silver wiring, 2 AV nipping, 3 flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, 4 papilloedema.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with headache. On auscultation he has a loud second heart sound. Which of the following could explain this finding?
explanation: Systemic hypertension makes the aortic valve close forcefully, giving a loud A2. Aortic regurgitation softens A2.
topics: Loud second heart sound; Essential hypertension

stem: A 35-year-old executive has a reproducible blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg and is referred to clinic to look for an underlying cause. What is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension?
explanation: Renal disease (parenchymal and renovascular) is the commonest secondary cause; primary aldosteronism is the commonest endocrine cause.
topics: Secondary hypertension; Renal disease; Primary aldosteronism

stem: A 60-year-old man is referred by his family doctor because his blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite four drugs, and a secondary cause is suspected. What is the commonest cause of poorly controlled hypertension?
explanation: Apparent resistant hypertension is most often non-adherence (pseudo-resistance); exclude it, white-coat effect and NSAIDs before seeking secondary causes.

stem: Which of the following drugs is not first line antihypertensive?
Which of the following is not considered as a first line treatment for hypertension?

A 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is reviewed in the diabetes clinic. Her blood pressure was 145/95 mmHg and lisinopril was started. Baseline blood tests showed potassium 4.5 mmol/L, creatinine 159 µmol/L (1.8 mg/dL) and eGFR 47 mL/min/1.73 m². Three months later, potassium is 4.9 mmol/L, creatinine 177 µmol/L (2.0 mg/dL) and eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73 m². What is the most appropriate course of action?
option_D: Stop lisinopril and arrange investigations to exclude renal artery stenosis
explanation: A creatinine rise < 30% (eGFR fall < 25%) with K⁺ < 6 after an ACE inhibitor is expected; continue the drug and monitor.
topics: ACE inhibitors; Renal function monitoring; Hypertension in diabetes

stem: All of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of hypertension are true EXCEPT:
option_A: Among people aged 60 years or older, average systolic blood pressure is higher in women than in men
option_B: Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life
option_C: Systolic blood pressure continues to rise with age throughout adult life
option_D: In industrialised nations, blood pressure rises steadily during the first two decades of life
option_E: Worldwide, around one-third of adults aged 30–79 years have hypertension
answer_text: Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life
explanation: Systolic BP rises throughout life; diastolic plateaus or falls after 50–60 as arteries stiffen, hence isolated systolic hypertension in the elderly.

stem: Disease of which organ is the most common cause of mortality in hypertensive patients?
explanation: Heart disease (CHD, LVH, heart failure) is the commonest cause of death in hypertension; stroke is most tightly linked to BP level.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has had hypertension that is difficult to control since the age of 26 years, requiring increasing doses of medication. Her current regimen is labetalol 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 40 mg once daily, clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily and amlodipine 5 mg once daily. She appears well; blood pressure is 168/100 mmHg and heart rate 84 bpm. Cardiac examination is unremarkable, peripheral pulses are good and there is no oedema. There is no hirsutism, abnormal fat distribution or genital abnormality. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L and fasting glucose 6.3 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis despite an ACE inhibitor suggests primary aldosteronism (Conn's); check aldosterone:renin ratio.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has resistant hypertension despite four antihypertensive drugs. She has no cushingoid features. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L and bicarbonate 32 mmol/L. What is the best initial test to establish the diagnosis?
explanation: Screen for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone:renin ratio (correct K⁺ first); confirm by suppression test, then adrenal CT and venous sampling.

stem: A 65-year-old engineer who never sees a doctor and takes no medications is brought to the emergency department with a headache that has worsened over the past day and confusion that began an hour ago. Blood pressure is 230/140 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm and oxygen saturation 95%. He moves all limbs equally and has no cranial nerve deficit but is clearly delirious. The apex beat is forceful and displaced with an S4 gallop; the lungs are clear. Creatinine is 212 µmol/L (2.4 mg/dL), urine shows 2+ protein and haematuria, haematocrit is 0.32 with a normal platelet count, and the blood film shows schistocytes. Urgent brain MRI shows old microvascular changes but no acute infarct or haemorrhage. Which is the most reasonable approach to his blood pressure?
option_C: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg followed by a continuous infusion, aiming for a mean arterial pressure of about 125 mmHg in the first hour
answer_text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg followed by a continuous infusion, aiming for a mean arterial pressure of about 125 mmHg in the first hour
explanation: Malignant hypertension with encephalopathy and AKI: IV labetalol infusion, lowering MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the physiology of renal perfusion is true?
option_A: Because of tight precapillary regulation, the glomerular capillary endothelium is relatively shielded from pressure injury
option_B: Renal cortical blood flow is less than renal medullary blood flow, and together with the high metabolic needs of the cortex this leaves the cortex bordering on hypoxia
option_C: Renal perfusion is tightly matched to the metabolic needs of the kidney
option_D: Urinary albumin excretion predicts systemic atherosclerotic events and can appear years before clinical atherosclerotic disease
option_E: Venous blood returning from the renal cortex has a lower oxygen content than venous blood returning from the renal medulla
answer_text: Urinary albumin excretion predicts systemic atherosclerotic events and can appear years before clinical atherosclerotic disease
explanation: Albuminuria reflects generalised endothelial dysfunction and predicts CV events years ahead; hence urine ACR in the hypertension work-up.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding renal artery stenosis is true?
option_A: An abnormally reduced renal artery flow velocity by Doppler ultrasound is predictive of haemodynamically significant stenosis
option_B: Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical
option_C: In the general population, the presence of fibromuscular dysplasia is rare (<1% prevalence)
option_D: Levels of renin activity observed in renal artery stenosis are predictive of response to medical therapy
option_E: Usually the first clinical presentation of renal stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia is reduced renal function
answer_text: Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical
explanation: Early renal artery stenosis raises renin (renin-dependent hypertension); a significant stenosis increases peak Doppler velocity.
topics: Renal artery stenosis; Fibromuscular dysplasia; Renin

stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness and blurred optic disc margins (papilloedema) on fundoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Severe hypertension with papilloedema (acute organ damage) is a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension): admit for controlled IV treatment.

stem: How would you best label this patient’s hypertensive state?

A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness and papilloedema on fundoscopy. Which of the following is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive in this situation?
explanation: Hypertensive emergency needs a titratable IV drug (labetalol, nicardipine or nitroprusside); lower MAP by ≤ 20–25% over the first hours.
topics: Hypertensive emergency; Sodium nitroprusside; Intravenous antihypertensives

stem: A 45-year-old man with hypertension attends his GP for review. His last clinic reading was 156/80 mmHg, and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring shows a daytime average of 138/85 mmHg. He is already taking the maximum dose of ramipril. Which agent would be most appropriate to add?
explanation: Daytime ABPM 138/85 is above the < 135/85 target on maximum ACEi: step 2 adds a CCB or thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide).

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding hypertension in pregnancy is NOT correct?
option_A: A rise above booking readings of more than 30 mmHg systolic or 15 mmHg diastolic suggests hypertension
option_B: Pre-eclampsia occurs in around 5% of pregnancies
option_C: A urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension
option_D: A rise in blood pressure before 20 weeks suggests pre-existing hypertension
option_E: In gestational hypertension the blood pressure rises in the second half of pregnancy
answer_text: A urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension
explanation: Gestational hypertension is new BP ≥ 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria; proteinuria makes it pre-eclampsia. Labetalol is first line.
topics: Hypertension in pregnancy; Pre-eclampsia; Gestational hypertension

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with lethargy and a blood pressure of 250/150 mmHg. Her family say she complained of severe headache and visual disturbance earlier in the day. She has a history of asthma but no known kidney disease. Fundoscopy shows retinal haemorrhages. Which of the following is the best approach?
explanation: Hypertensive emergency with asthma: avoid labetalol; use a nitroprusside (or nicardipine) infusion, lowering MAP ≤ 25% in the first hour.

stem: A 50-year-old construction worker continues to have a blood pressure of 160/95 mmHg even after a third agent is added to his antihypertensive regimen. Physical examination is normal, electrolytes are normal and he takes no over-the-counter medications. Which of the following is the best next step?
option_C: Check chest x-ray for coarctation of the aorta
explanation: Before calling hypertension resistant, exclude non-adherence (pill count, drug levels) and confirm with ABPM; then seek secondary causes.

stem: You see a 45-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus for the first time in clinic. Her systolic blood pressure was above 140 mmHg at each of her last two clinic appointments, home blood pressure monitoring over the past week averaged 150/90 mmHg, and her clinic blood pressure today is 164/92 mmHg. What is the best next step in her blood pressure management?
option_A: Ask her to keep a written record of her home blood pressure and bring it to a return appointment
option_B: Advise a heart-healthy, low-sodium diet and refer her to a dietitian
option_C: Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to a heart-healthy diet
option_D: Prescribe a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker in addition to a heart-healthy diet
option_E: Arrange an echocardiogram to assess for end-organ damage
answer_text: Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to a heart-healthy diet
explanation: In diabetes with confirmed hypertension, start an ACE inhibitor alongside lifestyle advice (reduces albuminuria and nephropathy).
topics: Hypertension in diabetes; ACE inhibitors; Home blood pressure monitoring

stem: All of the following are antiplatelet drugs EXCEPT:
explanation: Warfarin is an anticoagulant (vitamin K epoxide reductase; factors II, VII, IX, X). Aspirin, clopidogrel and dipyridamole are antiplatelets.

stem: A 64-year-old female comes to your surgery with a past medical history of hypertension. She is on an ACE inhibitor as well as on a range of other medications. Which one of the following would be most likely to blunt the antihypertensive effects of an ACE inhibitor?
explanation: NSAIDs block renal prostaglandins, causing salt retention that blunts ACEi; with a diuretic they form the 'triple whammy' for AKI.

stem: Loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide have which of the following effects?
option_A: Diuresis due to inhibition of potassium and water reabsorption
option_B: Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption
option_C: Diuresis due to inhibition of water reabsorption only
option_D: Increased serum potassium levels due to enhanced distal tubule function
answer_text: Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption
explanation: Loop diuretics block the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the thick ascending limb, the most potent diuresis; they cause hypokalaemia and alkalosis.

stem: In which of the following situations are beta-adrenoceptor antagonists (beta-blockers) indicated?
explanation: Evidence-based beta-blockers cut mortality by about a third in chronic HFrEF (start low when euvolaemic). They are harmful in acute LVF and cardiogenic shock.
topics: Beta-blockers; Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

stem: A 71-year-old woman with hypertension presents with fatigue and rapid, irregular palpitations. She normally takes enalapril. Her pulse is irregularly irregular at 125 beats/min and her blood pressure is 128/86 mmHg; cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal. A 12-lead ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a poorly controlled ventricular rate and no other abnormality. Which of the following drugs is most suitable to control her heart rate?
explanation: AF rate control without heart failure: a beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB first (target < 110/min). Her CHA2DS2-VASc is 3, so anticoagulate too.

stem: Which of the following drugs is known to be effective in preventing stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation?
explanation: Oral anticoagulants cut AF stroke by ~two-thirds; apixaban beat warfarin with less bleeding (ARISTOTLE). Aspirin is not recommended.

stem: Which of the following antiplatelet drugs is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor?
explanation: Dipyridamole inhibits platelet phosphodiesterase and adenosine reuptake (raises cAMP). Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block P2Y12.

stem: All of the fallowing drugs improve the prognosis in heart failure Except:
Digoxin toxicity may be precipitated by all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Digoxin is renally excreted, so hepatic impairment matters little. Renal impairment, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia and amiodarone/verapamil precipitate toxicity.

stem: A 47-year-old man is admitted with an acute coronary syndrome. He has a history of peptic ulcer disease, and his cardiologist decides to use clopidogrel. What is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
option_D: Blocks ADP binding to its platelet P2Y12 receptor
answer_text: Blocks ADP binding to its platelet P2Y12 receptor
explanation: Clopidogrel is a prodrug (CYP2C19) that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Omeprazole may reduce its activation; prefer lansoprazole.

stem: Which of the following beta-blockers has been shown to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
explanation: Mortality benefit in HFrEF is proven for bisoprolol, carvedilol and metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF); short-acting metoprolol tartrate was inferior.
topics: Beta-blockers; Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; Metoprolol succinate

stem: All of the following drugs used in the acute management of ST-elevation myocardial infarction are correctly matched to their mechanism of benefit EXCEPT:
option_B: Abciximab – inhibition of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor
option_C: Beta-adrenergic antagonists – reduced myocardial oxygen consumption
option_D: Clopidogrel – inhibition of the platelet adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor
explanation: GTN is mainly a venodilator: its benefit is preload (not afterload) reduction. Avoid in hypotension, RV infarction and after PDE-5 inhibitors.

stem: A 48-year-old woman who has been treated for essential hypertension for 3 months presents with a persistent dry cough that has not responded to linctus or antibiotics. Which antihypertensive is most likely responsible?
explanation: ACE inhibitors cause dry cough in 10–15% (bradykinin accumulation), often weeks after starting; switch to an ARB.

stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with a transient ischaemic attack and commenced on clopidogrel. He already takes a statin. After a week of treatment, he presents to his GP complaining of severe diarrhoea. His GP suspects that clopidogrel is the cause and decides to switch him to combination antiplatelet treatment. This includes modified-release dipyridamole. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation: Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that also blocks adenosine reuptake; MR dipyridamole + aspirin is used after TIA/stroke if clopidogrel is not tolerated.

stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted following an acute coronary syndrome. He receives aspirin, clopidogrel, nitrates and morphine. His 6-month risk score is high and percutaneous coronary intervention is planned. He is therefore given intravenous tirofiban. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
option_A: Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2
explanation: Tirofiban (like eptifibatide, abciximab) blocks platelet GP IIb/IIIa, the final common pathway of aggregation; now mainly bail-out during PCI.
topics: Tirofiban; Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors; Acute coronary syndrome

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a hot, red, swollen leg. On examination, the left leg is tender and hot to touch, with evidence of a recent superficial laceration he sustained whilst gardening. His blood tests show raised inflammatory markers and a negative D-dimer. He is treated for cellulitis with clarithromycin due to being penicillin-allergic. Which of his regular medications should be concurrently suspended?
explanation: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and risking rhabdomyolysis; withhold the statin during the course.

stem: A 24-year-old man with no previous medical problems faints during exercise. He recovers quickly with no neurological deficit, and the ECG shows sinus rhythm. Which is the most useful diagnostic test?
explanation: Exertional syncope in a young person suggests structural disease (HCM, AS, anomalous coronaries); echocardiography is the key test.

stem: While on call, you are bleeped to see a man who has had a massive rectal bleed. He is drowsy, with a blood pressure of 65/40 mmHg and a pulse of 130 beats/min. While IV access is obtained, he arrests and CPR is started. The monitor shows organised QRS complexes, but there is no pulse. CPR continues and adrenaline 1 mg IV has just been given. What is the most important next step in management?
option_A: Rapid IV infusion of blood products via the major haemorrhage protocol
answer_text: Rapid IV infusion of blood products via the major haemorrhage protocol
explanation: PEA from massive haemorrhage will not reverse without volume: give blood products rapidly via the major haemorrhage protocol during CPR.
topics: Pulseless electrical activity; Hypovolaemia; Major haemorrhage

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with chest pain of several days' duration. The pain is sharp and stabbing, located at the left sternal border, and worsened by coughing and by palpation. She has no family history of heart disease and no diabetes, hypertension, smoking or hyperlipidaemia. Physical examination, ECG and chest X-ray are all normal. Which further investigation is indicated?
explanation: Sharp localised pain reproduced by palpation with normal ECG and CXR is musculoskeletal (costochondritis); no further tests, reassure and analgesia.

stem: In the management of cardiac arrest, which of the following most accurately describes basic life support (BLS)?
option_A: Administration of intravenous drugs and external defibrillation (the two ‘D’s)
option_C: Support of airway, breathing and circulation (ABC)
option_D: Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure (ABCDE)
option_E: Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure, treatment of fibrillation (ABCDEF)
answer_text: Support of airway, breathing and circulation (ABC)
explanation: BLS is support of airway, breathing and circulation without equipment: call for help, CPR 30:2 and early AED. Drugs belong to ALS.

stem: Which of the following statements is true of a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest?
option_A: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be carried out for 1 minute before the rhythm is reassessed
option_B: Intravenous amiodarone will restore cardiac output
option_C: It is initially managed with immediate defibrillation
option_D: Reversible causes include hyperthyroidism and hypercalcaemia
option_E: Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia
answer_text: Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia
explanation: PEA is non-shockable: CPR, adrenaline 1 mg ASAP then every 3–5 min, and treat the 4 Hs and 4 Ts (e.g. hypoxia, hypothermia).

stem: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour. Which of the following is true of atrial myxoma?
option_B: It occurs more commonly in the right atrium than in the left atrium
option_C: Surgery is not indicated because atrial myxomas are benign
option_D: Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke
option_E: The tumour commonly obstructs the aortic valve
answer_text: Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke
explanation: Atrial myxoma (75% left atrial, from the septum) can obstruct the mitral valve, embolise and cause fever/high ESR (IL-6); excise surgically.

stem: A patient presents with an incidental finding of a mass in the left atrium whilst undergoing an echocardiogram for hypertension. What is the most likely cardiac tumour in this situation?
explanation: The commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults is myxoma, a pedunculated LA mass on the septum; metastases are commoner overall.

stem: A 24-year-old man with no prior medical problems faints while having exercise. He has a quick recovery and has no neurologic deficits. ECG shows a normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most useful diagnostic test?
The following are recognized causes of prolonged PR interval except
Common causes of empyema are the following EXCEPT:
option_C: Rupture of sub-phrenic abscess through the diaphram

stem: A country with a population and environment very similar to China is moving from the first stage of the epidemiological transition ('pestilence and famine') to the second ('receding pandemics'). Regarding the expected pattern of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in this country, which of the following is true?
option_A: As this nation enters the stage of receding pandemics, you would expect the majority of CVD morbidity and mortality to be due to cardiomyopathies secondary to infectious agents
option_B: Each nation or geographical location progresses through the five stages of epidemiologic transition identically in regard to CVD risk
option_C: In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality
option_D: One would expect a very homogeneous epidemiologic pattern of CVD risk throughout this nation over time
option_E: You anticipate that CVD mortality will inexorably climb as this nation progresses through the five stages of the epidemiologic transition
answer_text: In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality
explanation: In China-like populations, as CVD peaks, stroke mortality exceeds coronary mortality (high hypertension and salt intake).

stem: A 67-year-old man complains of exertional breathlessness, leg oedema and waking at night acutely short of breath. You assess his volume status by examining the jugular venous pulse (JVP). Which of the following statements about JVP measurement is true?
option_A: If done properly, the angle of inclination matters little to the measurement of JVP
option_B: In normal patients, the JVP rises with inspiration due to the augmented volume loading of the right heart
option_C: Measurement of the elevation of the top of the JVP and the sternal inflection point (angle of Louis) will provide a highly accurate measurement of central venous pressure
option_D: The external jugular is preferred over the internal jugular vein due to its ease of visibility
option_E: Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal
answer_text: Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal
explanation: The RA lies ~5 cm below the sternal angle, so venous pulsation above the clavicle when sitting upright means a raised JVP.
topics: Jugular venous pressure; Physical examination; Heart failure

stem: Which of the following statements regarding blood pressure measurements is true?
option_A: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries
option_B: Systolic leg blood pressures are usually as much as 20 mmHg lower than arm blood pressures
option_C: The concept of 'white coat hypertension' (pressures measured in clinical settings significantly higher than elsewhere) has been shown to be a myth
option_D: An inter-arm systolic difference of 25 mmHg is within normal limits
option_E: Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small results in a marked underestimation of the true blood pressure
answer_text: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries
explanation: Pulse amplification makes systolic pressure higher and diastolic lower in distal arteries (leg SBP > arm, basis of the ABPI).
topics: Blood pressure measurement; White coat hypertension

stem: Which of the following statements regarding normal depolarization patterns of the heart is true?
option_A: Each normal sinus beat is initiated by spontaneous depolarization in the atrioventricular (AV) node
option_B: The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium
option_C: The right bundle branch bifurcates into an anterior and posterior fascicle
option_D: The SA node is unique in its ability to spontaneously depolarize, a quality known as automaticity
option_E: Within the ventricular myocardium, depolarization sweeps from epicardium to endocardium
answer_text: The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium
explanation: Normal conduction: SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles (endocardium to epicardium).

stem: All of the following ECG waveforms are matched correctly to the cardiac cycle that they represent EXCEPT:
option_B: PR interval – conduction from the atria through the AV node and His–Purkinje system
explanation: The P wave is atrial depolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden in the PR segment/QRS. T = ventricular repolarisation.

stem: Which of the following mean QRS vectors in the frontal electrocardiographic plane is matched appropriately to its designation?
option_E: All of the above are incorrect
explanation: Normal QRS axis is −30° to +90°, so −20° is normal; −30° to −90° is left axis deviation.

stem: What is the primary finding on the ECG shown?
