option_E: ST elevation in the anterior precordial leads; suspect anterior myocardial ischaemia
explanation: Sinus rhythm with normal axis, intervals, R-wave progression and no ST shift or tall T waves: a normal ECG.

stem: A large snowstorm hits your area on a Thursday, and the roads are largely impassible until the following Monday. On Monday morning, a 48-year-old man is brought by EMS to the emergency department after being found with altered mental status by a neighbor. He is obtunded and unable to provide a history. You note a left brachial artery hemodialysis fistula in place. His initial ECG is shown in Figure V-19. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities would you expect to find in this patient?
The SA node serves as the dominant pacemaker of the heart in normal sinus rhythm. What property of SA nodal cells allows it to act as the primary pacemaker?
option_A: Location near the superior lateral area of the right atrium
option_B: More numerous intercalated discs of any other myocardial tissue
option_D: Only cells with the ability to spontaneously depolarize
option_E: Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells
answer_text: Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells
explanation: SA node cells depolarise spontaneously in phase 4 (funny current) faster than any other tissue, so they reach threshold first and dominate.
topics: Sinoatrial node; Automaticity; Cardiac action potential

stem: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus and osteoporosis is brought to the emergency department after a fall at home, followed immediately by intense left hip pain. She was found by a neighbour after several hours and cannot remember whether she lost consciousness. She is exquisitely tender over the left hip, and the leg is shortened and externally rotated. Her mucous membranes are dry and skin turgor is reduced. Blood pressure is 170/80 mmHg and heart rate 130 beats/min. Her rhythm strip is shown (arrows mark P waves). What is the most appropriate first step for her tachycardia?
explanation: Multifocal/sinus tachycardia driven by pain, dehydration and hypoxia after a hip fracture: treat the cause (analgesia, IV fluids, oxygen).
topics: Multifocal atrial tachycardia; Sinus tachycardia; Hip fracture

stem: After a snowstorm has kept people indoors for 4 days, a middle-aged woman is brought to the emergency department obtunded. Her neighbours had not seen her since the snow started, and the police found her unconscious on the floor. A radial pulse is barely palpable and blood pressure is 60 mmHg systolic. She has an arteriovenous dialysis fistula in the left arm. Her ECG is shown. What electrolyte abnormality do you expect?
explanation: Missed dialysis with a sine-wave ECG is pre-terminal hyperkalaemia: IV calcium, insulin–glucose and salbutamol, then urgent dialysis.
topics: Hyperkalaemia; End-stage renal disease; Sine-wave ECG

stem: An 87-year-old man with an orthotopic heart transplant presents with a mild resting tachycardia. Which of the following best explains his heart rate response?
option_B: The denervated donor heart lacks resting vagal tone and responds only to circulating catecholamines
option_D: The transplant procedure permanently damages the SA node
answer_text: The denervated donor heart lacks resting vagal tone and responds only to circulating catecholamines
explanation: A denervated transplanted heart lacks vagal tone, so it runs at its intrinsic rate (~90–110/min) and responds only to circulating catecholamines.

stem: Regarding donor heart allocation in the United States, which of the following statements is true?
option_A: Allocation is based solely on the severity of the recipient’s illness
option_B: Donor hearts can be shared nationally without time constraints
option_C: There is a physiologic limit of approximately 3 hours of ischemic time, necessitating regional allocation
option_D: Time on the waiting list is not considered in allocation
answer_text: Time on the waiting list is not considered in allocation

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with breathlessness on exertion. He had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy 5 years ago and has done well apart from one cytomegalovirus reactivation in the first year. For the past 3 months, he has become limited by breathlessness on progressively less exertion. He is adamant that he has no chest pain or pressure. He takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisolone and is fully adherent. Echocardiography shows normal LV function and wall thickness, and his resting ECG shows sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Late after transplant, breathlessness without angina suggests cardiac allograft vasculopathy (denervated heart); diagnose by angiography.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attending a travel clinic complains of a painless swelling of one leg. The skin is thickened with a woody texture, and a bedside ultrasound shows patent veins without thrombus. You suspect lymphoedema due to the most common cause of secondary lymphoedema worldwide. What cause do you suspect?
option_A: Cancer involving the inguinal lymph nodes
explanation: Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) is the commonest cause of secondary lymphoedema worldwide; cancer treatment in high-income countries.

stem: A woman has chronic lymphoedema of the leg following recurrent streptococcal lymphangitis in childhood. She finds the swelling unsightly and asks about treatment. All of the following are reasonable treatments for chronic lymphoedema EXCEPT:
explanation: Lymphoedema is protein-rich fluid, so diuretics do not help. Use decongestive therapy, compression, skin care and exercise.

stem: Mr. George is a 52-year-old man with longstanding hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. He presents complaining of several months of breathlessness with exertion, acute episodes of shortness of breath when recumbent, and lower extremity edema. On examination, he has an elevated jugular venous pulse and an S4 on auscultation. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with a large left atrium. You suspect this patient has the syndrome of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Drugs targeting which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?

You are evaluating a 64-year-old woman with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. She presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. You note that she has gained 11 kg since her last cardiology appointment 2 months ago. Physical examination confirms findings associated with acute decompensated heart failure, including pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pulse, abdominal ascites, lower extremity edema, and a square wave blood pressure Valsalva response. Her extremities are warm, and blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 75 bpm. Her laboratory studies return with a sodium of 128 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL (which is increased from her prior level of 1.2 mg/dL). Chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar filling pattern consistent with pulmonary edema. What is the next most appropriate step?
option_C: Insert a large-bore central IV line and prepare for ultrafiltration
option_D: Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring
option_E: Start dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/min and titrate to a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hr

stem: Which of the following statements regarding nesiritide is true in patients with acute decompensated heart failure requiring invasive hemodynamic monitoring?
option_A: Nesiritide has no significant effect on blood pressure
option_B: Nesiritide improves renal perfusion in states of acute decompensated heart failure
option_C: Nesiritide is associated with a decreased rate of rehospitalization, but not death, from acute decompensated heart failure
option_D: Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates
option_E: None of the statements are true
answer_text: None of the statements are true

stem: Mr. Jones is a 21-year-old man who presents to the emergency department with several days of worsening shortness of breath and lethargy 1 week after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. His family brought him in after he lacked the energy to rise from the couch unassisted. His blood pressure is 88/72 mmHg, heart rate is 115 bpm, and room air oxygen saturation is 90%. Physical examination reveals pulmonary crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, an audible S3 gallop, and cool extremities. He is lethargic and slow to respond to questions. Laboratory analysis reveals a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, elevated BNP level, and mildly elevated lactate. Bedside echocardiography reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15% with global hypokinesis. You start dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/ min and prepare to insert a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring. Which of the following hemodynamic parameters is most likely increased?
Which of the following medications has been shown to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?

You are seeing a patient with newly diagnosed nonischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. He is euvolemic and New York Heart Association (NYHA) class I in terms of symptoms severity. His blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, and heart rate is 80 bpm. You know that, eventually, you would like him on optimal doses of a B-blocker and an ACE inhibitor. Which of the following represents the appropriate order of initiation and dose titration of these medications?
option_A: Co-initiate ACE inhibitor and B-blocker at low dose. Titrate each up every 2–4 weeks to highest tolerated dose
option_B: Initiate ACE inhibitor and titrate to highest tolerated dose. Then initiate B-blocker and titrate to highest tolerated dose
option_C: Initiate ACE inhibitor at low dose. Then initiate B-blocker at low dose. Alternate titrating the dose up for each drug to the highest tolerated dose for both
option_D: Initiate B-blocker and titrate to highest tolerated dose. Then initiate ACE inhibitor and titrate to highest tolerated dose
option_E: The specific strategy does not matter so much as the goal of initiating both ACE inhibitor and B-blocker in a timely manner and titrating both to their optimal, highest tolerated doses
answer_text: The specific strategy does not matter so much as the goal of initiating both ACE inhibitor and B-blocker in a timely manner and titrating both to their optimal, highest tolerated doses

stem: A 72-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% has NYHA class II symptoms. She takes lisinopril 40 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Blood pressure is 102/82 mmHg and she is in sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min. Her eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.8 mmol/L. Which additional medication will further reduce her mortality?
explanation: HFrEF on ACEi, beta-blocker and MRA: add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin), which cuts CV death and admissions with or without diabetes.
topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; SGLT2 inhibitors; Dapagliflozin

stem: A 57-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 8 months ago, treated with primary PCI with an excellent result despite a late presentation. He is now asymptomatic on optimal medical therapy, with heart rate 65 beats/min and blood pressure 104/82 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and a QRS duration of 135 ms. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25% with a large anterior dyskinetic area consistent with aneurysm. Which therapy is indicated to reduce his mortality?
option_B: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator with cardiac resynchronization capability (coronary sinus lead)
explanation: EF ≤ 30% > 40 days after MI: a primary-prevention ICD reduces mortality (MADIT-II). CRT needs LBBB with QRS ≥ 150 ms.
topics: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; Sudden cardiac death; Post-myocardial infarction

stem: A 25-year-old man had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy 18 months ago. His resting heart rate has been consistently around 90 beats/min, and he feels well. What is the most appropriate next step regarding his resting heart rate?
option_A: Exercise treadmill ECG testing to evaluate for chronotropic competence
option_C: Initiate metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily
option_E: Refer for electrophysiology study to evaluate for ectopic atrial tachycardia
explanation: A resting rate of ~90/min in a well heart-transplant recipient is expected (denervation); reassure.

stem: A government committee on organ transplantation is considering a nationwide sharing strategy for donor hearts in a large country. Why is such a strategy not beneficial?
option_A: Blood groups are distributed non-randomly across the country, preventing true nationwide sharing
option_B: Regions use highly variable criteria for grading severity of illness
option_C: The financial structure of reimbursement would not allow it
option_D: The tolerable cold ischaemic time of a harvested heart is too short to allow nationwide sharing
answer_text: The tolerable cold ischaemic time of a harvested heart is too short to allow nationwide sharing
explanation: A donor heart tolerates only about 4 h of cold ischaemia, so it must be allocated within a limited radius of the donor.
topics: Heart transplantation; Organ allocation; Ischaemic time

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department for dyspnea on exertion. He had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischemic cardiomyopathy 5 years ago and, in general, has done quite well except for one cytomegalovirus reactivation within the first year. He reports that for the past 3 months, he has noticed that with decreasing amounts of exertion he has been having limiting dyspnea. He is adamant that he is experiencing no chest pain or pressure during these episodes. He has been perfectly compliant with his regimen of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisone. Echocardiography reveals a normal LV function with normal LV wall thickness. His resting ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at a rate of 80 bpm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

A 68-year-old woman with chemotherapy-related cardiomyopathy (EF 15%) has frequent admissions with acute decompensated heart failure despite optimal therapy. She is not a candidate for heart transplantation. Which of the following statements about other options to prolong her life is correct?
option_A: Continuous infusion of milrinone will improve cardiac function and survival
option_B: A left ventricular assist device can improve quality of life but provides no survival benefit over optimal medical care
option_C: A left ventricular assist device can improve survival over the initial 2–5 years more than optimal medical therapy
option_D: Stem cell implantation has been shown to prolong life in patients with end-stage cardiomyopathy
option_E: There are no other options for prolonging life, and we should consider palliative measures in the future
answer_text: A left ventricular assist device can improve survival over the initial 2–5 years more than optimal medical therapy
explanation: In transplant-ineligible stage D heart failure, a durable LVAD (destination therapy) improves survival; inotropes do not.
topics: Left ventricular assist device; Advanced heart failure

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of congenital heart disease (CHD) in high-income countries is true?
option_A: CHD is extremely rare, complicating fewer than 1 in 1000 live births
option_B: With advances in surgery and pre- and postnatal care, survival of neonates with CHD now approaches 90%
option_C: Because fewer women with CHD become pregnant, the incidence of CHD in neonates is declining
option_D: The population of adults with CHD is declining because of improved prenatal screening
option_E: Women with CHD have no increased risk of complications during pregnancy compared with the general population
answer_text: With advances in surgery and pre- and postnatal care, survival of neonates with CHD now approaches 90%
explanation: CHD affects ~1% of births and ~90% of neonates now survive, so adults with CHD now outnumber children.
topics: Congenital heart disease; Adult congenital heart disease; Epidemiology

stem: 1% of all live births. B. Given advances in surgical techniques and pre- and postnatal care, survival for a neonate with CHD now approaches 90%. C. Given the declining rates of pregnancy in women with CHD, the incidence of CHD in neonates is declining. D. The population of adults with CHD is declining given improved prenatal screening efforts. E. Women with CHD are at no increased risk for complications during pregnancy compared with the normal population.

A 62-year-old man is being assessed for mitral valve surgery for severe mitral regurgitation. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a small jet of right-to-left flow across the atrial septum, occurring when a small flap of tissue swings open (less than 1 mm). Which of the following explains this finding?
explanation: A flap that opens intermittently between atria is a PFO (~25% of adults), allowing paradoxical embolism; no treatment if incidental.
topics: Patent foramen ovale; Atrial septal defect

stem: A 21-year-old man has a newly diagnosed ventricular septal defect (VSD). Echocardiography confirms a 5-mm VSD in the muscular interventricular septum. Right heart catheterisation shows a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 20 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance of 2 Wood units and systemic vascular resistance of 6 Wood units, with a Qp:Qs of 1.25. What do you recommend?
option_A: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing to define peak oxygen consumption
option_B: Closure with a percutaneously deployed septal occluder device
option_C: Consideration of heart and lung transplant
option_D: No intervention now; annual cardiology assessments and reimaging if any new symptoms emerge
option_E: Surgical correction via open heart surgery and patch repair
answer_text: No intervention now; annual cardiology assessments and reimaging if any new symptoms emerge
explanation: A small restrictive VSD with Qp:Qs < 1.5 and normal pulmonary pressures needs no closure; review periodically and maintain dental hygiene.

stem: A 52-year-old patient presents with chest pain and raised cardiac enzymes. A superficial continuous murmur, not previously documented, is heard at the mid-sternal level. Echocardiography shows normal valves. Right heart catheterisation gives these oxygen saturations: superior vena cava 58%, right atrium 60%, mid-coronary sinus 91%, right ventricle 70%, pulmonary artery 70%. What abnormality accounts for these findings?
option_A: Anomalous left coronary artery off the main pulmonary artery
option_C: Coronary arteriovenous fistula to the coronary sinus
answer_text: Coronary arteriovenous fistula to the coronary sinus
explanation: A coronary sinus saturation of 91% (normally ~30–40%) means arterial blood is entering it: a coronary AV fistula, causing a continuous murmur and steal.
topics: Coronary arteriovenous fistula; Oxygen saturation step-up; Continuous murmur

stem: A 40-year-old man has a congenital bicuspid aortic valve. Which other structure is important to follow on his regular echocardiograms?
explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve carries an aortopathy, so measure the aortic root/ascending aorta on every echo; repair at 55 mm (50 mm with risk factors).

stem: All of the following are classic defining features of tetralogy of Fallot EXCEPT:
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and RV hypertrophy. Tricuspid atresia is a separate cyanotic lesion.
topics: Tetralogy of Fallot; Cyanotic congenital heart disease

stem: A 78-year-old man with a history of tobacco abuse, obesity, and diabetes mellitus is evaluated for dyspnoea on exertion. Echocardiography confirms severe aortic stenosis. Which of the following most likely contributed to the development of his lesion?
explanation: Calcific AS of a trileaflet valve at 78 shares atherosclerotic risk factors: age, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, lipids, CKD.
topics: Aortic stenosis; Calcific aortic valve disease; Diabetes mellitus

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with new exertional syncope and is found to have severe aortic stenosis. What is the average life expectancy of untreated patients with this presentation?
explanation: Untreated severe AS: average survival ~5 years after angina, 3 after syncope and 2 after heart failure; any symptom means valve replacement.

stem: An 82-year-old man with severe calcific aortic stenosis, who previously deferred surgery, now presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of multi-organ dysfunction. Which of the following would be a reasonable therapeutic option to improve his short-term perfusion to permit aortic valve replacement?
option_B: Digoxin 250 µg IV once and 125 µg orally daily thereafter
option_C: Metoprolol 5 mg IV serial dosing targeting a resting heart rate of 60–70 bpm
option_E: Phenylephrine continuous IV infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure of >65
explanation: Cardiogenic shock from critical AS: balloon aortic valvuloplasty temporarily relieves obstruction as a bridge to AVR/TAVI (restenosis within months).
topics: Aortic stenosis; Balloon aortic valvuloplasty; Cardiogenic shock

stem: An 85-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness and leg oedema. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25% with global hypokinesis, a calculated aortic valve area of 0.8 cm² and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step to determine whether he would benefit from aortic valve replacement?
option_A: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to evaluate ventricular scar and aortic valve mor phology
option_B: Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) to determine ventricular viability
option_C: Coronary angiography to evaluate for the presence of obstructive coronary disease
option_E: Right heart catheterization to document cardiac output and filling pressures
explanation: Low-flow low-gradient AS with poor EF: dobutamine stress echo separates true severe AS (gradient rises, area stays ≤ 1 cm²) from pseudo-severe and shows contractile reserve.
topics: Low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis; Dobutamine stress echocardiography

stem: Which of the following parameters is typically reduced in chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
explanation: In chronic severe AR diastolic pressure falls and pulse pressure widens; LV end-diastolic volume, stroke volume and afterload all increase.

stem: A 21-year-old woman with a connective tissue disease presents with acute breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. Echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with an avulsed right coronary cusp. While awaiting emergency surgery, which intervention is most likely to help maintain her end-organ perfusion?
option_A: Esmolol continuous IV infusion titrated to a heart rate of 60–70 bpm
explanation: Acute severe AR: nitroprusside (± dobutamine) increases forward flow as a bridge to surgery. IABP is contraindicated; beta-blockers lengthen diastole.

stem: What is the most common cause of obstruction to left ventricular inflow worldwide?
option_C: Infective endocarditis with large mitral valve vegetations
explanation: Rheumatic heart disease is by far the commonest cause of mitral stenosis/LV inflow obstruction worldwide; annular calcification in the elderly.

stem: In cases of severe mitral stenosis, which of the following parameters is typically increased?
explanation: In MS left atrial pressure rises to drive flow across the valve; LV end-diastolic pressure is normal or low and output falls.
topics: Mitral stenosis; Left atrial pressure; Haemodynamics

stem: In a patient with mitral stenosis, all of the following will raise left atrial pressure and may worsen pulmonary congestion EXCEPT:
explanation: Anything raising heart rate or output raises LA pressure in MS. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) lengthen diastole and lower LA pressure.

stem: An 84-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis develops new-onset atrial fibrillation. Which of the following interventions will NOT help lower her left atrial pressure?
option_D: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm
option_E: All of the above will help lower left atrial pressure
answer_text: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm
explanation: In MS, LA pressure falls with diuretics, valvotomy, cardioversion or rate control. Pacing at 90/min shortens diastole and raises it.

stem: A 34-year-old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis is asymptomatic, with a mitral valve area of 1.7 cm². On exercise his pulmonary artery systolic pressure reaches 40 mmHg. What management do you recommend?
option_C: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring
answer_text: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring
explanation: MVA 1.7 cm² is moderate MS; asymptomatic with exercise PASP < 60 mmHg, so review and serial echo every 1–2 years.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a 15-year history of non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) has severe functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation. He remains in NYHA class III despite optimal guideline-directed medical therapy and cardiac resynchronisation. He asks whether fixing his valve would improve his survival. What is the most accurate response?
option_A: Valve repair is only needed if you develop pulmonary hypertension or atrial fibrillation
option_B: Neither surgical nor percutaneous valve repair has ever been shown to improve survival in patients like you
option_C: Surgery should be considered only if repair is possible, because replacement would not improve survival
option_D: Surgical repair has not been shown to improve survival, but in selected patients like you transcatheter edge-to-edge repair has been shown to reduce mortality
option_E: Yes, your valve should have been fixed years ago
answer_text: Surgical repair has not been shown to improve survival, but in selected patients like you transcatheter edge-to-edge repair has been shown to reduce mortality
explanation: In secondary (functional) MR surgery does not improve survival, but transcatheter edge-to-edge repair reduced mortality in selected patients (COAPT).
topics: Secondary mitral regurgitation; Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair; Dilated cardiomyopathy

stem: During right and left heart catheterisation of a patient with stenosis of two valves, the following pressures are recorded: right atrium (mean) 15 mmHg; right ventricle 25/6 mmHg; pulmonary artery 25/12 mmHg; pulmonary artery wedge pressure 12 mmHg; left ventricle 105/6 mmHg; aorta 105/75 mmHg. Which two valves are stenosed?
explanation: Diastolic gradients RA > RVEDP and wedge > LVEDP mean tricuspid and mitral stenosis; no systolic gradients exclude pulmonary and aortic stenosis.
topics: Mitral stenosis; Tricuspid stenosis; Cardiac catheterisation

stem: You are evaluating a 50-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. She has severe tricuspid regurgitation, a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle, and signs of right heart failure. What is the best treatment for her severe tricuspid regurgitation?
option_A: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures
answer_text: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures
explanation: Functional TR from pulmonary hypertension is treated by diuretics, salt restriction and pulmonary vasodilator therapy; valve surgery is high-risk.
topics: Functional tricuspid regurgitation; Pulmonary arterial hypertension

stem: A 21-year-old woman who has never seen a doctor is found to have an ejection systolic murmur in the left second intercostal space, preceded by an ejection click. Echocardiography confirms pulmonary stenosis with a peak gradient of 70 mmHg and a doming pulmonary valve without regurgitation. What is the best treatment?
explanation: Doming pulmonary valve with peak gradient > ~64 mmHg is congenital pulmonary stenosis: percutaneous balloon valvotomy.

stem: A 77-year-old patient with severe aortic stenosis develops signs of acute pulmonary oedema and is found to have a new soft, short apical systolic murmur consistent with acute severe mitral regurgitation due to ruptured chordae. Which parameter will likely increase as a result of the new severe mitral regurgitation?
explanation: New severe MR gives the LV a low-pressure outlet, so EF rises while forward flow and the aortic gradient fall.
topics: Acute mitral regurgitation; Aortic stenosis; Ejection fraction

stem: A man with rheumatic heart disease and moderate mitral stenosis presents with atrial fibrillation at a ventricular rate of 60 beats/min. Which of the following is the appropriate thromboembolic prophylaxis?
option_E: More information is needed prior to initiating thromboembolic prophylaxis
explanation: AF with moderate–severe rheumatic MS needs warfarin (INR 2–3) regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc; rivaroxaban was inferior (INVICTUS).
topics: Rheumatic mitral stenosis; Atrial fibrillation; Warfarin

stem: All of the following are risk factors for the development of peripartum cardiomyopathy EXCEPT:
explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy risk factors: older age, multiparity, twins, pre-eclampsia/hypertension, African ancestry. Primiparity is not one.

stem: A 25-year-old man with a diagnosis of heart failure has used a wheelchair for many years and has severe scoliosis. His ECG shows tall R waves in V1 and V2 with deep Q waves in V5 and V6, and echocardiography shows severe global left ventricular dysfunction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A wheelchair-bound young man with scoliosis and DCM has Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin); tall R in V1–V2 is typical.

stem: Which of the following is the most common inheritance pattern for familial cardiomyopathies?
option_A: Autosomal dominant driven by exon duplication
option_B: Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations
option_C: Autosomal recessive driven by exon deletion
option_D: Autosomal recessive driven by exon duplication
answer_text: Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations
explanation: Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant missense mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3, TTN, LMNA); offer cascade screening.

stem: A 45-year-old man with obesity presents with several months of breathlessness, fatigue and a nocturnal cough. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a globally reduced ejection fraction of 25%. Which blood test is routinely recommended in all patients with newly diagnosed heart failure to identify a reversible cause?
explanation: TSH is part of routine tests in new heart failure, as hypo- and hyperthyroidism are reversible causes.
topics: Dilated cardiomyopathy; Thyroid function tests; Heart failure

stem: A 22-year-old student presents with lethargy and fatigue 3 days after a viral upper respiratory illness. He is obtunded, tachycardic and hypotensive, with cool peripheries and a raised jugular venous pressure. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30% with mild mitral regurgitation, and endomyocardial biopsy shows lymphocytic myocarditis. Which of the following statements about his prognosis and treatment is true?
option_A: His chance of survival is <10% without cardiac transplantation. Emergent transplant listing is warranted
option_B: His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical haemodynamic support is warranted
option_C: Immunosuppression with high-dose systemic steroids will increase his chance of survival
option_D: The presence and titer of anti-heart antibodies can help provide prognostic information for this patient
answer_text: His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical haemodynamic support is warranted
explanation: Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis has a good outcome if supported (inotropes, ECMO/VAD); LV function often recovers fully.
topics: Fulminant myocarditis; Cardiogenic shock; Mechanical circulatory support

stem: A 42-year-old woman with autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is brought in after collapsing at home. She reports several days of worsening lethargy and chest discomfort. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%, and endomyocardial biopsy shows diffuse inflammatory infiltrates with multinucleated giant cells and myocyte necrosis. Which of the following statements about her diagnosis is true?
option_A: Most patients with this form of cardiomyopathy recover with supportive care
option_B: Steroids alone are highly effective in treating this form of cardiomyopathy
option_C: The course is often rapidly progressive, with deterioration requiring urgent transplantation
option_D: Ventricular tachyarrhythmias are rare in this disease
option_E: None of the above is true
answer_text: The course is often rapidly progressive, with deterioration requiring urgent transplantation
explanation: Giant cell myocarditis (with autoimmune disease) progresses rapidly with heart block and VT; immunosuppression helps but many need urgent transplant.

stem: All of the following are associated with an elevated risk for development of cardiomyopathy during anthracycline chemotherapy EXCEPT:
option_E: All of the above are associated with elevated risk
answer_text: All of the above are associated with elevated risk
explanation: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity rises with cumulative dose (> 400–450 mg/m²), chest radiotherapy, heart disease, age extremes and trastuzumab.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with chest pain after a week of coryza, cough, fever and muscle aches. The pain is constant, radiates to his left shoulder, and is worse lying flat and on deep inspiration. There is a scratchy extracardiac sound with three components per heartbeat. His ECG is shown, and troponin I is undetectable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
option_A: Aspirin 75 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 80 mg daily
option_B: High-dose aspirin (750 mg–1 g every 8 hours) plus colchicine, with proton pump inhibitor cover
option_C: Heparin, aspirin and clopidogrel with immediate coronary angiography
option_D: Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks, then tapered over 2 months
answer_text: High-dose aspirin (750 mg–1 g every 8 hours) plus colchicine, with proton pump inhibitor cover
explanation: Viral pericarditis (rub, diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, normal troponin): high-dose aspirin or NSAID with PPI plus colchicine.

stem: You are caring for a 45-year-old man in the cardiac intensive care unit who was initially treated for acute coronary syndrome but is now diagnosed with acute pericarditis. Shortly after admission, he becomes hypotensive with elevated neck veins and cool extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
In a patient with cardiac tamponade, which of the following is likely to be increased during inspiration compared to expiration?
explanation: In tamponade inspiration increases RV filling (tricuspid inflow) while LV filling and SBP fall (pulsus paradoxus).
topics: Cardiac tamponade; Pulsus paradoxus; Ventricular interdependence

stem: All of the following ECG characteristics aid in differentiating acute pericarditis from acute myocardial infarction EXCEPT:
option_A: Absence of the development of Q waves
option_E: T-wave inversions after return of the ST segments to baseline
explanation: Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, no reciprocal change or Q waves. ST elevation in V2 occurs in both, so it does not help.
topics: Acute pericarditis; ST elevation; Myocardial infarction

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of Hodgkin disease treated with chemotherapy and mediastinal irradiation presents with signs of constrictive pericarditis. Echocardiogram shows pericardial thickening and an abrupt cessation of ventricular filling in early diastole. What is the best approach for treatment?
explanation: Post-radiotherapy constriction (knock, dip-and-plateau) is treated definitively by pericardiectomy; diuretics give only temporary relief.
topics: Constrictive pericarditis; Pericardiectomy; Radiation heart disease

stem: A 45-year-old man with a 3-month history of fevers, symmetrical arthralgia and fatigue develops sudden left hand weakness that resolves within 1 hour. Echocardiography shows a solitary 2-cm pedunculated mass in the left atrium arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_A: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass
option_C: Repeat blood cultures and evaluation for HACEK organisms
option_D: Serologies for ANAs, anti-DNA, and anticardiolipin antibodies
option_E: Whole-body PET scan to evaluate for malignancy
answer_text: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass
explanation: A pedunculated LA mass at the fossa ovalis with fever, arthralgia and TIA is myxoma: surgical excision without delay.
topics: Atrial myxoma; Transient ischaemic attack; Cardioembolism

stem: Which of the following malignancies carries the highest relative risk of metastasis to the heart?
explanation: Melanoma has the highest propensity for cardiac metastasis; lung and breast cancer are commonest by number.

stem: At a children's baseball game, a 12-year-old catcher is struck in the chest by a foul ball and immediately collapses in cardiac arrest. Which intervention is most critical for his survival?
option_A: Emergent transfer for percutaneous coronary intervention
option_B: Emergent transfer for repair of an acute aortic dissection
option_D: Prompt cardiac surgery to repair an avulsed aortic valve
explanation: Commotio cordis: a precordial blow on the T-wave upslope triggers VF in a normal heart; immediate CPR and defibrillation save life.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes asks about her future risk of heart attack and stroke. What is the most common cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus?
explanation: Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in type 2 diabetes (2–4× risk, often silent ischaemia).
topics: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; Coronary artery disease; Cardiovascular risk

stem: A 49-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with high-output heart failure. After treatment, his symptoms and left ventricular size improve rapidly. Which treatment most likely produced this improvement?
explanation: High-output heart failure in a heavy drinker that responds rapidly is wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency; give thiamine before glucose.
topics: Wet beriberi; Thiamine deficiency; High-output heart failure

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair and leg swelling. Her TSH is 79.4 mU/L. Which cardiovascular measurement is NOT expected to decrease?
explanation: Hypothyroidism lowers heart rate, stroke volume and output, raises SVR and prolongs (not shortens) the QT.

stem: In the current model describing the steps of atherosclerosis initiation and evolution, which of the following constitutes the first step?
option_A: Arterial endothelial cells overexpress adhesion receptors for leukocytes
option_C: Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima
option_D: Macrophages and other leukocytes are recruited to the arterial intima
option_E: Macrophages become lipid-laden foam cells via endocytosis
answer_text: Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima
explanation: Atherogenesis begins with LDL retention in the intima; oxidation, endothelial activation, monocyte recruitment and foam cells follow.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the pathophysiologic consequences of an atheroma is true?
option_A: An atheroma resulting in total vascular occlusion invariably causes infarction
option_B: An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina
option_C: Most atheromas will eventually produce symptoms in the patient
option_D: Upon initial formation, the atheromatous plaque usually grows inward toward the vessel lumen
option_E: Vessels affected by atherogenesis tend to contract and get smaller in diameter
answer_text: An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina
explanation: Arteries remodel outward, so a plaque does not narrow the lumen until it exceeds ~40% of the area within the internal elastic lamina (Glagov).

stem: Under the 2013 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline (whose statin benefit groups were retained in 2018), all of the following are statin benefit groups EXCEPT:
option_A: All individuals with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
option_B: Individuals with a raised high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol or ASCVD risk
option_C: Individuals with LDL cholesterol of 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) or more without a secondary cause
option_D: Individuals aged 40–75 years without ASCVD or diabetes, with LDL 1.8–4.9 mmol/L (70–189 mg/dL) and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or more
option_E: Individuals aged 40–75 years with diabetes but no ASCVD, with LDL 1.8–4.9 mmol/L (70–189 mg/dL)
answer_text: Individuals with a raised high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol or ASCVD risk
explanation: Statin benefit groups: clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L, diabetes aged 40–75, 10-year risk ≥ 7.5%. Raised hs-CRP alone is not one.

stem: A 50-year-old man with obesity attends his annual check-up. He has no known vascular disease and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 6%. His lipid profile shows total cholesterol 5.7 mmol/L (220 mg/dL), triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L (283 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol 0.75 mmol/L (29 mg/dL) and LDL cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (132 mg/dL). He is concerned about his low HDL. Which intervention aimed at his low HDL has been shown to lower his cardiovascular risk?
option_B: A cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitor
option_E: Weight loss and regular physical activity
answer_text: Weight loss and regular physical activity
explanation: HDL-raising drugs (CETP inhibitors, niacin, fibrates) did not cut events; weight loss and exercise improve HDL and overall risk.
topics: Low HDL cholesterol; Lifestyle modification; Cardiovascular risk

stem: All of the following are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand EXCEPT:
option_E: All of the above are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand
explanation: Myocardial oxygen demand depends on heart rate, contractility and wall stress (preload and afterload); rhythm itself is not a primary determinant.

stem: During an exercise stress test, how does the normal heart meet its increased oxygen demand?
option_A: Increased myocardial oxygen extraction during near-constant coronary blood flow
option_B: Increased oxygen extraction from the ventricular chambers
option_C: Relative expansion of the diastolic time period allowing increased coronary flow
option_D: Vasodilation of epicardial coronary arteries leading to decreased resistance and increased flow
option_E: Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow
answer_text: Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow
explanation: The heart already extracts ~70–75% of oxygen at rest, so extra demand is met by arteriolar dilatation and increased coronary flow.
topics: Coronary blood flow; Coronary autoregulation; Exercise physiology

stem: A man develops angina during an exercise stress test. Which of the following biochemical changes would NOT be expected in his ischaemic myocardium?
option_C: A shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism
option_D: Depletion of myocardial stores of high-energy phosphates
explanation: Ischaemia shifts to anaerobic glycolysis: lactate and H⁺ accumulate (pH falls), ATP depletes, calcium rises and potassium leaks out.

stem: Which of the following is an unusual site for radiation of anginal pain?
explanation: Angina radiates to arms, neck, jaw, epigastrium and back; radiation to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericarditis.

stem: Ms. Wilson is a 66-year-old postmenopausal postal employee who experiences chest pressure and dyspnea while walking her mail route. What term and CCS functional class best describe her angina?

A 50-year-old accountant with a history of cigarette use completes an exercise treadmill ECG stress test. He develops upsloping ST depressions in leads II, III, and aVF. His peak heart rate is 130 bpm, and his blood pressure increases from 120/80 to 155/95 mmHg. What is the appropriate interpretation of this stress test?
option_A: Negative stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
option_B: Negative stress test; nonspecific ST changes
option_C: Nondiagnostic stress test; normal blood pressure response
option_D: Positive stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
option_E: Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response
answer_text: Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response

stem: Mr. Brian, a 57-year-old hockey team coach with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco abuse, presents with chest discomfort that initially occurred with vigorous exertion but now at rest. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
option_E: More information is required before making a diagnosis

stem: A 62-year-old man with an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (ECG shown) develops cardiogenic shock while being prepared for primary PCI: BP 78/50 mmHg, cool peripheries, clear lung fields and a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L. Which agent is most appropriate first to support his blood pressure?
explanation: Cardiogenic shock after MI: urgent PCI, with noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor (SOAP II), ± dobutamine. Routine IABP is not recommended.

stem: A 72-year-old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 20%) presents in cardiogenic shock with pulmonary oedema: BP 82/50 mmHg, cool extremities, SpO2 84% despite high-flow oxygen and a respiratory rate of 34/min. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
option_B: Furosemide 60 mg IV once perfusion pressure is supported
explanation: Morphine is not recommended in acute heart failure, especially in shock (hypotension, respiratory depression, worse outcomes).
topics: Cardiogenic shock; Morphine; Acute heart failure

stem: A 52-year-old man develops acute pulmonary oedema and hypotension 4 days after an inferior myocardial infarction, with a new apical systolic murmur; acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture is suspected. What would a pulmonary artery catheter most likely show?
option_A: Low RA pressure, normal wedge, high CO
option_B: Normal RA pressure, low wedge, high SVR
option_C: Elevated wedge with prominent v waves
option_D: Equalization of pressures in all chambers
option_E: Low CO, low wedge, high RA pressure
answer_text: Elevated wedge with prominent v waves
explanation: Acute MR (papillary rupture) into a small non-compliant LA gives a high wedge pressure with giant v waves. A saturation step-up in the RV suggests VSD.
topics: Mitral regurgitation; Papillary muscle rupture; Pulmonary artery catheter

stem: All of the following statements about sudden cardiac death (SCD) are true EXCEPT:
option_A: Coronary artery disease is the commonest underlying substrate in adults
option_B: In about two-thirds of cases SCD is the first manifestation of heart disease or occurs in patients previously thought to be at low risk
option_C: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are commonly encountered initial rhythms in SCD arrests
option_D: A parental history of SCD increases the risk in offspring
option_E: Most victims have a previously documented left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less
answer_text: Most victims have a previously documented left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less
explanation: Most sudden cardiac deaths occur in people without known heart disease or with EF > 35%; CAD underlies ~80% of adult cases.

stem: A 56-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine blood pressure check and examination. He has no immediate concerns and his past medical history includes hypertension and asthma. He feels well in himself. On examination, he appears well and observa tions are normal except for a raised blood pressure of 155/87 mmHg. Upon auscultation of the heart, the GP notices an S4 heart sound. The GP then requests an ECG recording. Which part of the ECG does this sound coincide with?
explanation: S4 is atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it falls just after the P wave; S1 coincides with QRS. No S4 in AF.
topics: Fourth heart sound; Cardiac cycle; Left ventricular hypertrophy

stem: A 70-year-old man with mild chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus and heart failure is admitted with reduced urine output, weakness and breathlessness. He takes several medications but cannot remember their names. Blood results are pending, and his ECG is shown. Based on the information available, what is the best initial step in management?
option_D: Administration of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
explanation: Peaked T waves with flat P waves are hyperkalaemia: give IV calcium gluconate first, then insulin–glucose and salbutamol.

stem: A surgical colleague asks you to review a 54-year-old woman with ECG abnormalities the day after a subtotal thyroidectomy for toxic multinodular goitre. Her only medication is fentanyl for postoperative pain. She has no history of syncope and no family history of sudden cardiac death. Examination is unremarkable apart from a clean incision at the base of the neck. Her ECG is shown. What is the best next step?
option_C: Stat noncontrast CT scan of the brain
option_E: Reassure the patient that her ECG is normal for a woman her age
explanation: Long QT from ST-segment lengthening the day after thyroidectomy suggests hypocalcaemia (parathyroid injury): measure ionised calcium.

stem: A 60-year-old smoker with diabetes has bilateral pitting leg oedema, a raised JVP, a pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge.
explanation: Raised JVP with giant v waves, pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge (louder on inspiration) is tricuspid regurgitation.
topics: Leg oedema; Tricuspid regurgitation; Constrictive pericarditis

emq_options: A) Cor pulmonale | B) Amlodipine-induced oedema | C) Congestive heart failure | D) Tricuspid regurgitation | E) Constrictive pericarditis | F) Mitral regurgitation | G) Mitral stenosis | H) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease | I) Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis | J) Restrictive cardiomyopathy
stem: A 55-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension on regular treatment and no diabetes has bilateral pitting leg oedema; the JVP is normal and all investigations are normal.
explanation: Bilateral ankle oedema with normal JVP and investigations in a treated hypertensive is amlodipine oedema (arteriolar dilatation); it responds poorly to diuretics.
