A 46 year old man has recently fractured his leg, which is in a plaster cast. He suddenly becomes very breathless, unwell and collapses. The attending doctor suspects a pulmonary embolus from a deep vein thrombosis. The doctor performs an ECG. What is the most common ECG change in patients with pulmonary embolism?
explanation: The commonest ECG finding in PE is sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 and RBBB are uncommon.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with idiopathic (primary) pulmonary arterial hypertension is evaluated for therapy. Which of the following therapies may be indicated?
explanation: Bosentan (endothelin receptor antagonist) treats PAH; others are PDE-5 inhibitors, riociguat and prostacyclin agents. Monitor LFTs.
topics: Pulmonary arterial hypertension; Bosentan; Endothelin receptor antagonists

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with worsening breathlessness and palpitations. Examination shows an elevated JVP, and the chest X-ray shows prominent proximal pulmonary arteries with a paucity of peripheral vascular markings. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
option_B: Dysfunctional breathing studies and Nijmegen questionnaire
explanation: Raised JVP with pruned peripheral vessels suggests pulmonary hypertension; transthoracic echo is the first test, then RHC.

stem: A 23 year old woman diagnosed with primary pulmonary hypertension is evaluated for therapy. Which of the following therapies may be indicated?
40-year-old woman develops sudden-onset dyspnoea at rest following hip replacement surgery. On examination she is tachycardic and her electrocardiogram (ECG) shows right axis deviation.
A 35-year-old businessman returns from a trip abroad and collapses at the airport with haemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain. He has a sinus tachycardia and his ECG shows right axis deviation.
Which of the following sets of pulmonary function test results is most consistent with heritable (familial) pulmonary arterial hypertension?
option_A: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
option_B: Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
option_C: Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased MIP
option_D: Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
answer_text: Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
explanation: PAH is vascular, so volumes, spirometry and muscle strength are normal; the typical abnormality is an isolated low DLCO.
topics: Pulmonary arterial hypertension; Pulmonary function tests

stem: A 47-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and right heart failure despite maximal medical therapy is referred for transplantation. Which of the following statements is true?
option_B: Patients with idiopathic PAH have worse 5-year survival after transplantation than all other recipient groups
option_C: Single-lung transplantation is the preferred procedure
option_D: Her right ventricular function will recover after lung transplantation
option_E: She is at high risk of recurrent PAH in the transplanted lungs
answer_text: Her right ventricular function will recover after lung transplantation
explanation: RV dysfunction in PAH recovers after bilateral lung transplantation as afterload falls; heart–lung only for complex disease.

stem: In a patient with COPD, the presence of distended neck veins and bilateral leg oedema is most suggestive of:
explanation: Raised JVP and leg oedema in COPD are cor pulmonale (hypoxic pulmonary hypertension); LTOT improves survival.

stem: On precordial examination in a patient with cor pulmonale, which finding is most likely?
explanation: RV hypertrophy in cor pulmonale gives a left parasternal heave, loud P2 and functional TR.

stem: A 66-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressive shortness of breath and sharp right-sided chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration. She also has mild pain in the right leg. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable; heart rate is 96/min and respiratory rate 12/min. She denies weight loss or long-haul flights but had a nasal polypectomy 3 weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pleuritic pain and breathlessness with calf pain 3 weeks after surgery is PE: Wells score, CTPA and anticoagulate meanwhile.

stem: 19-A 30-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath. This began insidiously over several months. She has no cough and no chest pain. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern. Arterial blood gases reveal hypoxia and hypercapnia; a lung perfusion scan is normal. Right heart catheterisation reveals that right-sided pressures are markedly raised. Which diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?

A 50-year-old woman presents with breathlessness that has increased over several months. She has peripheral oedema and clinical evidence of right-sided heart failure without signs of left ventricular failure. She is a non-smoker with no chronic cough or sputum, and her chest X-ray lung fields and spirometry are normal. What is the most likely cause of her cor pulmonale?
explanation: Cor pulmonale with normal lung fields and spirometry suggests CTEPH from recurrent small emboli; V/Q scan, endarterectomy may cure.
topics: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; Cor pulmonale

stem: A 40-year-old woman has had increasing fatigue and breathlessness for several years. Chest X-ray shows right ventricular enlargement and enlarged central pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary embolism has been excluded by CT pulmonary angiography, and other causes of pulmonary hypertension have been ruled out. Right heart catheterisation shows a pulmonary artery pressure of 75/30 mmHg. What is the best next step in management?
option_A: Acute drug testing with short-acting pulmonary vasodilators
answer_text: Acute drug testing with short-acting pulmonary vasodilators
explanation: In idiopathic PAH, perform acute vasoreactivity testing at RHC; the ~10% responders get high-dose CCBs, others combination PAH therapy.
topics: Pulmonary arterial hypertension; Vasoreactivity testing; Right heart catheterisation

stem: A 35-year-old woman complains of slowly progressive breathlessness. She has no cough, sputum, pleuritic chest pain or history of thrombophlebitis, but has taken appetite suppressants at various times. Examination reveals a raised JVP, a palpable right ventricular heave and a loud P2. The chest X-ray shows clear lung fields, oxygen saturation is 94% and the ECG shows right axis deviation. A perfusion lung scan is normal, with no segmental defects. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pulmonary hypertension with clear lungs, normal perfusion scan and prior appetite suppressants is drug-induced PAH; confirm by RHC.
topics: Pulmonary arterial hypertension; Drug-induced pulmonary hypertension

stem: A 70-year-old man has cough, haemoptysis and breathlessness. He has finger clubbing and localised wheeze over the right lower lobe; CT shows a rounded mass in the right lower zone. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Haemoptysis, clubbing and localised wheeze with a mass in a 70-year-old is bronchial carcinoma: bronchoscopy and biopsy (± EBUS).

stem: A 78-year-old man has recurrent blood-streaked sputum with cough and breathlessness. He is breathless and anaemic with finger clubbing; pulse 86/min regular, BP 125/75 mmHg; localised wheeze (rhonchi) is heard over the right middle zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 78-year-old man has recurrent blood-streaked sputum with cough and breathlessness. He is breathless and anaemic with finger clubbing; pulse 86/min regular, BP 125/75 mmHg; localised wheeze (rhonchi) is heard over the right middle zone. Three weeks later he is found to have leg oedema and a serum sodium of 122 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause?

A 78-year-old man has recurrent blood-streaked sputum with cough and breathlessness. He is anaemic with finger clubbing, and a localised wheeze is heard over the right middle zone. Six weeks later he is more breathless; there is stony dullness from the right base up to the mid zone, with absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over this area, and the trachea is central. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds and a central trachea is a pleural effusion, likely malignant; aspirate for cytology.

stem: A 73-year-old heavy smoker with bronchial carcinoma develops nausea, vomiting, irritability and a seizure. Hb 9.8 g/dL; serum sodium 104 mmol/L (135–145). Which complication has developed?
explanation: Na⁺ 104 with seizure in lung cancer is SIADH (small cell); give hypertonic saline boluses, raising Na⁺ ≤ 8–10 mmol/L in 24 h.
topics: SIADH; Small cell lung cancer; Hyponatraemia

stem: Each of the following is a risk factor for lung cancer EXCEPT:
explanation: Lung cancer risks: smoking, radon, asbestos, metals (chromium, nickel, arsenic), pollution, radiotherapy. Lead is not a carcinogen here.

stem: A breathless patient with lung cancer has bilateral hilar enlargement and a pleural effusion on chest X-ray. What is the next step?
option_A: CT of chest, abdomen and head for staging
option_D: Palliative radiotherapy because the patient is not a candidate for curative resection
explanation: Effusion in suspected lung cancer: ultrasound-guided aspiration for cytology diagnoses and stages (M1a) and relieves breathlessness.
topics: Malignant pleural effusion; Pleural aspiration; Lung cancer

stem: Which of the following is a cutaneous manifestation of bronchogenic carcinoma?
explanation: Dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic skin manifestation of lung cancer; screen adults presenting with it.

stem: A 70-year-old heavy smoker has haemoptysis, finger clubbing and has lost 2 stones (13 kg) in weight over the last month. There is reduced air entry and wheeze in the right middle zone, and the chest X-ray shows a homogeneous opacity in the middle of the right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Haemoptysis, weight loss, clubbing and localised wheeze with an opacity in a heavy smoker is bronchogenic carcinoma; urgent CT and tissue.

stem: A 70-year-old heavy smoker has haemoptysis, finger clubbing and has lost 2 stones (13 kg) in weight over the last month. There is reduced air entry and wheeze in the right middle zone, and the chest X-ray shows a homogeneous opacity in the middle of the right lung. Some weeks later he develops a plethoric (moon) face, weight gain and striae. What is the likely cause?
explanation: Cushingoid features in a smoker with lung cancer are ectopic ACTH (small cell or carcinoid); often hypokalaemic alkalosis dominates.
topics: Ectopic ACTH syndrome; Cushing's syndrome; Small cell lung cancer

stem: A smoker with a lung mass develops Cushingoid features. Which test best distinguishes pituitary ACTH (Cushing disease) from ectopic ACTH secretion?
explanation: High-dose dexamethasone suppresses pituitary (Cushing disease) but not usually ectopic ACTH; petrosal sinus sampling is more reliable.
topics: Ectopic ACTH syndrome; Dexamethasone suppression test

stem: A 70-year-old heavy smoker has haemoptysis, finger clubbing and has lost 2 stones (13 kg) in weight over the last month. There is reduced air entry and wheeze in the right middle zone, and the chest X-ray shows a homogeneous opacity in the middle of the right lung. Later he has fatigue and concentrated urine; serum sodium 123 mmol/L and potassium 4.0 mmol/L. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hyponatraemia with normal K⁺ and concentrated urine in lung cancer is SIADH; fluid restriction, treat tumour, tolvaptan if refractory.

stem: A man with a central bronchial carcinoma develops increasing breathlessness, with reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right chest. His chest X-ray is shown. What is the diagnosis?
option_A: Lung collapse due to bronchial obstruction
answer_text: Lung collapse due to bronchial obstruction
explanation: A central tumour occluding a bronchus causes collapse: opacification with volume loss and the mediastinum pulled towards it.
topics: Lung collapse; Lung cancer; Chest X-ray

stem: An elderly man who is a heavy smoker has weight loss, haemoptysis, fatigue, constipation and thirst; he has diabetes mellitus. Chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass, and PET-CT shows no distant metastasis. What is the most likely type of lung cancer?
explanation: A central (hilar) tumour in a smoker with hypercalcaemia (thirst, constipation) is squamous cell carcinoma, which secretes PTH-related peptide. Small cell causes SIADH and ectopic ACTH instead.
topics: Squamous cell carcinoma; Hypercalcaemia; Lung cancer

stem: An elderly man who is a heavy smoker has weight loss, haemoptysis, fatigue, constipation and thirst; he has diabetes mellitus. Chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass, and PET-CT shows no distant metastasis. What is the most likely cause of his hypercalcaemia?
explanation: With no metastases on PET, hypercalcaemia is humoral: PTHrP from the squamous tumour, with a suppressed PTH. Treat with IV saline then a bisphosphonate.
topics: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy; PTH-related peptide; Paraneoplastic syndromes

stem: An elderly man who is a heavy smoker has weight loss, haemoptysis, fatigue, constipation and thirst; he has diabetes mellitus. Chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass, and PET-CT shows no distant metastasis. Lung function tests show good pulmonary reserve. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Non-metastatic non-small cell cancer in a patient fit for surgery (adequate FEV1/TLCO) is resected, usually by lobectomy with nodal sampling.
topics: Non-small cell lung cancer; Lung cancer surgery

stem: An elderly man who is a heavy smoker has weight loss, haemoptysis, fatigue, constipation and thirst; he has diabetes mellitus. Chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass, and PET-CT shows no distant metastasis. Lung function tests show good pulmonary reserve. One year later he develops contralateral chest pain; a pleural effusion is found and aspiration confirms malignant cells. What is the best treatment to prevent recurrence of the effusion?
explanation: A symptomatic recurrent malignant effusion is drained and then controlled by talc pleurodesis (or an indwelling pleural catheter if the lung is trapped). Repeated aspiration only buys days.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and haemoptysis. She is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lung. She has been a smoker for as long as she can remember. She has lived in central London for almost 30 years now and she worked in a shipbuilding yard for most of her working life. Both her father and mother died of lung cancer. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her cancer?
explanation: Smoking causes ~85% of lung cancer, especially squamous and small cell; asbestos multiplies its effect.
topics: Lung cancer; Smoking; Squamous cell carcinoma

stem: A middle-aged man is diagnosed with lung cancer. He worked in a shipbuilding yard for most of his life. He is distraught with the diagnosis as he says he has never smoked in his life. Which of the following types of lung cancer is he most likely to suffer from?
explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer in never-smokers; asbestos raises risk of all types.

stem: A 53-year-old woman is diagnosed with lung cancer. Her main symptoms on presentation included breathlessness and haemoptysis. She complained of stretch marks on her abdomen and that her skin bruised easily. On examination you note purple abdominal striae. Which of the following types of lung cancer is she most likely to suffer from?
explanation: Cushing's (striae, bruising) in lung cancer means ectopic ACTH from small cell carcinoma (or carcinoid).
topics: Small cell lung cancer; Ectopic ACTH syndrome

stem: A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with lung cancer. Which of the following extrapulmonary manifestations is he most likely to suffer from?
explanation: Clubbing is the commonest extrapulmonary sign of lung cancer (up to a third); new clubbing in > 40s needs an urgent CXR.
topics: Finger clubbing; Paraneoplastic syndromes; Lung cancer

stem: A 66-year-old woman with history of weight loss presents to the respiratory clinic with an 8-week history of nonproductive cough and chronic clearing of throat. She has a 52-pack year smoking history and quit 25 years ago. She was subsequently diagnosed with carcinoma of the lung. Which of the following is NOT a complication of carcinoma of the lung?
explanation: Lung cancer causes hypercalcaemia (PTHrP, bone metastases), not hypocalcaemia; SIADH, HPOA, adrenal metastases and Horner's are recognised.

stem: A 65-year-old factory worker presents with a dry cough, right-sided chest pain and finger clubbing. He has lost 4 kg in weight in the last 2 weeks and has a 30-year smoking history. The right lower chest is dull to percussion with reduced expansion, and a chest X-ray shows a right peripheral lung mass with a small pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A peripheral mass with clubbing, weight loss and effusion in a smoker is non-small cell lung cancer; clubbing is uncommon in small cell.
topics: Non-small cell lung cancer; Finger clubbing

stem: A 50-year-old heavy smoker of 30 pack years presents to his GP with weight loss of 8 kg over 4 months and a chronic cough with two episodes of haemoptysis. He denies any history of fever. Chest radiograph shows a rounded lesion measuring 5 cm in diameter in the right upper lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 46-year-old woman was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the lung at bronchoscopy 1 week ago. She presents to the emergency department acutely short of breath with a non-productive cough and a central chest ache that is worse on inspiration. She is apyrexial; SpO2 91% on 40% oxygen, respiratory rate 30/min, BP 100/65 mmHg, pulse 110/min. Expansion is reduced on the right, with dullness to percussion throughout the right side and reduced breath sounds; the trachea is deviated to the right and the apex beat is not palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Whole-hemithorax dullness with the trachea pulled towards it is lung collapse from an obstructing tumour; an effusion pushes it away.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with 4 days of haemoptysis. He has lost weight over the last 2 months without night sweats. He has smoked 30 cigarettes per day for 40 years and worked in construction, where he may have been exposed to asbestos. He returned from a holiday in Guyana 1 week ago. His chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely cause of the X-ray findings?
explanation: A thick-walled cavitating mass in a smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss is most likely cavitating squamous carcinoma.
topics: Lung cancer; Cavitating lung lesion; Squamous cell carcinoma

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with 24 hours of central chest pain and a month of progressive shortness of breath. Pulse 105/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, SpO2 96% on air, respiratory rate 16/min; she is apyrexial. The chest is clear and the heart sounds are normal without murmurs. ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Haemoglobin 110 g/L, WCC 9 × 10⁹/L, platelets 340 × 10⁹/L, urea and electrolytes normal, CRP 67 mg/L. Her chest X-ray (shown) shows a widened superior mediastinum. What should the next investigation be?
explanation: A widened mediastinum with inflammation in a young woman suggests lymphoma; contrast CT chest, abdomen, pelvis to stage and find biopsy sites.

stem: A 63-year-old woman had a CT pulmonary angiogram for left-sided pleuritic chest pain. There was no pulmonary embolism, but a 15-mm spiculated nodule at the apex of the right lung was noted (shown). Her pain resolved within 24 hours and she is otherwise asymptomatic; she has smoked 10 cigarettes per day for 40 years. What is the best next step?
explanation: A spiculated solid upper-lobe nodule ≥ 8 mm in a smoker (Brock risk > 10%) needs PET-CT next (BTS).

stem: A 63-year-old woman had a pulmonary nodule identified incidentally on a CT pulmonary angiogram. She has a 20 pack-year smoking history but no past medical history, is asymptomatic with performance status 0 and has normal pulmonary function. PET-CT (shown) shows FDG avidity in the right upper lobe nodule with no nodal or distant uptake. What should be the next step?
explanation: An FDG-avid nodule without nodal or distant uptake in a fit patient is presumed stage I: lobectomy (SABR if unfit).
topics: Solitary pulmonary nodule; Lobectomy; Non-small cell lung cancer

stem: A 51-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She is a non-smoker with no significant past medical history. She needs 40% oxygen to maintain saturations of 92%; she is apyrexial, BP 101/62 mmHg, pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 30/min. What does her chest X-ray (shown) demonstrate?
explanation: Right hemithorax opacification with volume loss and the mediastinum pulled right is right lung collapse; bronchoscopy for the cause (e.g. carcinoid).

stem: A 54-year-old woman attends the rapid-access lung cancer clinic with haemoptysis and an abnormal chest X-ray. CT shows a large cavitating right upper lobe mass and bronchoscopic biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What does her PET-CT scan (shown) demonstrate?
option_A: Uptake confined to the right upper lobe lesion
option_B: Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and a spinal metastasis
option_C: Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and indeterminate uptake in pulmonary vessels
option_D: Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and right hilar lymph node
option_E: Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion, a spinal metastasis and a sternal metastasis
answer_text: Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and right hilar lymph node
explanation: PET-CT shows uptake in the right upper lobe primary and right hilar node (N1); sample PET-positive nodes (EBUS) before deciding.
topics: PET-CT; Lung cancer staging; Squamous cell carcinoma

stem: A 59 year old smoker presents with a new cough. CT reveals a 4-cm peripheral tumour in the left lower lobe with an ipsilateral enlarged hilar lymph node. Due to emphysema, CT-guided biopsy is high risk. PET shows high FDG avidity in the tumour and indeterminate hilar uptake. What should be the next investigation?
explanation: EBUS-TBNA of PET-avid hilar nodes gives diagnosis and stage in one low-risk procedure (NICE NG122).

stem: An 84-year-old retired shipyard insulation worker who smokes a pipe has a 3-month history of a nagging left-sided chest ache, worst in the axilla and radiating to the spine. Examination shows dullness from the left base to the mid zone and erythema ab igne over the left chest wall. What is the most likely cause of his chest pain?
explanation: Persistent dull chest wall pain with effusion decades after asbestos exposure is mesothelioma; CT and pleural biopsy.

stem: A 67-year-old man undergoing CT colonography is found to have a 6-mm nodule in the right lower lobe. Which feature increases the risk of malignancy in a pulmonary nodule?
explanation: Upper-lobe location raises nodule malignancy risk (Brock), as do age, female sex, emphysema, size, spiculation and part-solid nature.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has CT for suspected interstitial lung disease, which shows mild basal interlobular septal thickening and a 1.5-cm spiculated right upper lobe nodule. What is true regarding PET scanning for pulmonary nodules?
option_D: It is not useful in nodules < 1 cm in diameter
option_E: It offers no more information than a standard CT
answer_text: It is not useful in nodules < 1 cm in diameter
explanation: PET-CT is unreliable for nodules < 8–10 mm, misses low-avidity tumours (carcinoid, AIS) and is falsely positive in inflammation.

stem: A 63 year old female non-smoker with a 5-cm lesion in the right mid-zone undergoes bronchoscopy with tumour biopsy. Which is the most common histological type of lung cancer?
explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer (40–50%), especially in never-smokers and women; test for EGFR, ALK, ROS1 and PD-L1.
topics: Adenocarcinoma of lung; Lung cancer histology

stem: A 73-year-old woman with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer develops increasingly painful wrists. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Painful wrists/ankles with clubbing in NSCLC is hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (periostitis); NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, treat tumour.
topics: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy; Non-small cell lung cancer

stem: A 56-year-old smoker with a new cough has a CT showing a 4-cm peripheral left lung mass with an enlarged ipsilateral hilar lymph node and a pleural effusion; pleural fluid cytology is positive for malignant cells. What is the correct stage?
explanation: A malignant pleural effusion is M1a, so the cancer is stage IVA regardless of T and N; treatment is systemic.
topics: Lung cancer staging; Malignant pleural effusion; TNM staging

stem: A 36-year-old non-smoker has isolated haemoptysis. CT shows collapse of the left upper lobe with a vascular tumour at the left upper lobe orifice. What is the most likely tumour type?
explanation: A vascular endobronchial tumour causing collapse in a young non-smoker is a bronchial carcinoid; resection has an excellent prognosis.

stem: A 64 year old woman with breast cancer metastatic to liver, lungs and bone develops increasing breathlessness despite antibiotics. CT shows diffuse interstitial thickening radiating from the hila. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Beaded septal and bronchovascular thickening radiating from the hila in metastatic breast cancer is lymphangitis carcinomatosa.

stem: A 28-year-old man has a large anterior mediastinal mass with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Anterior mediastinal mass with cervical and axillary nodes in a young adult is lymphoma (the 4 Ts: thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma).

stem: A 72 year old man with a history of benign asbestos pleurisy presents with a right-sided pleural effusion, pleural plaques and mediastinal pleural thickening. What is the most likely reason for his presentation?
explanation: A unilateral effusion with mediastinal pleural thickening after asbestos exposure is highly suspicious of mesothelioma; pleural biopsy.

stem: A 72-year-old smoker has a 5-cm peripheral left lung mass, left hilar lymphadenopathy, an indeterminate liver lesion and a palpable, hard 2-cm left supraclavicular lymph node. What should be the next diagnostic test?
explanation: Biopsy the palpable supraclavicular node (N3): it gives histology, molecular markers and the highest stage with least risk (NICE NG122).
topics: Lung cancer; Supraclavicular lymph node; Tissue diagnosis

stem: A 55-year-old woman with a left apical lung cancer and suspected mediastinal node involvement undergoes mediastinoscopy under general anaesthesia, followed by radiotherapy. She has been hoarse since waking from the procedure, but laryngoscopy shows normal vocal cord movement. What is the most likely cause?
option_D: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement by the tumour
explanation: Hoarseness right after anaesthesia with normal cord movement is intubation-related laryngeal trauma; a nerve palsy would paralyse the cord.

stem: A 73-year-old heavy smoker man with bronchial carcinoma developed nausea, vomiting, irritability and confusion. Investigations revealed Hb 9.8 g/dl, serum Na+ 104 mEq/L (normal 135–145 mEq/L). Which of the following is the most probable cause?

A 73-year-old heavy smoker man with bronchial carcinoma consults a physician because of progressive confusion and lethargy. Blood tests reveal serum Na+ 104 mEq/L, and chest imaging shows a central lung mass. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely responsible?
Which of the following is the strongest determinant of prognosis in lung cancer?
explanation: TNM stage at diagnosis is the strongest prognostic factor (stage IA ~70–90% vs stage IV < 10% 5-year survival).

stem: Causes of dyspnoea in bronchial carcinoma may be the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causes hoarseness and bovine cough, not breathlessness.
topics: Lung cancer; Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy; Dyspnoea

stem: A woman with systemic sclerosis is found to have a 3-cm lung lesion that is FDG-avid on PET-CT. Which statement is most accurate?
option_B: The findings on PET/CT make infection very likely
option_C: The findings on PET/CT make infection very unlikely
option_D: The findings on PET/CT make malignancy very likely
option_E: The findings on PET/CT make malignancy very unlikely
explanation: FDG uptake also occurs in infection and inflammation, so an avid lesion still needs tissue diagnosis.

stem: A 75-year-old man with previous asbestos exposure has a pleural effusion suspicious for mesothelioma. Which statement about this condition is true?
option_A: Cigarette smoking increases the likelihood of developing the condition
option_B: Death is usually due to widespread distant metastases
option_C: Exposure can be brief (1–2 years) and the latency may be 40 years or more
option_D: Repeated pleural fluid cytology usually gives a definitive diagnosis
option_E: Combined surgical resection and chemotherapy significantly improves survival
answer_text: Exposure can be brief (1–2 years) and the latency may be 40 years or more
explanation: Mesothelioma can follow brief asbestos exposure with a 30–40+ year latency; smoking does not raise its risk; cytology is often negative.

stem: A 64-year-old man has facial swelling and distended neck veins, and superior vena cava obstruction is suspected. Which CT finding is most likely?
option_A: A central mass obstructing right main bronchus
option_B: An apical mass invading the chest wall
option_E: Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes compressing the SVC
answer_text: Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes compressing the SVC
explanation: SVC obstruction is usually malignant (lung cancer, lymphoma) from mediastinal nodes compressing the SVC; stent for rapid relief.
topics: Superior vena cava obstruction; Lung cancer

stem: A 64-year-old man has facial swelling and distended neck veins from superior vena cava obstruction caused by enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. He has no stridor or confusion, and no tissue diagnosis has yet been made. Initial management includes all of the following EXCEPT:
option_B: Elevation of the head of the bed
explanation: In SVC obstruction without stridor or cerebral oedema, get tissue first; emergency radiotherapy may obscure the diagnosis.
topics: Superior vena cava obstruction; Oncological emergencies

stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer develops acute paraplegia from suspected metastatic spinal cord compression. What is the first step in management?
explanation: Suspected MSCC with deficit: give high-dose dexamethasone immediately, then whole-spine MRI within 24 h and definitive treatment.
topics: Metastatic spinal cord compression; Dexamethasone; Oncological emergencies

stem: A 74-year-old man who has smoked 40 cigarettes per day for 30 years presents with increasing shortness of breath. He takes diclofenac and paracetamol for joint pain. His chest X-ray shows a spiculated left hilar mass with dense consolidation of the left lower lobe beyond it, and air bronchograms indicate that the lobar bronchus is still patent. Which finding would be expected on examination over the left lower lobe?
explanation: Consolidation with a patent bronchus gives bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance and whispering pectoriloquy.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of increased shortness of breath. He has smoked 40 cigarettes per day for the past 30 years. Medications include diclofenac and paracetamol for joint pain. He comes to the clinic with a chest X-ray from his GP which shows a spiculated left hilar mass. What would the classical respiratory findings over the abnormal area be?

A 68-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes per day has a proven diagnosis of bronchial carcinoma, and radical radiotherapy is being considered. Which of the following is the most significant contraindication to radical radiotherapy?
explanation: A malignant pleural effusion (M1a, stage IV) cannot be included in a radical radiotherapy field, so radical treatment is inappropriate.

stem: 52-A 64-year-old mechanic and lifelong smoker noticed haemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows left upper-lobe collapse and predominantly left-sided hilar enlargement and mediastinal widening. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 42-year-old man has had a grade III chondrosarcoma of the right maxilla resected. He now has breathlessness and a dry cough, and a chest X-ray suggests lung metastases. Which radiological feature of lung metastases is characteristic of this tumour?
explanation: Calcified lung metastases are characteristic of bone/cartilage sarcomas (osteo-, chondrosarcoma) and thyroid or mucinous cancers.

stem: A 66-year-old man with COPD is referred by his GP to the rapid-access chest clinic after several courses of antibiotics and steroids for an exacerbation that has not fully resolved. His chest X-ray shows a suspicious 3-cm mass at the right hilum with background changes of COPD. Blood tests: Hb 142 g/L, platelets 323 × 10⁹/L, WBC 9.1 × 10⁹/L, Na 128 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, urea 6.4 mmol/L, creatinine 99 µmol/L. There is no clubbing, and a fixed monophonic wheeze is heard in the right lung. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation: A central mass with fixed monophonic wheeze and hyponatraemia in a smoker suggests small cell lung cancer (SIADH).

stem: A 50-year-old man with long-standing COPD develops insidious aching in the distal limbs, particularly both wrists, and has lost 4.5 kg (10 lb). The skin over the wrists is warm and red, and there is bilateral finger clubbing. Plain X-rays of the wrists show periosteal thickening, reported as possible osteomyelitis. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Clubbing with painful symmetrical periostitis is HPOA, usually from lung cancer; COPD does not cause clubbing, so get a chest X-ray.
topics: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy; Lung cancer; Finger clubbing

stem: After an adrenalectomy a patient becomes breathless and cyanosed. His chest X-ray is shown. What is the cause?
explanation: Dense hemithorax opacity with volume loss after upper abdominal surgery is collapse from retained secretions; analgesia, physiotherapy.

stem: An overweight middle-aged man sees his GP after his wife complains about his loud snoring. He drinks large amounts of alcohol in the evenings before bed. Which of the following symptoms is he most likely to report?
explanation: Daytime sleepiness is the cardinal OSA symptom; obesity and evening alcohol worsen airway collapse.

stem: You see a 55-year-old female for the first time. She has a 2-year history of chronic daily cough; thick, malodorous sputum and occasional haemoptysis. She has been treated with antibiotics for recurrent respiratory infections, but is frustrated with her continued symptoms. She has never smoked. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second:forced vital capacity (FEV1:FVC) ratio is 60% and a CT scan shows bronchial wall thickening and luminal dilatation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A 67-year-old obese man presents with loud chronic snoring and gasping episodes during sleep. His wife has witnessed episodes where it appears as if he has stopped breathing. He reports unrefreshing sleep, multiple awakenings from sleep and morning headaches. He has excessive daytime sleepiness, which is interfering with his daily activities. He has been treated for hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux and type 2 diabetes. For adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, which one of the following is the most effective treatment?
option_E: Weight reduction to achieve a body mass index <30 kg/m2
explanation: Continuous positive airway pressure splints the pharynx open during sleep and is the most effective treatment for symptomatic moderate-to-severe OSA, improving sleepiness, quality of life, driving safety and blood pressure. Mandibular advancement devices are an alternative for mild disease or CPAP intolerance, upper-airway surgery helps only selected patients, and modafinil treats residual sleepiness but not the apnoeas. Weight loss should be advised for everyone but rarely cures severe OSA on its own and takes time.

stem: A 53-year-old man has had a non-productive cough for 3 months. His spirometry is normal and he already takes omeprazole for reflux. Which statement about his management is true?
option_B: A trial of an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) is warranted
option_C: He should see an ENT surgeon
option_D: His cough has become a habit and he must get used to it
option_E: His reflux medication should be increased
explanation: Chronic cough (> 8 weeks) always needs a chest X-ray and spirometry to exclude serious disease before treating common causes.

stem: A 24-year-old man with cystic fibrosis asks about ivacaftor. Ivacaftor corrects the function of which CFTR defect?
explanation: Ivacaftor is a CFTR potentiator for gating mutations, classically G551D; F508del needs a corrector plus ivacaftor.

stem: A 56-year-old non-smoking man with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the left lung (EGFR mutation positive) is evaluated. What is the treatment of choice?
option_D: EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g. erlotinib or osimertinib)
answer_text: EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g. erlotinib or osimertinib)
explanation: Metastatic EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma is treated first line with an oral EGFR TKI (osimertinib preferred).
topics: Lung adenocarcinoma; EGFR mutation; Tyrosine kinase inhibitors

stem: A 24-year-old patient with cystic fibrosis fails to recover from an exacerbation, and sputum cultures now isolate Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which statement regarding P. aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis is true?
option_A: Intravenous antibiotic therapy is rarely required
option_B: It is a benign coloniser of the bronchiectatic airways
option_C: It is one of the earliest bacteria isolated in sputum from CF patients
option_D: Nebulised azithromycin 3 times a week suppresses infection
option_E: Nebulised tobramycin is an effective treatment in chronic colonisation
answer_text: Nebulised tobramycin is an effective treatment in chronic colonisation
explanation: Chronic Pseudomonas in CF accelerates decline; long-term nebulised tobramycin (or colistin, aztreonam) reduces exacerbations.
topics: Cystic fibrosis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Nebulised antibiotics

stem: A 61 year old woman on IV daptomycin for staphylococcal discitis, previously improving, spikes a fever after 2 weeks with rising WCC (including eosinophilia) and new bilateral upper zone consolidation on CXR. What should be the treatment?
explanation: Fever, eosinophilia and new infiltrates after 2 weeks of daptomycin is drug-induced eosinophilic pneumonia: stop it and give steroids.
topics: Eosinophilic pneumonia; Daptomycin; Drug-induced lung disease

stem: A 70 year old woman with a 6-week history of cough, low-grade fever, and malaise, on nitrofurantoin for UTIs, has bi-basal infiltrates on CXR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chronic cough, fever and bibasal infiltrates on long-term nitrofurantoin is nitrofurantoin lung; stopping the drug is diagnostic and therapeutic.

stem: A 75-year-old woman has a 10-year history of daily non-productive cough. She has back pain from a vertebral fracture, and the chest X-ray shows a large hiatus hernia and kyphosis. What is the most likely cause of her cough?
explanation: Chronic dry cough with a large hiatus hernia and kyphosis is most likely GORD; trial a PPI.
topics: Chronic cough; Gastro-oesophageal reflux; Hiatus hernia

stem: A 42-year-old non-smoking woman has a 4-month history of breathlessness occurring only in the daytime, which began after an upper respiratory tract infection with nasal blockage. Her D-dimer was positive but CTPA is normal, and spirometry is normal. What should be the next investigation?
option_C: Dysfunctional breathing studies and a Nijmegen questionnaire
option_E: Lung volume and gas transfer studies
answer_text: Dysfunctional breathing studies and a Nijmegen questionnaire
explanation: Daytime-only breathlessness after a viral illness with normal imaging and spirometry suggests dysfunctional breathing; Nijmegen questionnaire.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with COPD presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after returning from a 3-week holiday. SpO2 is 84% on room air; there is reduced air entry and mild bilateral ankle oedema, and the D-dimer is elevated. What is the most likely cause of her chest pain?
explanation: Sudden pleuritic pain with hypoxaemia after travel and a raised D-dimer in COPD is most likely PE; CTPA (CXR to exclude pneumothorax).

stem: A 45-year-old non-smoking man with finger clubbing, noted since his teens and also present in his father, presents with a sprained wrist. He has no other symptoms. What is the next step the family physician should take?
option_A: Check bloods (including LFTs, thyroid function tests and ESR)
option_E: Sweat test to exclude cystic fibrosis
explanation: Lifelong familial clubbing without symptoms is hereditary clubbing: reassure. New clubbing needs investigation.

stem: A patient with known bronchiectasis and a long-standing right apical cavity from old tuberculosis now coughs up 50 mL of fresh red blood. The chest X-ray shows a rounded mass partially filling the cavity. What is the likely cause of his haemoptysis?
explanation: A mass within an old TB cavity with an air crescent is an aspergilloma (mycetoma), which causes haemoptysis.

stem: A 32-year-old patient with cystic fibrosis presents with massive haemoptysis (250 mL of fresh red blood) but is haemodynamically stable. What is the most useful investigation?
explanation: Massive haemoptysis in CF comes from bronchial arteries: bronchial artery angiography localises and embolises the bleeding.
topics: Massive haemoptysis; Cystic fibrosis; Bronchial artery embolisation

stem: A 57 year old woman with a 3-year history of chronic productive cough (with green sputum) and frequent brief antibiotic responses is investigated. What is the best investigation?
Acute coryza is most commonly caused by which of the following?
explanation: The common cold (acute coryza) is caused mainly by rhinoviruses; symptomatic treatment only.

stem: A 45 year old man with a history of spontaneous VTE and family history presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and a swollen right calf after ACL reconstruction abroad and a recent long- haul flight. What should the next test be?

A 28-year-old woman recovering from ACL repair in an above-knee cast has near-syncope on standing, with BP 80/45 mmHg and sinus tachycardia. The chest X-ray is clear and the D-dimer is elevated, and she then has a cardiac arrest. What should the immediate management include?
explanation: Cardiac arrest from suspected massive PE: immediate thrombolysis during CPR, continuing CPR for 60–90 min.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a cough every May that resolves by autumn, with nasal discharge and watering eyes. Examination and spirometry are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Seasonal cough with rhinorrhoea and watery eyes every May with normal spirometry is seasonal allergic rhinitis; antihistamine and nasal steroid.

stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding breathing during sleep?
option_A: Abnormal ventilatory drive is present in obstructive sleep apnoea
option_C: Forty per cent of middle-aged women snore
option_E: Palatoglossus and genioglossus contract actively during expiration
explanation: Normal sleep reduces ventilatory drive and muscle tone, so mild hypoventilation (small PaCO2 rise) is normal.

stem: A 55-year-old man with excessive daytime sleepiness, an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 18 and a BMI of 36 kg/m² undergoes a sleep study. What is the likely result?
explanation: Epworth 18 in an obese man suggests significant OSA; AHI 20/h is moderate (mild 5–14, moderate 15–29, severe ≥ 30).

stem: A 72-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease, hypertension and childhood poliomyelitis has increasing breathlessness and nocturnal symptoms. His chest X-ray is under-inspired, a sleep study shows significant nocturnal hypoventilation, and arterial blood gases show decompensated type 2 respiratory failure. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: New respiratory muscle weakness decades after polio is post-polio syndrome, causing nocturnal then daytime hypercapnia; nocturnal NIV.
topics: Post-polio syndrome; Nocturnal hypoventilation; Type 2 respiratory failure

stem: Which of these associations between pathophysiological features and conditions is correct?
option_B: Eventration of diaphragm and foramen of Bochdalek
explanation: Spinal TB (Pott disease) causes angular thoracic kyphosis/kyphoscoliosis and can lead to restrictive ventilatory failure.

stem: Dyspnea that associate with wheezing can be caused by the following EXCEPT;
A woman with history of bronchial carcinoma 2 months ago developed cough and dyspnea. Which of the following is the best treatment of choice for her persistent obstructive symptoms?
A 28-year-old man of Chinese origin on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis telephones 2 weeks into therapy complaining of painful eyes and blurred vision. What is the likely cause?
option_A: Drug resistance to ethambutol and pyrazinamide
explanation: Painful eyes and blurred vision on TB treatment is ethambutol optic neuritis: stop it and get urgent ophthalmology review.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with a 28-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive shortness of breath. All of the following are recognised pulmonary complications of rheumatoid arthritis EXCEPT:
explanation: RA causes effusions, ILD, nodules, bronchiolitis obliterans and bronchiectasis; apical fibrobullous disease belongs to ankylosing spondylitis.
topics: Rheumatoid arthritis; Interstitial lung disease; Pleural effusion

stem: At what lung volume does the outward recoil of the chest wall equal the inward elastic recoil of the lung?
explanation: At FRC the inward recoil of the lung equals the outward recoil of the chest wall; FRC rises in emphysema and falls in fibrosis or obesity.

stem: A 65-year-old man has stridor-like, low-pitched wheeze heard over the central airway. His flow–volume loop is shown. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Flattening of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs of the flow–volume loop is a fixed central obstruction such as subglottic stenosis.
topics: Upper airway obstruction; Flow–volume loop; Subglottic stenosis

stem: A 22-year-old pregnant woman presents with acute dyspnoea. Arterial blood gas shows a raised A–a gradient and the chest X-ray is normal. What is the next best step in diagnosis and management?
option_A: Initiate therapy with amoxicillin for acute bronchitis
option_B: Perform a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram
option_D: Reassure the patient that dyspnoea is normal
option_E: Treat with clonazepam for a panic attack
answer_text: Perform a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram
explanation: Acute dyspnoea with a raised A–a gradient in pregnancy needs imaging for PE (CTPA or V/Q); D-dimer is unhelpful in pregnancy.

stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with myasthenia gravis?
option_A: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
option_B: Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
option_C: Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
option_D: Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
answer_text: Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
explanation: Myasthenia: respiratory muscle weakness gives low TLC, raised RV, normal FEV1/FVC and low MIP.
topics: Myasthenia gravis; Pulmonary function tests; Neuromuscular disease

stem: A 36-year-old woman rescued from a house fire remains obtunded, with seizures, hypotension and a bitter almond odour on her breath. Which test will confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: Coma, seizures, shock and bitter almond breath after a house fire suggest cyanide; red cell cyanide confirms, but give hydroxocobalamin without waiting.

stem: A 28-year-old has recurrent sinus and lung infections and cystic fibrosis is suspected. Which finding best confirms the diagnosis?
option_A: DNA analysis showing one F508del allele
explanation: Sweat chloride ≥ 60 mmol/L on two occasions with a compatible picture confirms cystic fibrosis.

stem: A 42-year-old man has progressive dyspnoea and weight loss. Bronchoalveolar lavage returns milky fluid containing PAS-positive material. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Milky BAL with PAS-positive material is pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (usually autoimmune anti-GM-CSF); CT shows crazy paving.

stem: A patient has symptomatic pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with hypoxaemia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Symptomatic PAP is treated by whole-lung lavage; inhaled GM-CSF is a newer option. Steroids do not help.

stem: A 52-year-old man has obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Which statement is true?
option_A: Mutation of the PHOX2B gene is associated with this condition
option_B: CPAP alone is always adequate therapy
option_C: Intubation is mandatory for acute hypercapnia
option_D: Coexistent obstructive sleep apnoea occurs in only 25% of cases
option_E: Weight loss will lead to improvements in PaCO2 over time
answer_text: Weight loss will lead to improvements in PaCO2 over time
explanation: Obesity hypoventilation (daytime PaCO2 > 6 kPa, BMI ≥ 30) improves with weight loss; CPAP or bilevel NIV at night.

stem: A 52-year-old man with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness and a high BMI is thought to have obstructive sleep apnoea. He has no significant cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease and no symptoms of another sleep disorder. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Uncomplicated adult with high probability of OSA: a home sleep apnoea test is the first step; full polysomnography if complex or inconclusive.
topics: Obstructive sleep apnoea; Home sleep apnoea testing

stem: A 48-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnoea refuses CPAP. Which statement about untreated obstructive sleep apnoea is correct?
option_A: It has no significant effect on mortality
option_B: It is not associated with depression
option_C: It increases the risk of motor vehicle accidents
option_D: It has no effect on blood pressure
option_E: Its complications are prevented by sleeping with extra pillows
answer_text: It increases the risk of motor vehicle accidents
explanation: Untreated OSA roughly doubles to triples the risk of road accidents; advise not to drive while sleepy.

stem: The polysomnogram shown demonstrates a waxing and waning (crescendo–decrescendo) breathing pattern with central apnoeas. Which patient is most likely to have this pattern?
option_A: A 6-year-old with enlarged tonsils and adenoids
option_C: A 48-year-old obese man with loud snoring
option_D: A 52-year-old menopausal woman with frequent awakenings
option_E: A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 15%), raised JVP and oedema
answer_text: A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 15%), raised JVP and oedema
explanation: Crescendo–decrescendo breathing with central apnoeas is Cheyne–Stokes respiration, typical of advanced heart failure.
topics: Cheyne–Stokes respiration; Central sleep apnoea; Heart failure

stem: A 48-year-old man has symptomatic obstructive sleep apnoea with an apnoea–hypopnoea index of 42/hour. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
explanation: AHI ≥ 30/h is severe OSA: CPAP is first line and improves sleepiness and BP. Oral devices suit mild disease; weight loss helps but is not enough alone.

stem: A 25-year-old with cystic fibrosis is referred for lung transplantation. What is the main impediment to long-term survival after transplantation?
explanation: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (chronic allograft dysfunction) is the main barrier to long-term survival after lung transplant.
topics: Lung transplantation; Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome; Chronic lung allograft dysfunction

stem: A 42-year-old man in haemorrhagic shock has a lactate of 4.8 mmol/L. Which factor is least important in determining oxygen delivery to his tissues?
explanation: O2 delivery = cardiac output × (1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + small dissolved fraction), so PaO2 matters least once saturated.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is intubated for pneumonia on a background of COPD. All of the following are measures that prevent ICU complications EXCEPT:
explanation: Tight glucose control (4.4–6.1 mmol/L) increased mortality (NICE-SUGAR); target ~8–10 mmol/L.
topics: Critical care; ICU complications; Glucose control

stem: All of the following statements regarding shock pathophysiology are true EXCEPT:
option_A: Hypotension inhibits the vasomotor centre, reducing adrenergic output
option_B: Metabolic derangements raise extracellular osmolarity, pulling fluid from cells
option_C: Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to lactate accumulation
option_D: Proinflammatory mediators contribute to organ failure
option_E: Severe stress increases cortisol, promoting gluconeogenesis and lipolysis
answer_text: Hypotension inhibits the vasomotor centre, reducing adrenergic output
explanation: Hypotension reduces baroreceptor firing, which increases (not inhibits) sympathetic output in shock.

stem: A patient with a C2–3 spinal cord transection is in shock. Which haemodynamic profile is expected?
option_A: Low CO, high SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
option_B: Low CO, high SVR, high RA pressure, high PCWP, low SvO2
option_C: High CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, high SvO2
option_D: Low CO, normal SVR, high RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
option_E: Low CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
answer_text: Low CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
explanation: High cervical cord transection: neurogenic shock with low SVR, low filling pressures, bradycardia, low CO and low SvO2.

stem: All of the following statements about the epidemiology of sepsis are true EXCEPT:
option_A: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms
option_B: In septic shock, blood cultures are positive in 40%-70%
option_C: Most sepsis occurs in patients with significant comorbidities
option_D: Respiratory infections are the most common cause of sepsis
option_E: Incidence of severe sepsis is ~3 per 1000 and rising
answer_text: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms
explanation: Gram-negative organisms remain the commonest isolates in sepsis (~60%); respiratory infection is the commonest source.

stem: A 62-year-old has pneumonia, hypotension responsive to fluids, pH 7.46, PaCO2 32, PaO2

A 62-year-old man with right lower lobe pneumonia is confused, with RR 28/min, HR 118/min and BP 84/50 mmHg, which rises to 112/70 mmHg after 2 L of IV crystalloid without vasopressors. ABG on air: pH 7.46, PaCO2 4.3 kPa (32 mmHg), PaO2 10.1 kPa (76 mmHg); lactate 1.6 mmol/L. How should his condition be classified?
option_E: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome without infection
explanation: Pneumonia with confusion and hypotension responding to fluids is sepsis (Sepsis-3); septic shock needs vasopressors and lactate > 2.

stem: A 68-year-old man with previous splenectomy is in septic shock with no clear source. Local rates of cephalosporin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae exceed 1%. Which empirical regimen is most appropriate?
explanation: Asplenic septic shock: cefotaxime/ceftriaxone for encapsulated organisms plus vancomycin where resistant pneumococci are prevalent.

stem: All of the following therapies initially looked promising but have not improved mortality in sepsis EXCEPT:
option_B: Red cell transfusion only when haemoglobin falls below 70 g/L
option_C: Intensive insulin therapy for tight glucose control
option_D: ACTH stimulation testing to select patients for steroid therapy
answer_text: Red cell transfusion only when haemoglobin falls below 70 g/L
explanation: A restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb 70 g/L) is safe in sepsis (TRISS); activated protein C and tight glucose control failed.

stem: Which of the following conditions can produce true coma, rather than being a state that mimics coma?
explanation: Diffuse metabolic encephalopathy causes true coma; vegetative state, akinetic mutism, catatonia and locked-in syndrome mimic it.

stem: A 74-year-old man has a large subdural haematoma with uncal herniation (MRI shown). What is the cause of his coma?
option_A: Compression of the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries
option_B: Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge
option_C: Compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle
option_D: Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum
option_E: Entrapment of the ventricles causing hydrocephalus
answer_text: Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge
explanation: In uncal herniation, coma results from the midbrain being pushed against the opposite tentorial edge, distorting the reticular activating system.

stem: A 44-year-old man is found comatose, flushed, with 5 mm pupils, muscle spasms and rapid breathing. What is the most likely cause of his coma?
explanation: Coma without focal signs, with flushing, reactive pupils, twitching and hyperventilation suggests drug intoxication; toxicology screen.

stem: In which patient is intraparenchymal intracranial pressure monitoring preferred over a ventriculostomy?
option_A: A 24-year-old with traumatic brain injury and GCS 6
option_B: A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure and INR 3.5
option_C: A 48-year-old man with subarachnoid haemorrhage and hydrocephalus
option_D: A 68-year-old with a large haemorrhagic stroke and midline shift
answer_text: A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure and INR 3.5
explanation: With coagulopathy (fulminant hepatic failure) an intraparenchymal ICP monitor is preferred; an EVD carries more bleeding risk.
topics: Intracranial pressure monitoring; Acute liver failure

stem: A 56-year-old woman with subarachnoid haemorrhage has an external ventricular drain in place, and her intracranial pressure rises to 45 mmHg. What is the next management step?
option_C: No action, as cerebral perfusion pressure is adequate
option_D: Open the ventriculostomy to drain CSF to an ICP below 20–25 mmHg
option_E: Hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 4 kPa (30 mmHg)
answer_text: Open the ventriculostomy to drain CSF to an ICP below 20–25 mmHg
explanation: With an EVD in place and ICP 45 mmHg, drain CSF first (target < 20–25 mmHg), then osmotherapy if needed.

stem: A 67-year-old man has been in the ICU with sepsis for 3 weeks and now cannot be weaned from the ventilator. He has symmetrical weakness of all limbs, worse distally, with absent tendon reflexes and reduced distal sensation; nerve conduction studies show an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy after weeks of sepsis causing failure to wean is critical illness polyneuropathy.
topics: Critical illness polyneuropathy; Ventilator weaning; ICU-acquired weakness

stem: A 56-year-old woman with a subarachnoid haemorrhage improves initially, but on day 7 has an abrupt neurological decline. CT shows no new blood. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Neurological decline on day 7 after SAH without new blood is vasospasm (delayed cerebral ischaemia).
topics: Subarachnoid haemorrhage; Cerebral vasospasm; Delayed cerebral ischaemia

stem: A 56-year-old woman develops delayed neurological deterioration on day 7 after a coiled aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT shows no new blood, and CT angiography confirms severe cerebral vasospasm. She is already taking nimodipine. What treatment do you recommend now?
option_E: IV noradrenaline to raise blood pressure and referral for balloon angioplasty
answer_text: IV noradrenaline to raise blood pressure and referral for balloon angioplasty
explanation: Symptomatic vasospasm after a secured aneurysm: euvolaemia and induced hypertension (noradrenaline) plus angioplasty.

stem: A 21-year-old with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a white cell count of 156 × 10⁹/L starts induction chemotherapy. Which is NOT a feature of tumour lysis syndrome?
explanation: Tumour lysis causes high K⁺, phosphate and urate with hypocalcaemia (calcium bound by phosphate), not hypercalcaemia.

stem: All of the following are important in preventing tumour lysis syndrome EXCEPT:
option_B: Adequate IV hydration (about 3 L/m² per day)
option_C: Rasburicase for patients at high risk
option_D: Frequent serum biochemistry (every 4–6 hours) in high-risk patients
explanation: TLS prevention: hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase and monitoring; dialysis is for established TLS, not prophylaxis.

stem: In which of the following patients presenting to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea would a positive D-dimer result prompt further testing for pulmonary embolism?
option_A: A 24-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant
option_B: A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who has calf pain after prolonged air travel and a normal alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient
option_C: A 56-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer
option_D: A 62-year-old man who had hip replacement surgery 4 weeks ago
option_E: A 72-year-old man who had an acute myocardial infarction 2 weeks ago
answer_text: A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who has calf pain after prolonged air travel and a normal alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient
explanation: A positive D-dimer is meaningful only in low/intermediate-probability outpatients without pregnancy, cancer or recent surgery.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with acute breathlessness 2 days after developing calf pain and swelling following a 9-hour car journey. BP 98/60 mmHg, HR 114/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 92% on room air, weight 89 kg; the lungs are clear and the right leg is swollen and tender. ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.3 kPa (25 mmHg), PaO2 9.1 kPa (68 mmHg). Kidney and liver function are normal, and CT confirms pulmonary embolism. All of the following agents can be used alone as initial therapy EXCEPT:
option_D: Unfractionated heparin IV adjusted to maintain activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) two to three times the upper limit of normal
option_E: Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3
answer_text: Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3
explanation: Warfarin cannot be used alone initially (slow onset, early prothrombotic effect); LMWH, fondaparinux, UFH or apixaban/rivaroxaban can.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding pulmonary embolism is true?
option_A: Airway resistance usually decreases in the setting of an acute pulmonary embolism
option_B: Almost all patients with pulmonary embolism have evidence of deep vein thrombosis at the time
option_C: Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism
option_D: Hypotension in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism is often due to acute left ventricular systolic dysfunction
option_E: The size of the arterial-alveolar gradient is invariably correlated with the size of the pulmonary embolism
answer_text: Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism
explanation: PE typically causes alveolar hyperventilation with hypocapnia; hypotension results from RV failure.

stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension is admitted with pulmonary embolism. BP 132/62 mmHg, HR 85/min, SpO2 95% on room air; echocardiography shows normal right heart size and function and troponin is undetectable. Doppler shows extensive femoral–popliteal DVT. He is started on LMWH with warfarin and asks whether he should have an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter. What is the most appropriate answer?
option_A: “No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point.”
option_B: “No, there are currently no indications for IVC filter placement in the setting of deep vein thrombus or pulmonary embolism.”
option_C: “We will need to go back to review your images and see how large your pulmonary embolus clot burden is before deciding whether an IVC filter is appropriate for you or not.”
option_D: “Yes, given the presence of residual lower extremity thrombus, we will schedule you for IVC filter insertion.”
option_E: “Yes, given your age and gender, we will schedule you for an IVC filter insertion.”
answer_text: “No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point.”
explanation: An IVC filter is only for contraindication to or failure of anticoagulation; it does not improve survival.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with morbid obesity (weight 140 kg), hypertension and diabetes is on day 4 after open gastric bypass surgery. She develops sudden breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia and a sense of impending doom. CT pulmonary angiography shows a saddle pulmonary embolism. Her blood pressure is 70/45 mmHg and urine output is poor. After intravenous 0.9% saline and dobutamine, her blood pressure improves only modestly. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Massive PE with shock 4 days after major surgery (thrombolysis contraindicated): surgical or catheter embolectomy.

stem: A 70-year-old postoperative male (72 hours after hip replacement) presents with left leg swelling, shortness of breath, hypotension, and an oxygen saturation of 78%. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a partial right bundle branch block. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
If the chest X-ray is normal, which investigation is most appropriate to support the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism?
option_A: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan or CT pulmonary angiogram

stem: What is the immediate treatment for a haemodynamically unstable patient with suspected pulmonary embolism?
explanation: Haemodynamically unstable (high-risk) PE: systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) after starting heparin; embolectomy if contraindicated.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with an 8-month history of productive cough with yellowish sputum, occasional hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, and finger clubbing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which investigation is considered the gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of bronchiectasis?
option_C: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
answer_text: High-resolution CT scan of the chest

stem: Which two complications are most important to monitor for in patients with bronchiectasis?
An 18-year-old woman has an acute pulmonary embolism at 9 weeks of pregnancy. There are no obvious risk factors. What is the most appropriate treatment for the remainder of her pregnancy?
explanation: PE in pregnancy: weight-adjusted LMWH for the rest of pregnancy and ≥ 6 weeks postpartum; warfarin and DOACs are avoided.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with asthma and severe rheumatoid arthritis presents with 3 days of cough, wheeze and fever following a cold. She has taken naproxen for several years without any respiratory symptoms. Chest X-ray is clear, peak flow is 380 L/min (predicted 510 L/min) and CRP is 49 mg/L. She has already received nebulised salbutamol in the clinic with only partial improvement. Which single treatment is most appropriate now?
explanation: Moderate viral-triggered asthma exacerbation with partial SABA response: oral prednisolone 40–50 mg for ≥ 5 days.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a non-productive cough. He has mildly raised liver enzymes, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and anaemia and he is positive for cold agglutinins. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Mycoplasma (cold agglutinins, haemolysis) lacks a cell wall: use a macrolide (erythromycin) or doxycycline, not beta-lactams.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted with acute breathlessness. Arterial blood gas on air: PaO2 7.4 kPa, PaCO2 3.8 kPa, pH 7.45. Peak expiratory flow is 250 L/min (about 50% of predicted) and the chest X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
explanation: Acute severe asthma with PaO2 < 8 kPa: oxygen to 94–98% and high-dose nebulised salbutamol first.
topics: Acute severe asthma; Salbutamol; Arterial blood gas

stem: A 59-year-old man is reviewed in clinic 3 months after coronary artery bypass grafting. He is breathless on exertion and particularly when lying flat in bed. The operation went well and he has no angina. His medications are ramipril 10 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. He looks well; BP 123/72 mmHg, pulse 70/min and regular, BMI 31 kg/m², and the chest is clear. Hb 131 g/L, WCC 5.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 178 × 10^9/L, Na+ 138 mmol/L, K+ 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 110 µmol/L. Vital capacity is 88% of predicted sitting and falls to 55% of predicted lying down. What is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
explanation: A fall in VC > 20–25% from upright to supine indicates diaphragm weakness — here phrenic palsy after cardiac surgery.
topics: Diaphragmatic paralysis; Phrenic nerve injury; Lung function tests

stem: An anxious 22-year-old woman has had mild exertional breathlessness and intermittent double vision over the last few weeks. Chest X-ray, lung function tests and ECG are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fluctuating diplopia with breathlessness in a young woman suggests myasthenia gravis; antibodies, EMG and CT for thymoma.

stem: A 37-year-old man with increasing breathlessness is found to have unilateral emphysema. Which of the following is most likely to have predisposed him to this?
explanation: Unilateral hyperlucent emphysematous lung is Swyer–James (MacLeod) syndrome after childhood obliterative bronchiolitis.

stem: In which of the following respiratory diseases is finger clubbing NOT a feature?
explanation: Clubbing is not a feature of chronic bronchitis/COPD; it occurs in cancer, fibrosis, asbestosis and chronic suppurative lung disease.

stem: Which one of the following features is seen least frequently in patients with obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome?
explanation: OSA is 2–3 times commoner in men, so female gender is the least frequent feature listed.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who does not smoke is found to have normal lung volumes but a reduced transfer factor for carbon monoxide (TLCO) of 45% of predicted. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Isolated low TLCO with normal volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease, e.g. arteriovenous malformation (HHT); bubble echo or CTPA.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with shortness of breath, wheeze and rhinorrhoea. On examination, you note a bilateral expiratory wheeze. Blood results are as follows: Hb 120 g/L; Platelets 228 * 10^9/L; WBC 14.2 * 10^9/L; Eosin

A 62-year-old man presents with breathlessness, wheeze and rhinorrhoea. On examination there is bilateral expiratory wheeze. Blood results: Hb 120 g/L, platelets 228 × 10^9/L, WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 2.2 × 10^9/L, Na+ 138 mmol/L, K+ 4.1 mmol/L, urea 5.8 mmol/L, creatinine 62 µmol/L, CRP 8 mg/L. p-ANCA is positive. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
explanation: Late asthma with eosinophilia and positive p-ANCA suggests EGPA; montelukast may unmask it and is best avoided.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is started on varenicline to help her stop smoking. Which one of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
explanation: Nausea is the commonest varenicline adverse effect (~a third); vivid dreams and insomnia also occur.

stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the smoking cessation clinic. Which one of the following conditions would contraindicate the prescription of bupropion?
explanation: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in epilepsy.

stem: A 77-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted with worsening breathlessness. His GP started amoxicillin 5 days ago. BP 88/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 36/min. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. Arterial blood gas on air: pH 7.37, PaCO2 5.5 kPa, PaO2 9.1 kPa. What is the most suitable antibiotic therapy?
explanation: CURB-65 ≥ 3 pneumonia failing amoxicillin: IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.

stem: A 22-year-old with cystic fibrosis is assessed for lung transplantation after multiple chest infections and a poor response to chest physiotherapy, nutritional supplementation and a trial of lumacaftor/ivacaftor. He meets the criteria and is placed on the transplant waiting list. Chronic infection with which organism would be a contraindication to transplantation?
explanation: Chronic Burkholderia cepacia (especially cenocepacia) infection worsens transplant survival and is usually a contraindication.
topics: Cystic fibrosis; Burkholderia cepacia; Lung transplantation

stem: A 64-year-old woman with asthma is referred with worsening breathlessness over the past few months. Her asthma was diagnosed in her teens; she uses an inhaled corticosteroid and rarely needs her salbutamol. She has no wheeze or nocturnal symptoms, her inhaler technique is excellent and she is adherent. She has no other medical problems and does not smoke. She is comfortable at rest, SpO2 is 96% on air, BMI is 30 kg/m² and the chest is clear. Chest X-ray shows a normal heart size and clear lung fields. Lung function: FEV1 3.30 L (96.1%), FVC 3.92 L (88.6%), FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLCO 77.4%, KCO 101.9%. What is the likely cause of her breathlessness?
explanation: No obstruction, clear CXR and a slightly low TLCO with normal KCO (small alveolar volume) point to obesity as the cause of breathlessness.
topics: Obesity; Gas transfer; Lung function tests

stem: A 76-year-old woman with alcohol dependence is in hospital receiving antibiotics for a urinary tract infection. Over the last few days she has developed a cough productive of thick, blood-stained, jelly-like sputum and feels very nauseous. Chest X-ray shows bilateral cavitating upper-lobe opacities. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Upper-lobe cavitating pneumonia in an alcohol-dependent inpatient is classically Klebsiella pneumoniae ('redcurrant jelly' sputum).

stem: A 55-year-old man attends his GP with 7 day history of general fever and malaise, and a 2 day history of non-productive cough. His eyes have also been sticky and sore for the last few days. He appears visibly unwell, with a fever of 38.2°C and a respiratory rate of 20 /min. There is also some mild splenomegaly. He has no history of recent foreign travel and denies any tuberculosis exposure or contact with anyone who has been ill. He is, however, the proud new owner of George, a red-crested Australian King Parrot, who he has had for a month. What is the most likely cause of this gentleman’s symptoms?

A 54-year-old man who lives alone and works at a bird sanctuary is admitted with a 10-day history of worsening breathlessness, cough and fever. He is started on intravenous co-amoxiclav, but after 72 hours there is no clinical improvement. PCR of a respiratory sample is positive for Chlamydia psittaci. What is the most appropriate action?
explanation: C. psittaci is intracellular, so beta-lactams fail: switch to doxycycline 100 mg bd for 10–14 days (macrolide if pregnant).

stem: A 29-year-old man on an expedition on Mount Everest develops a headache at about 5000 m, followed by poor coordination and slurred speech. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Ataxia and slurred speech after ascent is high-altitude cerebral oedema: descend immediately and give dexamethasone (and oxygen).

stem: A 34-year-old man climbing Mount Kilimanjaro has had nausea and headache for 2 days. At 4500 m he develops breathlessness and a cough with pink frothy sputum, and there are bibasal crackles. Other than descent, what is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Pink frothy sputum and crackles at altitude is HAPE: descent, oxygen and nifedipine to lower pulmonary artery pressure.

stem: A 28-year-old man develops nausea and a severe headache whilst trekking in Nepal. Within the next hour he becomes ataxic and confused. A diagnosis of high altitude cerebral oedema is suspected. Other than descent and oxygen, what is the most important treatment?

A 48-year-old male patient with a medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with painful swelling in the left submandibular and submental areas. There was tenderness on palpation over the swelling with discharging pus. A facial and oral incision and drainage (R&D) was performed under general anaesthesia. Post-operatively 72-hours later the patient developed a new oxygen requirement with oxygen saturations dropping to 89%. He had a regular heart rate of 75 beats per minute and remained apyrexial. An urgent portable chest radiograph was requested. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old man with tetraplegia and a long-term indwelling urinary catheter presents with fever, breathlessness and cough. He has had recurrent urinary tract infections for years and takes long-term prophylactic therapy to suppress them. There is mild bilateral wheeze and a diffuse erythematous rash. Chest X-ray shows diffuse alveolar infiltrates. WBC 13.5 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 50%, lymphocytes 30%, eosinophils 20%). What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_A: Sepsis with ARDS secondary to urinary tract infection
option_C: A drug reaction to one of his medications
answer_text: A drug reaction to one of his medications
explanation: Fever, wheeze, rash, infiltrates and 20% eosinophils on long-term UTI suppression is a drug (nitrofurantoin) reaction; stop it.
topics: Nitrofurantoin; Drug-induced lung disease; Eosinophilic pneumonia

stem: A 68-year-old woman with asthma attends for a routine review. She has occasional palpitations and tremor, but her breathlessness is well controlled. She was admitted with mild heart failure 2 months ago and has occasional postprandial acid reflux. Her medications are lisinopril, digoxin, furosemide, an as-required short-acting inhaled beta-agonist and theophylline, and she takes an over-the-counter tablet (name unknown) for reflux. Her heart rate is 112/min, heart sounds are normal and there is a mild tremor of the outstretched hands. What is the best next step?
option_A: Chest X-ray to exclude heart failure
option_D: Lorazepam 0.5 mg orally three times daily
option_E: Stop the beta-agonist and substitute inhaled ipratropium
explanation: Tachycardia and tremor on theophylline (narrow range 10–20 mg/L, raised by cimetidine) suggest toxicity: check the level.

stem: A 40-year-old man with alcohol dependence develops cough and fever. His chest X-ray (shown) demonstrates a cavity with an air–fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe. What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: A cavity with air–fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe in an alcoholic is an aspiration abscess from anaerobes.
topics: Lung abscess; Aspiration pneumonia; Chest X-ray

stem: A 25-year-old man is referred for evaluation of infertility.
